members.name: tier
members.description:
**The styled tier, so the tooltip this renders is the styled one.**

`tag()` builds a child's tag name from this prefix, and the base declares
`helix-headless-`. Every other styled component that renders a child
overrides it; the three charts that draw a tooltip did not, so a
`helix-bar-chart` on a page put a `helix-headless-tooltip` in its shadow
root: the behavior with none of the surface. What showed was the browser's
own popover defaults, a white 1.5px border, square corners, `0.25em` of
padding and the page's font size, which is why the reading bubble looked
like no other tooltip on the site.

Measured before the fix: the chart's bubble computed
`border: 1.5px solid rgb(255, 255, 255)`, `border-radius: 0px`,
`padding: 3.5px`, `font-size: 14px`. The masthead's, a `helix-tooltip`,
had the component's own `none`, `radii-sm`, `2xs xs` and `text-xs`.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the columns are made of.

**A third axis on the chart, not on the bar.** A bar is a mark inside a
drawing and nobody writes markup for one; the chart is what a consumer
addresses, so the choice belongs here and reaches every column at once.

`glass` lets the gridlines read through the columns, which is what puts a
chart in the same language as a glass header rather than leaving it the one
opaque slab on the page.

**`gradient` was here and is `wash` now, which is #156.** The two set
different properties, `fill-opacity` against `fill`, and a chart forced into
both renders as a translucent gradient that is distinct from either: one
enum was holding two independent things, which is the mistake `Card`'s own
doc warns about arriving on the component that borrowed the word.

Absent is solid, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default,
so the stylesheet describes only the departure. The strength is the
theme's: `glass` scales with `--helix-material-opacity`, so a language that
is more see-through everywhere is more see-through here.

Styled rather than headless, because what a bar is filled with is a
treatment and this tier is where treatments live. The gradient it points at
is drawn below, which is an element and therefore that tier's business.

**This paints a mark rather than a ground, and the axis still reads the
same way.** On a surface the points are how much of the page shows through;
on a series they are how much ink the mark has, and the order is the same:
`glass` admits most, `frosted` admits less, absent is opaque. The two
factors, 0.62 and 0.88, carry the relationship the surface tokens carry
between `material-translucent` and `material-translucent-strong`, so a
chart and a card mean the same thing by the word.

**`transparent` is where this one stops.** A mark with no ink is not a
material choice, it is an absent series, and a chart says that by not
having the datum rather than by painting it invisibly. See 270.

members.name: wash
members.description:
How a column's fill is distributed across it.

`gradient` fades each column toward its base, into the wash the headless
tier draws whether or not anything points at it.

**A chart-domain axis and deliberately not a library one.** It lives on this
family alone, and here it is a way of encoding data rather than a way of
expressing a theme: promoted to the registry it would put an attribute on
eighty-eight components that means nothing on eighty-seven. `wash` because
that is what the tier below already calls it, in `--chart-bar-wash` and in
the `bar-wash-start` and `bar-wash-end` stops.

members.name: glass
members.description:
Which series are glass rather than solid, by name.

Matched the way `outlined` is, against the column headings the table gives.

**Per series for the reason `emphasis` is, arrived at one axis later.** A
chart-wide material puts every column in the same substance, which is right
when the whole chart is joining the page's language and wrong the moment one
series is a different kind of fact from the others. The two axes take the
same shape because they answer the same question about the same thing: what
is *this series* made of, and how much ink does *this series* claim.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How much ink the columns claim.

The chart's treatment, which every series takes unless `outlined` or
`subtle` names it. `outlined` is the mark as its edge alone, `subtle` a wash
of the series color with that edge on it, and absent is the filled column,
per the rule that a reflected property takes no default.

**It composes with `material` rather than competing with it.** Emphasis
decides what is drawn and material decides how much of it comes through, so
`glass` thins whatever emphasis put there: the fill on a solid column, the
stroke on an outlined one. That corner was inert when the two were first
put side by side, `glass` setting a fill opacity on a mark whose fill is
`none`, and a combination that silently does nothing is the trap
`--card-backdrop` was for the one commit it shipped alone.

members.name: outlined
members.description:
Which series are drawn as an outline rather than a fill, by name.

Space separated and matched against the column headings the table gives,
the way `lines` and `secondary` are, so a chart says `outlined="Forecast"`
rather than counting columns. Names because they are what the table already
carries and what the legend already shows.

**The case this exists for is a series that is not a measurement.** A
forecast, a target, a budget: something drawn on the same axis as the
others and not the same kind of fact, which an outline says without a
second legend or a note under the chart.

Per series and not per bar, because a bar is a mark inside a drawing and
nobody writes markup for one, which is the same reason `material` sits on
the chart.

members.name: subtle
members.description:
Which series are drawn as a wash of their color, by name.

Matched as `outlined` is.

members.name: source
members.description: Resolves `for` and re-renders when the table behind it changes.

members.name: pointer
members.description:
Which reading a pointer is nearest, for a tooltip to sit on.

Public for the same reason `series` and `named` are: a protected member
cannot be cast onto across unrelated classes, so it would be invisible to
every chart that needs it. Reading where a pointer is resting is a fair
thing to ask a chart anyway.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

members.name: series
members.description: The columns of the table, one series each, or none if there is no table.

members.name: named
members.description:
What to call the drawing, the consumer's word or the table's own.

The fallback is the reason this is shared rather than copied: a caption is
already written, already the right words, and already the thing a reader
of the table sees. A chart that made the consumer say it twice would be
asking for the second one to drift.

members.name: sourceRows
members.description:
Every row of the table, with each cell's text as well as its number.

This is where a tooltip's content comes from, and it is deliberately not
`series`. A chart draws numbers; a reader resting a pointer on one wants
what the table says, which is `$128k` and not `128000`, and often wants
the column beside it that nothing plotted at all.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this paragraph.** It
is the source table's rows, and `rows` on a chart is a name a chart
wants for itself: `helix-heatmap` takes `rows="7"` to mean a calendar
week, and declaring that against a base class whose `rows` is a `Row[]`
getter is a type error at best. The same fault `MixinCollection` had,
where a slot counter called `rows` would have shared one field with a
consumer's data property. Name the member for what it holds rather than
for the shortest word available.

members.name: readings
members.description: How many readings there are, which is what the pointer maps onto.

members.name: direction
members.description:
Whether the categories run down the side rather than along the bottom.

Absent is columns. `horizontal` is the one to reach for when the category
names are words rather than dates: a row of long names either overlaps or
turns on its side, and neither is as readable as putting them down the left
where they read normally.

members.name: gridlines
members.description:
Which rules are drawn across the plot, if any.

Absent draws none. `value` rules the axis the columns are *measured* on,
`category` rules the axis they are *arranged* on with one through each
group, and `both` draws both. Which of those is horizontal turns with
`direction`, because a rule belongs to an axis and not to a screen edge.

**A bare `gridlines` means `value`**, and so does anything unrecognised: an
unrecognised value that draws nothing is indistinguishable from the
attribute being absent, which is the one thing a reader cannot debug.

`category` is the quieter half of this on a bar chart and is here for
completeness rather than because it is usually right: columns already
divide the categories by being separate columns, and a rule through each
one is a second statement of the same fact. It earns its place on a chart
of many thin bars, where the eye has stopped counting.

Furniture rather than data, so the rules are inside the `aria-hidden` plot
and reach no reader through the table.

members.name: lines
members.description:
Which series are drawn as a line instead of as columns, by name.

Space separated, matched against the column headings the table gives, so a
chart says `lines="Margin"` rather than counting columns. Names because
they are what the table already carries and what the legend already shows:
an index is a fourth place the column order is written down and the first
one to go stale when somebody moves a column.

**A combination chart is one scale, and that is the honest half of it.**
Both marks are measured against the same domain, so a line here says
something comparable to the columns beside it. The usual reason to reach
for a combination chart is the other thing, a count against a percentage on
a second axis, and that is deliberately not this: two scales on one frame
let the author put any two shapes in any relation by choosing the ranges,
and the reader has no way to see it happening.

A line among columns still measures from zero, because the columns do and
they share the axis. That is the trade for comparability, and it is why
this is a bar chart that can carry a line rather than a line chart that can
carry columns.

members.name: secondary
members.description:
Which series are measured against a scale of their own, by name.

Space separated and matched the way `lines` is, against the column headings
the table gives. Opt in: absent, every series shares one domain, which is
what makes a chart comparable and is the right default.

**Two scales on one frame let an author put any two shapes in any relation
by choosing the ranges, and a reader cannot see it happening.** That is not
a caveat, it is what the feature does: a line that crosses the columns
twice and a line that never touches them can be the same two series drawn
against different ranges. It earns its place when the two quantities are
genuinely incomparable, a count against a percentage, and it is a way to
mislead in every other case.

**So it draws its axes**, and that is not optional here. The chart renders
no value axis at all when there is one scale, because the columns are
measured against each other and a reader needs no numbers to do that. With
two, a reader has no way of knowing there are two, let alone which series
is on which, so both scales are labeled the moment this is set. An
unlabelled second axis is the deceptive case rather than the tidy one.

The grid stays on the primary axis, since a rule measured against two
scales at once is a rule that means nothing. The tooltip is unaffected: it
has always shown every column's own number, which is the reader's way out
of any scale question the picture raises.

members.name: scaled
members.description: The series names on the second scale, lowercased and trimmed.

members.name: lined
members.description: The series names drawn as a line, lowercased and trimmed for matching.

members.name: rulesValue
members.description: Whether the levels are ruled, which is every value but `category`.

members.name: rulesCategory
members.description: Whether each category is ruled, which only two values ask for.

members.name: renderPlot
members.description:
The columns themselves, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

`aria-hidden`, because the table it was read from is the readable version
and a screen reader hearing both hears the same numbers twice.

members.name: renderAxis
members.description:
The numbers along one scale, drawn only where there are two of them.

**A chart with one scale renders no axis, on purpose.** Columns measured
against each other need no numbers to be compared, and a row of them beside
a small chart is furniture that makes the drawing smaller for no reading a
reader was going to do. With two scales that argument inverts: a reader
cannot tell there are two, cannot tell which series is on which, and cannot
recover either from the picture. So this appears with `secondary` and never
without it.

**Beside the plot and not inside it**, which is the second thing this got
wrong. Inside, the numbers are drawn over the drawing, and a horizontal
chart shows it immediately: its value axis runs along the bottom, which is
where the last row of bars is. The vertical case has the same fault and
enough slack to hide it. The plot is also the pointer's catchment and the
tooltip's containing block, both measured from its box, so padding it to
make room would move every reading half an axis to the right.

A column of the host grid instead, which the stylesheet grows only when
`secondary` is set. That is what the property reflects for.

The primary hugs the edge the drawing starts at and the secondary the edge
it ends at: down the two sides for columns, along the bottom and top for
bars, which is where each axis is when the chart is turned.

members.name: renderGridlines
members.description:
The grid, behind everything, or nothing at all.

Across the measured axis, which turns with `direction`: a rule belongs to
the axis the bars are measured on and not the one they are arranged on, so
columns get horizontal rules and rows get vertical ones. Getting that
backwards draws a grid that divides the categories, which are already
divided by being separate bars.

Drawn before the baseline, so where a gridline and zero coincide the
baseline is what shows: zero is a fact about the data and a gridline is a
ruler.

members.name: renderBand
members.description:
The slot the pointer is resting in, drawn behind the columns.

**The honest version of the fade.** A group under the pointer already sets
`data-active` and the stylesheet dims the others, which says which group is
meant by making four of five quieter: it reads as the chart losing
confidence rather than as one column being pointed at. A band says the same
thing by lighting the region the pointer is actually in, and the region is
the whole slot, because that is the catchment the pointer resolves against.

Both are kept. The fade separates the active group from its neighbours and
the band says where the neighbourhood is, and on a chart of two categories
the fade alone is ambiguous about which half is lit.

members.name: renderLine
members.description:
One series drawn as a line across the categories, behind a seam.

Through the middle of each slot, which is where the group stands, so a
point sits over its own columns rather than over the gap between two of
them. The same arithmetic the category gridlines use, and for the same
reason: the reading is the thing, the boundary is only where the pointer
changes its mind.

`data-series` keeps the index the series has among *all* of them, not among
the lines, so the color a line takes is the color the legend gives it and
moving a column between marks does not repaint the chart.

members.name: renderTooltip
members.description:
What a pointer resting on a reading shows.

A seam over `drawTooltip`, which holds the markup every chart shares. The
usual reason to override is arrangement: every cell of the row is already
there, including the columns nothing was plotted from.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.description:

bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug

itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

so the stylesheet describes only the departure. The strength is the
theme's: `glass` scales with `--helix-material-opacity`, so a language that
is more see-through everywhere is more see-through here.

Styled rather than headless, because what a bar is filled with is a
treatment and this tier is where treatments live. The gradient it points at
is drawn below, which is an element and therefore that tier's business.

**This paints a mark rather than a ground, and the axis still reads the
same way.** On a surface the points are how much of the page shows through;
on a series they are how much ink the mark has, and the order is the same:
`glass` admits most, `frosted` admits less, absent is opaque. The two
factors, 0.62 and 0.88, carry the relationship the surface tokens carry
between `material-translucent` and `material-translucent-strong`, so a
chart and a card mean the same thing by the word.

**`transparent` is where this one stops.** A mark with no ink is not a
material choice, it is an absent series, and a chart says that by not
having the datum rather than by painting it invisibly. See 270.

attributes.name: wash
attributes.description:
How a column's fill is distributed across it.

`gradient` fades each column toward its base, into the wash the headless
tier draws whether or not anything points at it.

**A chart-domain axis and deliberately not a library one.** It lives on this
family alone, and here it is a way of encoding data rather than a way of
expressing a theme: promoted to the registry it would put an attribute on
eighty-eight components that means nothing on eighty-seven. `wash` because
that is what the tier below already calls it, in `--chart-bar-wash` and in
the `bar-wash-start` and `bar-wash-end` stops.

attributes.name: glass
attributes.description:
Which series are glass rather than solid, by name.

Matched the way `outlined` is, against the column headings the table gives.

**Per series for the reason `emphasis` is, arrived at one axis later.** A
chart-wide material puts every column in the same substance, which is right
when the whole chart is joining the page's language and wrong the moment one
series is a different kind of fact from the others. The two axes take the
same shape because they answer the same question about the same thing: what
is *this series* made of, and how much ink does *this series* claim.

attributes.name: emphasis
attributes.description:
How much ink the columns claim.

The chart's treatment, which every series takes unless `outlined` or
`subtle` names it. `outlined` is the mark as its edge alone, `subtle` a wash
of the series color with that edge on it, and absent is the filled column,
per the rule that a reflected property takes no default.

**It composes with `material` rather than competing with it.** Emphasis
decides what is drawn and material decides how much of it comes through, so
`glass` thins whatever emphasis put there: the fill on a solid column, the
stroke on an outlined one. That corner was inert when the two were first
put side by side, `glass` setting a fill opacity on a mark whose fill is
`none`, and a combination that silently does nothing is the trap
`--card-backdrop` was for the one commit it shipped alone.

attributes.name: outlined
attributes.description:
Which series are drawn as an outline rather than a fill, by name.

Space separated and matched against the column headings the table gives,
the way `lines` and `secondary` are, so a chart says `outlined="Forecast"`
rather than counting columns. Names because they are what the table already
carries and what the legend already shows.

**The case this exists for is a series that is not a measurement.** A
forecast, a target, a budget: something drawn on the same axis as the
others and not the same kind of fact, which an outline says without a
second legend or a note under the chart.

Per series and not per bar, because a bar is a mark inside a drawing and
nobody writes markup for one, which is the same reason `material` sits on
the chart.

attributes.name: subtle
attributes.description:
Which series are drawn as a wash of their color, by name.

Matched as `outlined` is.

attributes.name: for
attributes.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

attributes.name: direction
attributes.description:
Whether the categories run down the side rather than along the bottom.

Absent is columns. `horizontal` is the one to reach for when the category
names are words rather than dates: a row of long names either overlaps or
turns on its side, and neither is as readable as putting them down the left
where they read normally.

attributes.name: gridlines
attributes.description:
Which rules are drawn across the plot, if any.

Absent draws none. `value` rules the axis the columns are *measured* on,
`category` rules the axis they are *arranged* on with one through each
group, and `both` draws both. Which of those is horizontal turns with
`direction`, because a rule belongs to an axis and not to a screen edge.

**A bare `gridlines` means `value`**, and so does anything unrecognised: an
unrecognised value that draws nothing is indistinguishable from the
attribute being absent, which is the one thing a reader cannot debug.

`category` is the quieter half of this on a bar chart and is here for
completeness rather than because it is usually right: columns already
divide the categories by being separate columns, and a rule through each
one is a second statement of the same fact. It earns its place on a chart
of many thin bars, where the eye has stopped counting.

Furniture rather than data, so the rules are inside the `aria-hidden` plot
and reach no reader through the table.

attributes.name: lines
attributes.description:
Which series are drawn as a line instead of as columns, by name.

Space separated, matched against the column headings the table gives, so a
chart says `lines="Margin"` rather than counting columns. Names because
they are what the table already carries and what the legend already shows:
an index is a fourth place the column order is written down and the first
one to go stale when somebody moves a column.

**A combination chart is one scale, and that is the honest half of it.**
Both marks are measured against the same domain, so a line here says
something comparable to the columns beside it. The usual reason to reach
for a combination chart is the other thing, a count against a percentage on
a second axis, and that is deliberately not this: two scales on one frame
let the author put any two shapes in any relation by choosing the ranges,
and the reader has no way to see it happening.

A line among columns still measures from zero, because the columns do and
they share the axis. That is the trade for comparability, and it is why
this is a bar chart that can carry a line rather than a line chart that can
carry columns.

attributes.name: secondary
attributes.description:
Which series are measured against a scale of their own, by name.

Space separated and matched the way `lines` is, against the column headings
the table gives. Opt in: absent, every series shares one domain, which is
what makes a chart comparable and is the right default.

**Two scales on one frame let an author put any two shapes in any relation
by choosing the ranges, and a reader cannot see it happening.** That is not
a caveat, it is what the feature does: a line that crosses the columns
twice and a line that never touches them can be the same two series drawn
against different ranges. It earns its place when the two quantities are
genuinely incomparable, a count against a percentage, and it is a way to
mislead in every other case.

**So it draws its axes**, and that is not optional here. The chart renders
no value axis at all when there is one scale, because the columns are
measured against each other and a reader needs no numbers to do that. With
two, a reader has no way of knowing there are two, let alone which series
is on which, so both scales are labeled the moment this is set. An
unlabelled second axis is the deceptive case rather than the tidy one.

The grid stays on the primary axis, since a rule measured against two
scales at once is a rule that means nothing. The tooltip is unaffected: it
has always shown every column's own number, which is the reader's way out
of any scale question the picture raises.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on the footer whether there is an attribution in it.

A `<footer>` with nothing in it is still a block in the quote's flow and
still takes the container's gap, so every blockquote written without an
attribution reserved a full space below itself. There is no selector that
can ask, `slot:empty` being about a slot's fallback rather than its
assigned nodes, so the component asks and says so on the footer inside this
shadow root: an attribute on the host is a change to markup the consumer
rendered, which React reports on hydration.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: href
members.description:
Where the crumb goes, and nothing where it is the current page.

**Optional and reflected, because a stylesheet does select on it.**
`breadcrumb.css` writes `:host(:not([href])) [part="link"]` to take the
block padding off a crumb that is not a link, so the attribute is what
decides how tall a crumb is. Unreflected, an `href` set from script reached
the property, rendered the anchor, and left the host looking unlinked: the
crumb drew at 20px where a markup twin drew at 28.

*This said the opposite until 27 Aug 2026*, and named the reason as
"nothing selects on it", which was not true when it was written. The
paragraph is worth keeping because the rest of it is right and is what makes
this optional rather than defaulted: an `href` written onto every host would
be a link to the current page on every crumb nobody asked to be one. That is
the general rule as well, that a reflected property takes no default, so the
two agree.

Found by the picture comparison rather than by reading: React assigns a
matching property instead of an attribute, so every crumb in the React twin
of `breadcrumbs/links` lost its padding at once.

attributes.name: href
attributes.description:
Where the crumb goes, and nothing where it is the current page.

**Optional and reflected, because a stylesheet does select on it.**
`breadcrumb.css` writes `:host(:not([href])) [part="link"]` to take the
block padding off a crumb that is not a link, so the attribute is what
decides how tall a crumb is. Unreflected, an `href` set from script reached
the property, rendered the anchor, and left the host looking unlinked: the
crumb drew at 20px where a markup twin drew at 28.

*This said the opposite until 27 Aug 2026*, and named the reason as
"nothing selects on it", which was not true when it was written. The
paragraph is worth keeping because the rest of it is right and is what makes
this optional rather than defaulted: an `href` written onto every host would
be a link to the current page on every crumb nobody asked to be one. That is
the general rule as well, that a reflected property takes no default, so the
two agree.

Found by the picture comparison rather than by reading: React assigns a
matching property instead of an attribute, so every crumb in the React twin
of `breadcrumbs/links` lost its padding at once.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.

word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:

members.name: variant
members.description:
Whether the buttons are one bar or a spaced row.

Joined by default, which is what a button group has always meant here: one
control made of parts, sharing borders, reading as a segmented bar.

`spaced` is the same set with air between them, for a row of related but
separate actions. It exists because the semantics and the joining were one
thing and should not have been: `role="group"` and a shared name are what
make a set of buttons a set, and a consumer who wanted that *and* ordinary
spacing had to choose. `helix-flex` gives the spacing and no group; this
gave the group and no choice about the spacing.
Whether the buttons are one bar or a spaced row.
members.name: appearance
label
members.description:
Accessible name for the group.

On the host through internals, so an author's `aria-label` still overrides
it and nothing lands on the host that a consumer's markup did not have.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the buttons are stacked.

Unset is a row and stays unset, so a reflected default cannot appear on a
host whose server output never had it.

**A property and not an `auto`, which the splitter and the carousel earned
and this has not.** Turning those two changes what they *do*: a drag axis,
arrow keys, how many slides a page holds. A group of buttons turning is
paint, so there is no state to resolve and nothing to observe; what it needs
is for a consumer who knows the column is narrow to be able to say so.

**What it is for, measured.** Three buttons at 320 come to 322 and overflow
the page by 26. A row of joined buttons cannot answer that by wrapping,
which is the obvious reach and the wrong one: the group's whole contract is
buttons sharing edges as one shape, and a wrapped row carries the corners of
a first row into a second. Stacked, the same three keep one shape and one
column.

members.name: width
members.description: How much of the space available to it the button takes. - `auto` is the default and is never written: the button is as wide as its label, which is what a control in a toolbar or beside a field should be. - `standard` is one width for every button that takes it, so a column or row of actions lines up instead of following the length of each word. - `full` fills the container, for a single action at the foot of a form or a card, and on a phone where a control is a target before it is a label. **This was `fill`, and the name had to disclaim itself.** The paragraph here opened "Width and not weight", which is a sentence a name should not need: `emphasis` on this same element is documented as "How filled it is drawn", so a button carried a property called `fill` beside a property about being filled, meaning different things. `separation="filled"` and `ThemeIntent.separation`'s `fill` mechanism both mean a surface's own color, and every chart in the library writes `fill` for paint, which left this the only use of the word meaning geometry. `Dialog` had already made the same move for the same reason, its `appearance` becoming `size` for saying how wide a panel is, "which its own description admitted in as many words". `size` is not available here, because that rule's test is whether two of them sitting together could legitimately differ, and two buttons do: this is a width *policy* rather than a scale, and `standard` exists precisely to stop a row being ragged. Width and not weight, still. `emphasis` says how much a button matters and this says how much room it takes, and the three are independent: a `ghost standard` Cancel beside a `solid primary standard` Save is exactly the pairing a dialog wants. **A consumer's own anchor takes it as `data-button-width`**, the way it takes the emphasis as `data-button`: ```html Save ``` Both are one declaration in the base layer. They were not, and that was a real gap rather than a missing convenience: this class promises a link styled as a button and a real button are indistinguishable, and a dialog's button row is built on `standard`, so the one place the promise mattered most was the one place it did not hold.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How filled it is drawn.

**This was `appearance`, and the docstring above it always said what it
really was.** "How filled it is drawn", sitting beside `tone`, "What it
means": the axis was named correctly in prose and filed under the word
four axes shared. A Card's `outlined` says where a surface ends and this
one says how much ink a control claims, and one word cannot keep saying
both. `check:axes` holds the vocabulary now.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it, and undefaulted because
it reflects: a reflected property with a default writes its attribute
onto every host anybody renders. The resting treatment is the attribute's
absence, which each control names for itself, `outlined` on `Button` and
`ghost` on `IconButton`.

members.name: tone
members.description:
What it means.

Three and an accent, not the full status set. A tag reports a state and a
button performs an action: a success button and a warning button are not
things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page where the color
of a control means nothing in particular. `accent` is the second
emphasis, a rotation off the brand seed rather than a color of its own,
so it stays in relation when somebody rethemes.

members.name: type
members.description: What activating the button does to its form.

members.name: value
members.description:
What this button submits under its own `name`, the way a native submitter does.

**Reported for exactly the submission this button starts and not otherwise.**
A native submit button contributes `name=value` only when it is the one
that submitted, and every other button on the form contributes nothing. A
form-associated element reporting a value continuously would contribute on
every submission whoever started it, which is a different feature wearing
the same name, so `submit` below sets it, submits, and clears it inside one
synchronous call.

`CopyButton` has a `value` of its own meaning the text to put on the
clipboard, which is not this and is why it is declared there rather than
inherited.

members.name: formAction
members.description:
Where this button's submission goes, overriding the form's own.

**The five `form*` overrides work by writing the form and putting it back**,
which is the only mechanism available and is closer to the platform than it
sounds. `requestSubmit(submitter)` is how a native submitter carries these,
and it refuses ours twice over: the inner `<button>` is `type="button"` so
it is not a submit button, and it sits in this shadow root so its form owner
is not the consumer's form. Both throw. So the submission is started with no
submitter and the overrides are applied to the form for the duration of it.

the window is one call and a `finally` closes it whether or not a listener
refused. What a `submit` handler observes during that window is the form a
native submitter would have given it, which is the point.

members.description: How the submission is encoded, overriding the form's own.

members.name: formMethod
members.description: Which HTTP method the submission uses, overriding the form's own.

members.name: formNoValidate
members.description: Whether this submission skips the form's validation.

members.name: formTarget
members.description: Which browsing context the response lands in, overriding the form's own.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: expanded
members.description:
Whether this button is a disclosure trigger, and whether its panel is open.

**Set by whatever owns the panel, and a property rather than an attribute
for the reason `Menu` already states about its items**: an attribute
written onto a consumer's element after it upgrades is a hydration mismatch
waiting to happen. Measured 28 Aug 2026 against React 19.2.8, server markup
hydrated with the definitions loaded either side of `hydrateRoot`:
`Megamenu` and `SpeedDial` wrote `aria-expanded` onto the slotted trigger
and React reported "some attributes of the server rendered HTML didn't
match the client properties. This won't be patched up" in both orders;
`Popover` and `Menu`, which write nothing, were clean in both.

**A property crosses that gap because React never looks at one.** It diffs
the attributes it rendered, and this one is `attribute: false`, so the state
travels to the inner `<button>` and lands inside a shadow root React does
not own and cannot compare. The consumer's own element is left exactly as
they served it, which is what `Popover`'s note asks for, and the reader is
still told what the control does, which is what `SpeedDial`'s note asks
for. See #322.

`undefined` renders nothing at all, so a button that is not a trigger
carries no `aria-expanded`: the resting state is the attribute's absence,
which is the rule every reflected property here follows.

A consumer who wants to say this statically writes `aria-expanded` on the
host instead, which `AriaForwardController` carries to the same place.

members.name: submit
members.description:
Submits the form as this button, for the length of one call.

Everything a native submitter carries is written onto the form, the
submission is started, and everything is put back. See `formAction` for why
`requestSubmit(submitter)` is not available to a control inside a shadow
root.

`novalidate` is in the same list rather than reached by `form.submit()`,
which looks like the shortcut and is not: `submit()` skips the `submit`
event as well as the validation, so a consumer's handler would stop running
the moment somebody wrote `formnovalidate`. Turning the flag on and calling
`requestSubmit()` skips the validation alone, which is what the attribute
means.

members.name: commandForElement
members.description:
The element this button's command is sent to, resolved.

The platform's own accessor, and this element had the resolution and kept
it to itself: `linkCommand` writes the target onto the inner `<button>`,
where a consumer cannot reach it, and `commandFor` answers with an id
rather than an element. Writing assigns the inner control directly, which
is what an invoker without an id in the same tree needs.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends
exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: width
attributes.description: How much of the space available to it the button takes. - `auto` is the default and is never written: the button is as wide as its label, which is what a control in a toolbar or beside a field should be. - `standard` is one width for every button that takes it, so a column or row of actions lines up instead of following the length of each word. - `full` fills the container, for a single action at the foot of a form or a card, and on a phone where a control is a target before it is a label. **This was `fill`, and the name had to disclaim itself.** The paragraph here opened "Width and not weight", which is a sentence a name should not need: `emphasis` on this same element is documented as "How filled it is drawn", so a button carried a property called `fill` beside a property about being filled, meaning different things. `separation="filled"` and `ThemeIntent.separation`'s `fill` mechanism both mean a surface's own color, and every chart in the library writes `fill` for paint, which left this the only use of the word meaning geometry. `Dialog` had already made the same move for the same reason, its `appearance` becoming `size` for saying how wide a panel is, "which its own description admitted in as many words". `size` is not available here, because that rule's test is whether two of them sitting together could legitimately differ, and two buttons do: this is a width *policy* rather than a scale, and `standard` exists precisely to stop a row being ragged. Width and not weight, still. `emphasis` says how much a button matters and this says how much room it takes, and the three are independent: a `ghost standard` Cancel beside a `solid primary standard` Save is exactly the pairing a dialog wants. **A consumer's own anchor takes it as `data-button-width`**, the way it takes the emphasis as `data-button`: ```html Save ``` Both are one declaration in the base layer. They were not, and that was a real gap rather than a missing convenience: this class promises a link styled as a button and a real button are indistinguishable, and a dialog's button row is built on `standard`, so the one place the promise mattered most was the one place it did not hold.

attributes.name: emphasis
attributes.description:
How filled it is drawn.

**This was `appearance`, and the docstring above it always said what it
really was.** "How filled it is drawn", sitting beside `tone`, "What it
means": the axis was named correctly in prose and filed under the word
four axes shared. A Card's `outlined` says where a surface ends and this
one says how much ink a control claims, and one word cannot keep saying
both. `check:axes` holds the vocabulary now.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it, and undefaulted because
it reflects: a reflected property with a default writes its attribute
onto every host anybody renders. The resting treatment is the attribute's
absence, which each control names for itself, `outlined` on `Button` and
`ghost` on `IconButton`.

attributes.name: tone
attributes.description:
What it means.

Three and an accent, not the full status set. A tag reports a state and a
button performs an action: a success button and a warning button are not
things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page where the color
of a control means nothing in particular. `accent` is the second
emphasis, a rotation off the brand seed rather than a color of its own,
so it stays in relation when somebody rethemes.

attributes.name: type
attributes.description: What activating the button does to its form.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What this button submits under its own `name`, the way a native submitter does.

A native submit button contributes `name=value` only when it is the one
that submitted, and every other button on the form contributes nothing. A

clipboard, which is not this and is why it is declared there rather than
inherited.

What kind of attention the passage needs.

members.name: renderIcon
members.description:
The mark for the callout's tone, behind a seam.

layer, and a fallback with only the first is one a tier can restyle and
cannot change.

members.description:

members.name: toggleState
members.description:

members.name: stopInner
members.description:

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:

so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on

makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

attributes.name: tone
attributes.description:
What kind of attention the passage needs.

**`severity` was a sixth spelling of `tone`**, which is the axis for what a
thing means, and a subset of it: a callout reports a status and never a
brand role, so it takes four of the seven. One word per axis is the whole

declarations.description:
Regions are slots: `media`, `header`, the default slot for content, and
`footer`. An omitted region takes no space, so a card with only content needs
no wrapper markup at all.

`media` runs edge to edge and clips to the card's corners, so an image needs
no inset correction. Set `orientation="horizontal"` to move it alongside the
header, content, and footer stack rather than above it, or
`media-placement="end"` to put it under the content instead of over it, which
is what a chart concluding a card wants.

Regions are bare slots with no wrapper element, so an omitted one occupies no
space without the card having to detect that it is missing. Style slotted
content directly rather than reaching for a part: a header is whatever
element you slotted, not a wrapper around it.
