members.name: separation
members.description:
How the card separates itself from the page.

**One value per mechanism, and the theme has the same four.**
`ThemeIntent.separation` is `border | fill | shadow | space`, so these are
the component's words for what a theme states as a policy, one to one. It
was `appearance`, which is the library's word for four different questions
and is being retired from all of them: `outlined` on a Card says where the
surface ends and `outlined` on a Button says how much ink, and one word
cannot keep saying both.

- `outlined` is the default, and a hairline is usually enough. It costs
  less attention than a shadow: a screen of shadowed cards reads as a stack
  of things floating, none of them settled.
- `elevated` is lifted off the page instead of framed, for a card on a
  colored or busy background, where a line has to compete with whatever is
  behind it and a shadow does not.
- `filled` is told apart by its own color, with neither edge nor lift. For
  a dense surface where a border on every card is a grid of lines, and for
  a theme whose `separation` policy is `fill`, which pushes the surface
  ladder away from the page precisely so this reads.
- `plain` has no frame at all: the card is a layout and whatever it sits in
  is the surface. For a card inside something already bounded, where a
  second box adds a line and no meaning.

**`filled` is new and it closes a hole the engine could already see.**
`plain` clears the ground *and* the edge, so a surface with its own color
and neither edge nor lift was unsayable while being one of the four things
a theme could ask for.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the card is made of.

**A third axis, and it passes the test the other two answer to.**
`separation` is where the surface ends and `tone` is what it means; both of
those can be true at once with this, an elevated glass card being a
perfectly ordinary thing to want, so it is not a value of either.

**An attribute rather than a hook, because glass is not one declaration.**
It is a translucent ground *and* a backdrop filter, and either without the
other does nothing: a blur behind an opaque background is invisible, and a
translucent card over an unfiltered page is a smear. `--card-backdrop`
shipped on its own for exactly one commit and was that trap, a published
hook a consumer could set and see nothing happen. The component owns the
pair; a theme owns how strong it is.

Absent is opaque, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default,
so the stylesheet only describes the departure.

**The whole axis, which it did not used to be.** `glass` shipped alone,
so a card offered one point of a three-point language and said nothing
about the other two. `frosted` is the same pair turned up, the heavier
ground under the heavier blur, for a card that has to stay readable over
a busy page; `transparent` drops both, for one that is structure and
spacing with the page showing through. See 270.

members.name: orientation
members.description: Whether media sits above the content stack or beside it.

members.name: mediaPlacement
members.description:
Puts the media after the content instead of before it.

**A figure that concludes a card is the same region as one that opens it**,
and the only thing that differs is which edge it is flush against. Media is
the one region that escapes the inset, so a chart wanting to span the card
has nowhere else to be: slotted into the content it keeps the padding on
both sides, and there is no second bleeding region to add without saying
twice what this says once.

Reflected and undefaulted, so a card that has not asked reads as a card
with no attribute on it and the stylesheet only describes the departure.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

declarations.summary: Groups related content and actions into a single surface.

examples.description: A heading, some prose, and a footer, in the resting appearance.
Lifted off the page with a shadow rather than an outline.
Told apart by its own color, with neither edge nor lift.
Media beside the words rather than above them.
A whole card that navigates, with the heading carrying the link.
Glass, which is a pair: a ground that lets light through and a filter behind it.
The picture down one side, for a row in a list rather than a tile in a grid.
A hairline around the surface.
Neither border nor shadow, for a card inside something that has both.

declarations.description:
The track scroll-snaps, so a drag and a trackpad swipe move it with the
browser's own momentum and the controls only have to scroll.

Slides take the full track by default. `per-view` fits more than one across,
up to five, and is declared on the tier below because it decides how many
positions the track has rather than only how wide a slide is,
which is what a run of cards wants rather than a run of full-width panels.
declarations.name: HelixCarousel

cssProperties.description: Room inside the scroller so a slide's own shadow, border or focus ring is not clipped by it. Defaults to enough for `--helix-shadow-md`, which reaches 16px below the box it is on; a slide on `--helix-shadow-lg` reaches 44px and wants more.
cssProperties.name: --carousel-bleed

cssProperties.description: Height of a vertical track.
cssProperties.name: --carousel-block-size

cssProperties.description: Space between slides.
cssProperties.name: --carousel-gap

members.name: indicatorPlacement
members.description:
Which side of the slides the dots sit on.

Unset is `block-end`, under them. `block-start` puts them above,
`inline-start` and `inline-end` beside, where a run of dots becomes a
column.

**The sides of the content, not positions along a bar.** This was
`start | center | end`, which answered "where along the row" when the
question is "which edge", and could not say "above" at all. The logical
names rather than `top`/`left`, because the component is already careful
about writing direction everywhere else and an `inline-start` carousel
should put its dots on the right in Arabic without being told.

Independent of `controlsPlacement`. Both default to the block end, where
they share the row and split it, dots to the start and arrows to the end.
That is the arrangement the old shared bar gave, arrived at by two defaults
rather than by a rule about the pair, so moving one leaves the other alone.

members.name: indicatorAlign
members.description:
Where along that side the dots sit.

The second half of the answer to "where do they go". `indicatorPlacement`
says which edge and this says where along it, so the pair spells out the
nine positions a consumer asks for in words: bottom left, bottom center,
top right, and so on. One attribute with nine values was the alternative
and it multiplies rather than composing, since every value has to name both
facts and a consumer changing one has to rewrite the other.

**One word for both axes, because the edge decides which axis it is.** On a
block edge the run is a row and this is `justify-self`; on an inline edge it
is a column and the same question is `align-self`. A consumer should not
have to know which of those two words their edge wanted.

Logical, like the placement: `start` is the left in English and the right in
Arabic on a horizontal run, and the top on a vertical one.

Unset splits the row, dots to the start and arrows to the end, which is
what keeps two items in one grid cell from landing on each other. Beside the
slides, and over them, both center instead, because a column there has
nothing to split the edge with. Putting both groups on the same edge with
the same alignment does overlap them, and always did: that is what the two
different defaults exist to avoid.

members.name: controlsPlacement
members.description:
Which side of the slides the arrows sit on.

The same four sides as `indicatorPlacement` and the same default, so a
carousel that moves only one of them keeps the other where it was.
`inline-start` or `inline-end` stacks the arrows into a column, which is
what a vertical track usually wants.

`overlay` puts them on the slides, at the track's own edges, which is what a
full-bleed carousel wants: the slide is the page and the controls are on it
rather than in a bar beneath it. It carries its own treatment with it, a
surface and a shadow under each arrow, because a glyph drawn straight onto a
photograph is legible against about half of one.

**That was `appearance="hero"` and did not need to be.** A third axis for
something these two already describe: what `hero` meant was "the controls
are over the content", and the surface, the edge-to-edge arrows and the bar
that catches no presses all followed from it rather than being separate
decisions. One fewer property, and the two axes are now the whole of where
a carousel's chrome can go.

members.name: controlsAlign
members.description:
Where along that side the arrows sit. See `indicatorAlign`.

`overlay` answers it too, and the edge there is the whole slide: the bar is
stretched across the picture, so this moves the arrows up and down within
it rather than moving the bar. Centered unless asked otherwise, which is
where an arrow over a photograph belongs.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description:
Manual, so each slide can be wrapped without its markup being touched.

A slide has to be a `group` carrying `aria-roledescription="slide"` and a
position in the run, and those are the component's facts rather than the
consumer's element's. Writing them on is what a React consumer's hydration
reports and does not patch up, and on a slide that is itself a link it also
takes the link's role away. Assigning into a pane the component rendered
says the same thing to a screen reader and leaves the consumer's element
exactly as it was served. `Chat` and `DataTable` wrap their children the
same way and for the first of those two reasons.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the carousel.

members.name: index
members.description:
The slide in view, counted from zero.

Reading gives the real slide, in either mode. Writing sets it, the way a
script assigning to a native control does. Which mode the carousel is in is
read once, at the first update, from whether anything had declared an
`index` by then: declared, and the consumer owns it and the carousel only
announces where it would have gone; not declared, and the carousel owns it
and `default-index` says where it starts.

The same contract the four mixins carry, written out here rather than
extracted, because a slide is addressed by position and every one of those
mixins is keyed by a name. One consumer is not a mixin: if a second numeric
state turns up, this is what it is extracted from.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the track runs.

Behavior rather than presentation, which is why it is here: the scroll
position and the nearest-slide arithmetic are both single-axis, and a
styled-tier attribute cannot change which one they read. Two sites branch
on it, `scrollTo` and the drag settle, and nothing else in the component
knows about the axis at all.

A vertical track needs a height, which a horizontal one does not: width
comes from the page and height does not, so the styled tier gives it
`--carousel-block-size` and a consumer sets that to whatever the slides
want.

members.name: controls
members.description:
Whether the previous and next controls are shown.

`auto`, which is the resting behavior and what an absent attribute means,
shows them wherever the pointer can hover and hides them where it cannot.
`always` keeps them on every device, and `none` never renders them at all.

**Pointer and not width, which is the distinction this exists to make.** A
375px window on a desktop still has a mouse and still wants the arrows; a
tablet at 1024 has neither. `.claude/rules/helix.md` forbids a component
asking about the viewport, because the viewport is not the component's box,
and that objection does not reach `hover` and `pointer`: those describe the
input device, and the answer is the same whether this carousel is 300px in
a sidebar or runs the width of the page.

**Safe to hide because the arrows are not the keyboard's way in.** The
indicators carry a roving `tabindex` and handle the arrow keys, so every
slide is still reachable with the controls gone. Hiding a control that was
the only route to something would be a different change under this name.

**The rotation control is never hidden by this**, which is a decision
rather than a limit of scope: content that moves on its own has to offer a
way to stop it, so an autoplaying carousel keeps its pause control on a
touch device exactly as it does on a desktop.

members.name: defaultIndex
members.description: Slide to start on, where nothing declared one.

members.name: indexState
members.description: The slide in view, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: loop
members.description: Whether moving past either end wraps to the other.

members.name: autoplay
members.description: Whether the carousel advances on its own.

members.name: interval
members.description: How long each slide is held, in milliseconds.

members.name: rotating
members.description:
Whether rotation is running.

Absent until autoplay starts it.

members.name: perView
members.description:
How many slides are shown across the track at once. Absent shows one.

**Here rather than on the styled tier, because it decides how many places
the track can stop.** It was declared above as a width, which is what it
looks like from the stylesheet: one rule per value setting a custom
property, and the slides divide the track by it. But a carousel showing
four of six slides has three positions, not six, and everything that counts
positions is in this file. Left up there, `goTo` clamped to the last
*slide*, so three of the six indicators pointed at a scroll offset the
track had already reached and could not pass: pressing next walked the dots
to the end while the slides stopped moving a third of the way through.

No default, because it reflects. A reflected property with a value writes
its attribute on upgrade, and the host then carries something a consumer's
server markup never had, which React reports as a mismatch. The one-across
case is the absent attribute, and the styles read it that way.

members.name: positions
members.description:
How many distinct views the track holds, which is what the indicators count.

A window of `perView` slides sliding one at a time over `n` of them stops
`n - perView + 1` times, so six slides four across is three: 0 to 3, 1 to 4,
2 to 5. One at minimum, since a carousel showing everything it has still
has the one place to be.

members.name: panes
members.description:
The panes rendered for the slides, in order. Empty until the first render.

One per slide, and the box the track actually lays out: the slide itself is
assigned into it and takes its size from it, so every offset the scroller
is asked about is a pane's. Read fresh rather than cached, because a slide
arriving or leaving re-renders the run.

members.name: slides
members.description: The slides, in light-DOM order. Empty on the server, which has no tree.

members.name: handleIndicatorKeydown
members.description:
The arrows move between indicators, which is the tablist pattern.

One tab stop for the set and the arrows within it, so a reader does not
have to press Tab once per slide to get past a carousel of twelve. Moving
changes the slide, because an indicator that could be focused without
selecting would leave the highlight and the slide disagreeing with nothing
on screen saying which is which.

members.name: goTo
members.description: Moves to a slide, wrapping only where `loop` says to.

members.name: bleed
members.description:
The leading padding the track keeps for a slide to draw its own edge in.

A styled track carries one so a slide's shadow and focus ring have
somewhere to go: a scroll container clips at its padding box, and a slide
flush against that edge loses whatever it paints outside itself. The
headless tier has no stylesheet and so no padding, and this reads zero
there, which is why both tiers can share the arithmetic below.

Physical sides rather than logical, to match the physical `offsetLeft` and
`offsetTop` it is subtracted from. The bleed is one length on all four
sides, so the two agree whatever the writing mode; if that stops being
true, this is the method that has to know.

members.name: edgeOf
members.description:
Where a slide's leading edge sits, in the scroller's own coordinates.

**Both directions go through here, because they have to agree.** The
offsets are measured to the track's *border* box and `scrollTop` and
`scrollLeft` are measured from its content box, so the two differ by the
bleed: sending the carousel to a slide and reading back which slide it is
on used the same expression, and correcting one of them alone put a drag
one position off what the arrows did.

Unsubtracted, the leading slide's own offset *is* the bleed, so scrolling
to index 0 put its edge back on the clip edge. Measured on the insights
carousel: `scrollLeft` resting at 4 against a 4px bleed, the first card
shaved, and no scrolling done to cause it.

members.name: settling
members.description:
Whether the scroll now settling is one this component asked for.

Cleared by the first `scrollend` after it is set, and by a reader taking
hold of the track. The second half is not belt and braces: a `scrollTo`
whose target is already the scroll position fires no `scrollend` at all,
and the clamped end of a `per-view` track is exactly that case. Measured:
clicking past the last reachable slide moves `index` and produces no
`scrollend`, so a flag that only a `scrollend` could clear would stay set
and swallow the reader's next drag.

members.name: stop
members.description:
Stops rotation for good.

Hovering away or moving focus out does not start it again. The APG is
explicit that rotation resumes only when the reader asks for it, because a
carousel that starts moving again on its own is the thing the control
exists to escape.

members.name: runTimer
members.description:
Owns the timer, from the state rather than from the call site.

`start()` and `stop()` each held the interval and `connectedCallback`
started one, which the rules forbid: a DOM move re-ran connect and restarted
rotation the reader had stopped, and the server, which never runs connect at
all, rendered the control saying the opposite of what it would do. The
state is what is declared and the timer follows it, which also means one
place clears it.

members.name: nearest
members.description:
The slide the track is nearest to, or undefined when there is no track.

Shared by the two readers of the scroll position, which want the same
arithmetic and disagree about what to do with it: one commits where a drag
settled, the other follows it while it is still moving.

Only the leading edges a window can actually rest on. Past the last
position every remaining slide is on screen already, and taking the nearest
of *those* to the scroller's edge reported a place the reader could not get
back to: dragged fully right, a four-across six reported the sixth slide
and the dots jumped to an indicator that no longer existed.

members.name: handleTrackScroll
members.description:
Follows the track while a reader is still dragging it.

**`scrollend` is the only honest place to commit an index and much too late
to show one.** It fires once momentum has fully settled, which on iOS is
most of a second after the finger has left the glass, so the dots sat on
the old slide for the whole of the coast and then jumped. Reported exactly
that way, as the delay on the indicator being too great.

So showing and committing are separated. This moves the marker and nothing
else: no state is written and no event is dispatched, because neither is
true yet. A drag in flight is not a reader having chosen, `handleScroll`
still decides that, and a consumer holding `index` still hears once.

**The marker only, and not `aria-current` or the roving `tabindex`.** Those
describe where the reader *is*, which is a question with one answer per
settled position; moving them every frame of a drag would churn the
accessibility tree to report a place nobody has arrived at.

Coalesced to a frame, a scroll firing far more often than a screen
refreshes, and skipped while we are settling a scroll of our own: a click
has already moved the index and the track is following it, which is the
precedence `handleScroll` documents at length.

members.name: handleScroll
members.description:
Reads where a reader's drag settled, and only a reader's.

**The scroll we issued ourselves ends with a `scrollend` too, and taking it
as a reading is what makes the dots jump back.** This ran on every one, so
the index a reader had just chosen was overwritten by whichever slide
happened to be nearest the leading edge at the moment the animation
finished. Any disagreement there is enough: a snap settling a pixel short of
a midpoint, a target clamped by the scroller's own maximum, a fractional
layout, or a smooth scroll cut off by the next click. The component asked
for slide four, the pixels said three, and the pixels won.

Which is the wrong precedence in one direction only. A drag is the reader
moving the track and the index has to follow it; a click is the reader
moving the index and the track has to follow *that*. One `scrollend` cannot
tell those apart, so the flag does.

members.name: showing
members.description:
Where the track is right now, while a drag is still running.

Separate from `index`, which is where the reader has *arrived*. Undefined
whenever the two would agree, so the marker falls back to the committed
index the moment a drag settles and nothing has to keep them in step. See
`handleTrackScroll` for why they are not one value.

members.name: scrollFrame
members.description: The pending frame for the above, so a burst of scrolls costs one reading.

members.name: stopped
members.description:
Whether the reader has stopped it, as opposed to something pausing it.

The two were one flag and the difference matters: `focusin` bubbles, so
every focus move inside the carousel re-ran `stop()`, and a reader who
pressed Start had it undone by their very next Tab. Pausing on hover and on
focus is right; forgetting that the reader asked it to stop is not, and the
APG is explicit that rotation resumes only when the reader asks.

members.name: watcher
members.description:
Watches the light DOM for slides arriving and leaving.

**A manually assigned slot does not announce them.** `slotchange` fires when
an assignment changes, and under `slotAssignment: 'manual'` the only thing
that changes an assignment is this component calling `assign`, so a slide
appended by a consumer would reach no slot, render nowhere and be counted by
nothing. The default slot used to carry that duty and could, because it took
whatever was there. `Chat` watches for the same reason.

members.name: pause
members.description: Pauses without forgetting that the reader wanted it running.

members.name: assign
members.description:
Puts each slide into the pane rendered for it.

**The panes carry the ARIA and the consumer's element carries none**, which
is the whole reason this is a manual assignment rather than a plain slot.
The APG wants each slide to be a `group` with `aria-roledescription="slide"`
and a name saying where it sits in the run, and this used to be four
`setAttribute` calls onto the elements a consumer wrote. Two things were
wrong with that, and only one of them was about frameworks.

**A React consumer's slides are nodes React is in the middle of hydrating.**
The attributes landed before React reached them, so React found a DOM it had
not rendered and reported a mismatch it says it will not patch up. It means
it: the ARIA survived and the announcement was correct, so nothing looked
wrong and the console was the only tell. Deferring the write was tried
first, and a frame is a race rather than an ordering: measured in Chromium
on the landing page, a tab opened in the foreground still reported the
mismatch, and a tab opened hidden did not, only because `requestAnimationFrame`
had not run there yet. `Chat` reached this same conclusion for the same
reason and its comment on `shadowRootOptions` says so.

**And `role="group"` on a consumer's `<a href>` is not additive.** It
replaces the implicit link role, so six insight cards on the landing page
announced as groups and left the links list entirely. Every slide that is
itself a control had this, and no amount of deferring the write would have
helped, because the write was the bug. A pane around the slide is what the
pattern actually asks for: a group holding a link, rather than a link
relabeled as a group.

So nothing is written onto a consumer's element at all now, and the
mismatch is gone by construction rather than by timing.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: indicator-placement
attributes.description:
Which side of the slides the dots sit on.

Unset is `block-end`, under them. `block-start` puts them above,
`inline-start` and `inline-end` beside, where a run of dots becomes a
column.

**The sides of the content, not positions along a bar.** This was
`start | center | end`, which answered "where along the row" when the
question is "which edge", and could not say "above" at all. The logical
names rather than `top`/`left`, because the component is already careful
about writing direction everywhere else and an `inline-start` carousel
should put its dots on the right in Arabic without being told.

Independent of `controlsPlacement`. Both default to the block end, where
they share the row and split it, dots to the start and arrows to the end.
That is the arrangement the old shared bar gave, arrived at by two defaults
rather than by a rule about the pair, so moving one leaves the other alone.

attributes.name: indicator-align
attributes.description:
Where along that side the dots sit.

The second half of the answer to "where do they go". `indicatorPlacement`
says which edge and this says where along it, so the pair spells out the
nine positions a consumer asks for in words: bottom left, bottom center,
top right, and so on. One attribute with nine values was the alternative
and it multiplies rather than composing, since every value has to name both
facts and a consumer changing one has to rewrite the other.

**One word for both axes, because the edge decides which axis it is.** On a
block edge the run is a row and this is `justify-self`; on an inline edge it
is a column and the same question is `align-self`. A consumer should not
have to know which of those two words their edge wanted.

Logical, like the placement: `start` is the left in English and the right in
Arabic on a horizontal run, and the top on a vertical one.

Unset splits the row, dots to the start and arrows to the end, which is
what keeps two items in one grid cell from landing on each other. Beside the
slides, and over them, both center instead, because a column there has
nothing to split the edge with. Putting both groups on the same edge with
the same alignment does overlap them, and always did: that is what the two
different defaults exist to avoid.

attributes.name: controls-placement
attributes.description:
Which side of the slides the arrows sit on.

The same four sides as `indicatorPlacement` and the same default, so a
carousel that moves only one of them keeps the other where it was.
`inline-start` or `inline-end` stacks the arrows into a column, which is
what a vertical track usually wants.

`overlay` puts them on the slides, at the track's own edges, which is what a
full-bleed carousel wants: the slide is the page and the controls are on it
rather than in a bar beneath it. It carries its own treatment with it, a
surface and a shadow under each arrow, because a glyph drawn straight onto a
photograph is legible against about half of one.

**That was `appearance="hero"` and did not need to be.** A third axis for
something these two already describe: what `hero` meant was "the controls
are over the content", and the surface, the edge-to-edge arrows and the bar
that catches no presses all followed from it rather than being separate
decisions. One fewer property, and the two axes are now the whole of where
a carousel's chrome can go.

attributes.name: controls-align
attributes.description:
Where along that side the arrows sit. See `indicatorAlign`.

`overlay` answers it too, and the edge there is the whole slide: the bar is
stretched across the picture, so this moves the arrows up and down within
it rather than moving the bar. Centered unless asked otherwise, which is
where an arrow over a photograph belongs.

examples.description: Slides with controls and indicators, one at a time.
A carousel the page owns, so the slide it shows can be driven from elsewhere.
The slide in view, announced as it changes and not as it is dragged.
Full-bleed slides with the controls over the picture.

Advancing on its own, and stopping when a pointer rests on it.
More than one slide in view, which is what a shelf of cards wants.
Slides stacked and scrolled downward.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: send
members.description:
Offers what is written, and reports whether it stood.

Public because a consumer's own send control is as likely to ask as this
element's is, and because a keyboard shortcut somewhere else on the page is
a reasonable way to send.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on each tool box whether anything is in it.

They are boxes in a flex row, so an empty one still takes the gap beside it
and the send control drifts inward by one for every slot a consumer left
alone. No selector can ask this: a slot's assigned nodes are not its DOM
children, so `:empty` describes the fallback rather than the fill.

members.name: renderSend
members.description:
The control that offers the turn, behind a seam so a tier can draw its own.

**A glyph with the label as its accessible name, rather than the label as
text.** The word "Send" beside a field is the widest thing in the row and
says nothing a return key does not, and every composer a reader has used in
the last five years marks it rather than spells it. The return glyph is the
mark because Enter is what actually sends, which `submit-on` says out loud:
the control and the key are one affordance and should look like it.

`send-label` is unchanged and is now the accessible name rather than the
visible one, so a screen reader hears the same word it always did.

members.name: handleInput
members.description:
Records the draft, and stops the textarea speaking in this element's name.

**The stop is not incidental.** `input` is composed by specification, so the
`<textarea>` in this shadow root sent its own past this host and on through
whatever `<helix-chat>` it is slotted into, and neither element declares an
`input`: a consumer binding one on either received an undeclared event whose
target was a control they cannot reach. What a composer offers is
`helix-send`, once, when the reader is done. See 308.

members.name: handleKey
members.description:
Enter sends where that is what `submit-on` says, and never mid-composition.

**`isComposing` is the part that is easy to leave out and breaks a whole
writing system.** A reader typing Japanese, Chinese or Korean presses Enter
to accept the candidate their input method is offering, and a composer that
reads it as send fires off a half-finished word every time. The flag is on
the event for exactly this and costs one condition.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: separation
members.description:
Where the turn's surface ends.

**A bubble is one answer and not the only one, and the category has moved.**
Two people messaging read as two columns of bubbles, which is what the form
has looked like since it existed. An assistant answering does not: the reply
is a paragraph, often a long one with code and lists in it, and every AI
surface worth copying sets it as prose with the reader's own turns in
bubbles beside it. A component that can only draw bubbles cannot render the
conversation most people are now building.

- `filled` is the default and is told apart by its own ground, which is the
  bubble.
- `plain` has no ground and no edge: the turn is text on the transcript, and
  the space around it and the avatar beside it are what separate it. For an
  assistant's side of a conversation, and for any turn long enough that a
  fill reads as a wall.

**On this tier, because it is where the surface ends and nothing else.**
`check:axes` keeps `separation` off the headless tier for the reason it
keeps every painted axis off it: that tier has no ground to end. The two
values are a subset of the registry's four; `elevated` and `outlined` are
available and neither is a thing a turn should be, a lifted message reading
as a card and an outlined one as an input.

members.name: author
members.description:
Who said it.

Free text rather than a two-value union, because a conversation is not
always two-sided: a transcript with a system turn, a tool call and three
participants is the ordinary case for anything worth building this for.
`me` and `them` are the conventional values and the stylesheet knows them;
anything else is a name the consumer styles.

members.name: state
members.description:
What has happened to it.

Reflected, because every one of the four is a visual state and a stylesheet
has no other way to know. Absent is a settled message with nothing to
report, which is what most of a transcript is, and it is the absence of the
attribute rather than a value of it: there is no initializer, so nothing is
reflected until something happens.

members.name: at
members.description: When it was said, as anything `Date` parses.

members.name: locale
members.description:
Locale for the timestamp.

Empty is the runtime's own.

members.name: sendingLabel
members.description: What to call each state, for a reader who cannot see it.

members.name: retryLabel
members.description: Label for the control offered on a failed message.

members.name: moment
members.description: The timestamp, or nothing where there is not one to read.

members.name: renderMark
members.description:
The status glyph, behind a seam so a tier can draw its own.

`TONE_MARKS.danger` rather than a glyph chosen here: the library has one
status vocabulary, `Callout`, `Toast.Item` and `Announcement` all read from
it, and a reader meets these four marks in a passage, in a message and now
on a turn and has to read them as the same four things. It carries the
accessible name with it, which is the half that matters: `danger` is the
word the API uses and "Error" is the word a reader understands.

members.name: renderState
members.description:
What has happened to it, in words, and the way back from a failure.

A seam of its own, because the styled tier draws a failure as an icon and a
consumer may want neither. `sent` says nothing: every settled message is
sent, and a transcript that labels each one is a transcript of the word
"sent".

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on each region whether anything is in it.

Three of them need the answer and no selector can give it: a slot's assigned
nodes are not its DOM children, so `:empty` and `:has(*)` both describe the
fallback rather than the fill. `sources` and `actions` are regions that cost
a gap when they are boxes at all, which most turns should not pay. `content`
is the one that is not about space: a turn that is `streaming` with nothing
in it yet is what the typing indicator is drawn for, and "nothing in it yet"
is exactly this question.

members.name: handleFill
members.description:
A turn's own content arrives and changes no property here.

It is the streaming case that needs this rather than a tidiness one: the
first token of an answer is a light-DOM child appearing under an element
nothing else told to look again, and it is exactly the moment the typing
indicator has to stop being drawn.

members.name: handleRetry
members.description:
Retry is `helix-send` again, from the message rather than the composer.

**Not an event of its own**, because a retry is the same request: the reader
is offering what they wrote, and the only difference is which element is
offering it. A listener that wants to tell them apart has `event.target`,
which is the message on a retry and the composer on a first send, and that
is a distinction the DOM already makes without a second name for it.

Free text rather than a two-value union, because a conversation is not
always two-sided: a transcript with a system turn, a tool call and three
participants is the ordinary case for anything worth building this for.
`me` and `them` are the conventional values and the stylesheet knows them;
anything else is a name the consumer styles.

attributes.name: state
attributes.description:
What has happened to it.

Reflected, because every one of the four is a visual state and a stylesheet
has no other way to know. Absent is a settled message with nothing to
report, which is what most of a transcript is, and it is the absence of the
attribute rather than a value of it: there is no initializer, so nothing is
reflected until something happens.

attributes.name: at
attributes.description: When it was said, as anything `Date` parses.

attributes.name: locale
attributes.description:
Locale for the timestamp.

Empty is the runtime's own.

attributes.name: sending-label
attributes.description: What to call each state, for a reader who cannot see it.

attributes.name: retry-label
attributes.description: Label for the control offered on a failed message.

declarations.description:
Three regions stacked, and only the transcript scrolls: a composer that slid
away as the reader scrolled up to re-read would be the thing they were about
to type into.

**The transcript keeps its turns at the bottom when there are too few to fill
it**, which is what a conversation looks like. A new one starting at the top
of an empty column reads as a document.

The way back sits over the transcript rather than in the column, so offering
it does not move what the reader is reading, which is the whole point of
offering it.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the rows are still on their way.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What is said while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: slotCounted
members.description: Whether the rows have been looked at yet.

members.name: slotRows
members.description:
How many there were, the last time anyone looked.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this comment.**
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time claim and the runtime field is
whatever it is named, so a subclass declaring `@property() rows` for the
data a consumer hands it would share one field with this counter: the
slot count would overwrite the consumer's array on every `updated`, and
`hasRows` would read the array's length as a slot count. Nothing would
throw. `helix-data-table` takes exactly that property, which is what
found this before it happened.

members.name: countRows
members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: renderStatus
members.description:
The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description:
Nothing is assigned by name, so the turns land in the log and the rest does not.

The messages are ordinary children a consumer writes with no `slot`, and a
`role="log"` whose turns are somewhere else is a log of nothing. Manual
assignment is the only way to wrap them without editing the consumer's
markup, which is a change a React consumer's hydration reports and does not
patch up.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the conversation.

members.name: threshold
members.description:
How near the bottom still counts as being at it, in pixels.

A hook rather than a constant, because the right number depends on how tall
a turn is: a transcript of one-line replies wants a smaller threshold than
one of paragraphs, and a reader who has scrolled up by half a message has
not left.

members.name: pinned
members.description:
Whether the transcript follows new turns to the bottom.

Set it and this element defers: the reader's scrolling fires `helix-change`
and moves nothing until a new value arrives. `default-pinned` seeds a state
this element then owns, and it defaults to pinned because a conversation
opens at its most recent turn.

**Not reflected, and the default is why.** A reflected property that
defaults to true writes its attribute on upgrade whether or not the
consumer wrote one, so the server serves `<helix-chat label="x">` and the
client turns it into `<helix-chat label="x" pinned>`: a hydration mismatch a
React consumer reports and does not patch up. Nothing needs the attribute
either, because the one thing that changes with the pin is the way back, and
that is a part inside the shadow tree where a stylesheet can already reach
it. Measured rather than assumed: `label, pinned` after upgrade against
`label` from the server.

members.name: defaultPinned
members.description: Whether to open pinned, where nothing declared it.

members.name: watcher
members.description: Watches for turns arriving, since a manual slot hears nothing about them.

members.name: filled
members.description:
Which regions were given something, or undefined where nobody has counted.

**A slot that is assigned by hand has no children, so no stylesheet can ask
whether it was filled.** `[part="header"]:not(:has(> slot:has(*)))` is the
rule every other collection here hides an empty region with, and `:has()`
walks the DOM tree: with `slotAssignment: 'manual'` the assigned elements
are children of this host and never of the slot, so the test was false for
a filled header exactly as often as for an empty one and the rule never
matched. Measured on a chat with nothing slotted at all: the header was 25
pixels tall and drew its hairline under nothing, and so did the composer.

Undefined rather than empty on the way in, for `MixinCollection`'s reason:
the server has no children to count, and an unknown answer is not "empty".
It serves every region and the first assignment on the client settles them,
which is a shadow-root attribute rather than a host one and so is nothing a
consumer's hydration compares.

members.name: has
members.description: Whether a region has something in it, taking unknown for yes.

members.name: messages
members.description: The turns declared as children, in the order they are written.

members.name: log
members.description: The element that scrolls, once there is one.

members.name: atBottom
members.description: Whether the reader is within `threshold` of the bottom right now.

members.name: resume
members.description:
Puts the transcript back at its most recent turn.

Public because the way back is a slot, so the control offering it is the
consumer's and needs something to call. Pins again on the way, which is what
a reader asking to go to the bottom means.

members.name: requestPinned
members.description:
Asks to pin or unpin, and reports whether the request stood.

Announced before it is applied, so a consumer owning the pin hears the
reader's scroll and decides. `property` names it, which is what
`helix-before-pin`'s detail is for: a listener switching on the name is
switching on something with one meaning.

members.name: handleResume
members.description:
A press anywhere in the way back takes the reader back.

**The affordance was inert, in the component and in every example.** The
control is slotted so the consumer picks the words, and `resume()` was
public "because the control offering it is the consumer's and needs
something to call". True, and it left a button this element positions, lifts
and shows and hides doing nothing at all until somebody wired it, which none
of the five examples did: the one control whose whole job is to undo a
scroll shipped as decoration.

The region exists for exactly one purpose, so a press inside it has exactly
one meaning and this element is entitled to act on it. `resume()` stays
public for the other callers it was always for: a keyboard shortcut, or a
consumer's own control somewhere else on the page.

members.name: handleScroll
members.description:
The reader's own scrolling, which is the only thing that unpins.

**Bound to the transcript in the template, and it has to be.** This was a
capture listener on the host, on the reasoning that `scroll` does not bubble
so the capture phase is the only phase that reaches it. Not bubbling is not
the problem: `scroll` is not *composed*, and a non-composed event's
propagation path stops at the shadow root and never includes the host, in
any phase. So the listener never ran once, the pin never released, and a
reader who scrolled up to re-read was pulled back to the bottom by the next
turn to arrive, which this element's own description calls the most
got-wrong thing in the category.

Measured by dispatching both shapes at the transcript: with
`composed: false`, which is what the platform sends, the host saw zero and
`pinned` stayed true; with `composed: true` the host saw one and `pinned`
went false. Bound here, the phase and the bubbling never come up.

**The scroll this element does itself must not unpin it**, which is the
subtle half: `scrollTop = scrollHeight` fires the same event a reader's
wheel does. Reading the position rather than counting events is what makes
that harmless, since after a programmatic scroll the position is the bottom
and the answer is the one that was already true.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: A conversation: the turns, and where the reader is in them.

examples.description: A conversation with the four states a turn can be in, and a composer under it.
An assistant answering: what it drew the answer from, what can be done with it, and the wait before the first token.
The command palette: summoned from anywhere, anchored near the top, and gone when it is answered.
A turn sent and a transcript pinned, which are the reader's two asks.
The whole screen: a dialog at full size with the conversation filling it.
The floating one: an icon in the corner, and the conversation in a popover over the page.
The sidebar: a drawer from the trailing edge, with the conversation filling the panel.
