The palette is a dialog holding a filterable listbox, so what this tier adds
is where that dialog sits and how the list reads inside it. It opens against
the top of the window rather than centered, which is where every palette a
reader has used opens: a list that grows and shrinks as it is filtered would
otherwise walk up and down the screen under the words being typed.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it

different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all

writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute

opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-open` or
`helix-before-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the
element opens or closes itself, whether or not a consumer declared
`open`: a declared property is a seed and a correction, and a consumer
who wants the decision for themselves refuses it and assigns their own.
See 294.

members.name: announceToggle
members.description:
Says the state moved, under the platform's own name and in its shape.

**`<details>` fires `toggle` and a popover fires `toggle`, and sixteen
families here fired neither.** Two of them render a real `<dialog>` and
ten show a `popover="manual"` panel, so the browser was already firing
something on an element inside a shadow root, where `toggle` neither
bubbles nor composes and so reaches nobody. The rest, the disclosures,
have no native element to fire anything at all: `AccordionItem` and
`TreeItem` are `aria-expanded` and `hidden` written by hand, which is
`<details>`'s job done manually.

**From here rather than from `PopoverController`, which had it first.**
The controller covers eleven families and the mixin covers sixteen, and
the overlap is ten that would have announced twice. What `toggle` reports
is the *state*, and the state is this mixin's; the controller is a way of
putting a panel on the screen.

**`newState` and `oldState`, because that is the platform's shape**, so a
consumer arriving from `<details>` reads the same two words. Not
cancelable: the before events are the request, and a second cancelable
event for one transition is two answers to one question.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the overlay, which has no visible heading.

members.name: placeholder
members.description: Shown in the field before anything is typed.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: Words shown where the filter has matched nothing.

members.name: hotkey
members.description:
The key that opens it, as `mod+k` or `shift+p` or plain `k`.

Empty turns it off, for a consumer who opens the palette from a button or
from their own shortcut handler. There is no list of defaults to fight
with: one key, said once.

members.name: footed
members.description:
Whether the consumer put anything under the list.

Asked of the slot rather than of CSS. A wrapper holding a slot always has a
child element, which is the slot, so `:not(:has(*))` on it is never true
and an empty footer would draw its rule and its padding over nothing. Steps
was caught by the same thing.

members.name: handleHotkey
members.description:
Answers the hotkey from wherever the reader is.

On the document rather than on this element, which is never the thing with
focus: a palette that only answered when it already had focus would be a
palette nobody could open.

`preventDefault` because every key worth using is already the browser's.
Command-K focuses the address bar in some browsers and opens a search in
others, and a palette that opened underneath one of those would be a
palette the reader never sees.

members.name: handleChange
members.description:
Takes what the list announced and says it under this element's name.

The listbox says `helix-before-change`, which is the right word for a control that
holds a value and the wrong one for a palette: nothing here changed, a
command ran. It is stopped and re-announced rather than relayed, so a
consumer hears one event naming the element they put on the page.

members.name: activeOption
members.description:
The row under the keyboard, read from the attribute the listbox writes.

`data-active` rather than a reference the listbox hands over, because the
options are this element's own light DOM children and the attribute is
already published: asking the listbox would mean a second channel saying
what the markup says.

members.name: handleAlternate
members.description:
Takes the row's second destination, where the reader asked for it.

**Command intercepts rather than Listbox reporting, and that is the whole
design.** Enter belongs to the listbox: it owns the active row, it decides
what choosing means, and it announces `helix-before-change`. Teaching it about a
modifier would put a palette's idea of a second destination inside a
control that is also a select and a combobox, neither of which has one.

So this listens in the capture phase, before the listbox sees the key, and
only for the one combination that means something here. Anything else falls
straight through and the listbox behaves exactly as it always did.

`mod` is Command on a Mac and Control elsewhere, which is what `hotkey`
already means by it two methods up.

The pointer takes the same path for the same reason: a modifier-click on a
row is the same intent as a modifier-Enter on it, and both have to be
stopped before the row announces its ordinary selection.

members.name: renderDialog
members.description:
The surface the palette opens in, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

A method rather than a fragment inline, so a tier above can render its own,
wrap this one, pass it a property the base does not know about, or leave it
out, without reimplementing the whole template to do any of them. The tag is
interpolated rather than written, so `tier` resolves it: this renders the
headless element, and a styled subclass that sets `tier` renders the styled one
from the same template.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

attributes.name: default-open

The key that opens it, as `mod+k` or `shift+p` or plain `k`.

Empty turns it off, for a consumer who opens the palette from a button or
from their own shortcut handler. There is no list of defaults to fight
with: one key, said once.

declarations.description:
Takes the icon button's square box, then stacks its two faces in one grid
cell so the press never changes the button's size. See the stylesheet: a
control that resizes under the pointer at the moment a reader is looking at
it for reassurance reads as a second, accidental press.
declarations.name: HelixCopyButton

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How filled it is drawn.

**This was `appearance`, and the docstring above it always said what it
really was.** "How filled it is drawn", sitting beside `tone`, "What it
means": the axis was named correctly in prose and filed under the word
four axes shared. A Card's `outlined` says where a surface ends and this
one says how much ink a control claims, and one word cannot keep saying
both. `check:axes` holds the vocabulary now.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it, and undefaulted because
it reflects: a reflected property with a default writes its attribute
onto every host anybody renders. The resting treatment is the attribute's
absence, which each control names for itself, `outlined` on `Button` and
`ghost` on `IconButton`.

members.name: tone
members.description:
What it means.

Three and an accent, not the full status set. A tag reports a state and a
button performs an action: a success button and a warning button are not
things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page where the color
of a control means nothing in particular. `accent` is the second
emphasis, a rotation off the brand seed rather than a color of its own,
so it stays in relation when somebody rethemes.

members.name: value
members.description:
What goes on the clipboard.

**Narrows `Button.value`, which is the submit value, and the two agree.**
A copy button is `type="button"` and never submits, so the inherited
meaning has nothing to act on; where a consumer changes the type, what it
submits is what it copies, which is the reading anybody would expect of one
property called `value`. Declared here rather than inherited because the
clipboard is what this component is about and its own page should say so.

members.name: label
members.description:
What it is called, and says, before a press.

Defaulted rather than left empty. An icon-only control must be named, and
the name of this one is not a judgment call: every copy button in the
world is called Copy. A consumer with a better word still sets it.

members.name: copiedLabel
members.description:
What it is called, and says, after one.

`attribute` written out, because Lit lowercases a property name rather than
dash-casing it, and `copiedlabel` is not what anyone would type.

members.name: says
members.description:
The words for the state it is in, used twice on purpose.

The tooltip is the visible confirmation and the accessible name is the
spoken one, and they have to be the same words. A tooltip that changes to
Copied while the accessible name stays Copy tells a sighted reader it
worked and leaves a screen reader user pressing a button that never
acknowledges anything. Changing the name of the focused element is what
makes the announcement happen at all.

members.name: clipboard
members.description:
The write, the confirmation, the timer and the event, all of them shared.

**This was a second implementation of `CopyController` with the hard half
left out.** It reached straight for `navigator.clipboard.writeText` and had
no `execCommand` fallback, so it was inert in a sandboxed iframe without
`allow-same-origin`, which is the sandbox every example on the docs site
runs in: the guard on the API existing does not help there, because the
object exists and the write rejects. A copy button that does nothing is
indistinguishable from a broken one, and this one was doing nothing in the
one place a reader is most likely to try it.

The controller also carries the two things this had wrong on its own terms:
it checks the host is still connected after the await, because writing is
asynchronous and `hostDisconnected` clears a timer that does not exist yet,
and it registers itself so the timer is released without an override here.

members.name: icon
members.description:
Both faces, drawn rather than demanded.

Slot fallback, which is this library's answer for content a component has a
sensible default for: a copy button with no icons is not a copy button, and
making every consumer slot the same clipboard is asking them to supply the
one thing the component is sure about. Slotting anything replaces it, at
assignment time, with no property to set and nothing for the server and the
client to disagree about.

members.name: renderCopyIcon
members.description:
The mark for the resting state, behind a seam a tier can move.

Two seams and not one taking the state, because the two marks are two
decisions: a tier changing the clipboard for a house glyph has no reason to
touch the confirmation, and the stylesheet already treats them separately,
the check holding its green through a hover where this one does not.

members.name: renderCopiedIcon
members.description:
The mark for the moment after a press, behind a seam of its own.

Both slots render and CSS shows one, which is why this is a slot rather
than a branch: swapping which slot exists would unassign the consumer's
content on every press, and an element that leaves and re-enters the tree
loses focus with it, so the button a reader just pressed would stop being
the focused element mid-press.

members.name: renderTooltip
members.description:
The bubble the control sits inside, behind a seam.

It takes the control rather than rendering it, because this one wraps: a
tier above overriding it can drop the tooltip entirely and return the
button, put something else around it, or keep the tooltip and change only
how it is anchored, and every one of those is a normal thing to want.
Rendering the button here as well would make all three a rewrite.

members.name: type
members.description: What activating the button does to its form.

members.name: formAction
members.description:
Where this button's submission goes, overriding the form's own.

**The five `form*` overrides work by writing the form and putting it back**,
which is the only mechanism available and is closer to the platform than it
sounds. `requestSubmit(submitter)` is how a native submitter carries these,
and it refuses ours twice over: the inner `<button>` is `type="button"` so
it is not a submit button, and it sits in this shadow root so its form owner
is not the consumer's form. Both throw. So the submission is started with no
submitter and the overrides are applied to the form for the duration of it.

The whole submit algorithm runs synchronously inside `requestSubmit()`, so
the window is one call and a `finally` closes it whether or not a listener
refused. What a `submit` handler observes during that window is the form a
native submitter would have given it, which is the point.

members.name: formEnctype
members.description: How the submission is encoded, overriding the form's own.

members.name: formMethod
members.description: Which HTTP method the submission uses, overriding the form's own.

members.name: formNoValidate
members.description: Whether this submission skips the form's validation.

members.name: formTarget
members.description: Which browsing context the response lands in, overriding the form's own.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: expanded
members.description:
Whether this button is a disclosure trigger, and whether its panel is open.

**Set by whatever owns the panel, and a property rather than an attribute
for the reason `Menu` already states about its items**: an attribute
written onto a consumer's element after it upgrades is a hydration mismatch
waiting to happen. Measured 28 Aug 2026 against React 19.2.8, server markup
hydrated with the definitions loaded either side of `hydrateRoot`:
`Megamenu` and `SpeedDial` wrote `aria-expanded` onto the slotted trigger
and React reported "some attributes of the server rendered HTML didn't
match the client properties. This won't be patched up" in both orders;
`Popover` and `Menu`, which write nothing, were clean in both.

**A property crosses that gap because React never looks at one.** It diffs
the attributes it rendered, and this one is `attribute: false`, so the state
travels to the inner `<button>` and lands inside a shadow root React does
not own and cannot compare. The consumer's own element is left exactly as
they served it, which is what `Popover`'s note asks for, and the reader is
still told what the control does, which is what `SpeedDial`'s note asks
for. See #322.

`undefined` renders nothing at all, so a button that is not a trigger
carries no `aria-expanded`: the resting state is the attribute's absence,
which is the rule every reflected property here follows.

A consumer who wants to say this statically writes `aria-expanded` on the
host instead, which `AriaForwardController` carries to the same place.

members.name: submit
members.description:
Submits the form as this button, for the length of one call.

Everything a native submitter carries is written onto the form, the
submission is started, and everything is put back. See `formAction` for why
`requestSubmit(submitter)` is not available to a control inside a shadow
root.

`novalidate` is in the same list rather than reached by `form.submit()`,
which looks like the shortcut and is not: `submit()` skips the `submit`
event as well as the validation, so a consumer's handler would stop running
the moment somebody wrote `formnovalidate`. Turning the flag on and calling
`requestSubmit()` skips the validation alone, which is what the attribute
means.

members.name: commandForElement
members.description:
The element this button's command is sent to, resolved.

The platform's own accessor, and this element had the resolution and kept
it to itself: `linkCommand` writes the target onto the inner `<button>`,
where a consumer cannot reach it, and `commandFor` answers with an id
rather than an element. Writing assigns the inner control directly, which
is what an invoker without an id in the same tree needs.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.
The same asymmetry the listbox relies on for `aria-activedescendant`, and
the second place in this library where the id form is the one that cannot
work.

The id is looked up in the host's own root rather than the document, so a
button inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root
and not a coincidence in the page.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:
The element this button commands, or nothing.

Looked up in the button's own root rather than in the document, so a button
inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not
a coincidence in the page.

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

Only where the platform is absent, so a browser that has invokers sends
exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

Defaulted rather than left empty. An icon-only control must be named, and
the name of this one is not a judgment call: every copy button in the
world is called Copy. A consumer with a better word still sets it.

attributes.name: copied-label
attributes.description:
What it is called, and says, after one.

`attribute` written out, because Lit lowercases a property name rather than
dash-casing it, and `copiedlabel` is not what anyone would type.

attributes.name: type
attributes.description: What activating the button does to its form.

attributes.name: formaction
attributes.description:
Where this button's submission goes, overriding the form's own.

**The five `form*` overrides work by writing the form and putting it back**,
which is the only mechanism available and is closer to the platform than it
sounds. `requestSubmit(submitter)` is how a native submitter carries these,
and it refuses ours twice over: the inner `<button>` is `type="button"` so
it is not a submit button, and it sits in this shadow root so its form owner
is not the consumer's form. Both throw. So the submission is started with no
submitter and the overrides are applied to the form for the duration of it.

The whole submit algorithm runs synchronously inside `requestSubmit()`, so
the window is one call and a `finally` closes it whether or not a listener
refused. What a `submit` handler observes during that window is the form a
native submitter would have given it, which is the point.

attributes.name: formenctype
attributes.description: How the submission is encoded, overriding the form's own.

attributes.name: formmethod
attributes.description: Which HTTP method the submission uses, overriding the form's own.

attributes.name: formnovalidate
attributes.description: Whether this submission skips the form's validation.

attributes.name: formtarget
attributes.description: Which browsing context the response lands in, overriding the form's own.

attributes.name: command
attributes.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

attributes.name: commandfor
attributes.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

attributes.name: name
attributes.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

limitation and worth repeating where a consumer chooses between the two: use
`helix-table` where the content has to be in the served HTML.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the rows are still on their way.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What is said while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: slotCounted
members.description: Whether the rows have been looked at yet.

members.name: slotRows
members.description:
How many there were, the last time anyone looked.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this comment.**
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time claim and the runtime field is
whatever it is named, so a subclass declaring `@property() rows` for the
data a consumer hands it would share one field with this counter: the
slot count would overwrite the consumer's array on every `updated`, and
`hasRows` would read the array's length as a slot count. Nothing would
throw. `helix-data-table` takes exactly that property, which is what
found this before it happened.

members.name: countRows
members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: hasRows
members.description: Emptiness is a fact about the data here, not about slotted children.

members.name: renderStatus
members.description:
The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description:
Nothing is assigned by name, so the columns can be put in a header row.

`role="columnheader"` under `role="grid"` with no owning row is invalid, and
the columns are ordinary children a consumer writes with no `slot`. Manual
assignment is the only way to wrap them without editing the consumer's
markup, which is a change a React consumer's hydration reports and does not
patch up. The same arrangement `helix-table` arrived at, for the same reason.

members.name: rows
members.description:
The whole result, in the order it arrived.

A property and not an attribute: it is an array. Left alone this element
filters, sorts and pages it; in `server` mode it is the page the consumer
already fetched and none of the three is applied.

**Read, never written.** Sorting produces a new array rather than reordering
this one, because a consumer's array may be the same object their own state
holds and reordering it under them is a mutation they did not ask for.

members.name: key
members.description:
The field naming a row's stable identity.

**Needed before selection exists, not after.** Lit keys the rendered rows by
it, so a sort moves a row's element rather than rewriting every cell in
place, which is what keeps focus inside a cell and keeps a CSS transition
attached to the row it belongs to. Left unset the index is the key, which is
correct only while nothing reorders: it is why this defaults to something
that works and is worth setting anyway.

members.name: mode
members.description:
Whether this element does the work or asks the consumer to.

`client` filters, sorts and pages `rows` itself. `server` applies none of
them: `rows` is the page, `total` is the size of the whole result, and the
three events are requests the consumer answers by fetching. Past some size
the client cannot hold the data, so this is not an optimization, it is the
only mode that works, and it is here from the start because adding it later
inverts the data flow.

members.name: total
members.description:
How many rows the whole result has, where this element cannot count them.

Only read in `server` mode, where `rows` is one page and its length says
nothing about the result. Ignored in `client` mode rather than trusted,
because two sources for one count is the mistake, and here the array is the
one that cannot be stale.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the grid.

members.name: sort
members.description:
The order, as `field:direction`.

Set it and this element defers: a reader's click fires `helix-sort` and
changes nothing until a new value arrives. `default-sort` seeds an order this
element then owns.

members.name: defaultSort
members.description: Order to open on, where nothing declared one.

members.name: filter
members.description:
What the rows are narrowed to, as one query across every column.

One query rather than a predicate per column, which is what a reader means
by a search box above a table. It matches on each column's ordering value,
so search and sort cannot disagree about what a column holds.

members.name: defaultFilter
members.description: Query to open with, where nothing declared one.

members.name: page
members.description:
The page on show, from 1.

Clamped on the way out, so what this reports is the page it drew: a
bookmarked link to page 99 of a result that has since shrunk reads back as
the last page rather than as 99.

members.name: defaultPage
members.description: Page to open on, where nothing declared one.

members.name: pageSize
members.description:
How many rows a page holds. Zero is every row, which is what "no paging" means.

**It announces nothing, and that is not an omission.** Nothing in this
element ever asks for a different page size: a size selector is
`helix-pagination-size`, which a consumer puts in the `footer` slot and
answers themselves. Routing this through `requestChange` would announce an
event the element never has cause to fire.

members.name: defaultPageSize
members.description: Page size to open with, where nothing declared one.

members.name: paginated
members.description:
Whether to draw a pagination under the grid.

On by default once a page size is set, because a paged table with no way to
change pages shows a reader the first twenty rows and no way to know there
are more. Off for a consumer supplying their own through the `footer` slot,
which is why the slot replaces this rather than sitting beside it.

members.name: tableColumns
members.description: The columns declared as children, in the order they are written.

members.name: axes
members.description: The columns reduced to what the ordering needs.

members.name: template
members.description: The track list, from the columns if there are any.

members.name: view

type.text: { matched: number; rows: DataRow[]; total: number }

members.description:
The rows to draw, and the counts around them.

In `server` mode this element applies nothing: `rows` is already the page,
`total` is the result, and both counts come from the consumer. Anything else
would be this element filtering a page it was handed, which narrows one
screen and calls it a search.

members.name: pages
members.description: How many pages the result makes, which is at least one even when empty.

members.name: matched
members.description:
Rows after filtering, computed without paging.

Separate from `view` because `pages` needs it and `page` needs `pages`:
asking `view` for it would recurse through the clamp in `page`.

members.name: requestSort
members.description:
Asks for a different order, and reports whether the request stood.

Announced before it is applied, so `preventDefault()` is a refusal and the
order does not move, which is what makes a server-side sort expressible: the
consumer refuses the local reorder, fetches, and hands back a new set.

members.name: requestFilter
members.description: Asks for a different query.

members.name: requestPage
members.description: Asks for a different page.

members.name: search
members.description:
Narrows the rows, from a consumer's own search field.

Public because the query lives above the table in every design that has one,
and a consumer wiring their own input needs somewhere to send it. Returns
whether the change stood, the same as every other request here.

members.name: toggleSort
members.description:
Cycles the order by one column, which is what a click on its heading means.

Ascending, descending, then the order the rows arrived in. Public for the
same reason `search` is: a consumer's own heading UI needs a way to ask.

members.name: assign
members.description:
The columns into the header row, everything else into the toolbar and footer.

Manual assignment, so a consumer's own markup is never written to.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on the toolbar and the footer whether anything is in them.

**The stylesheet used to ask, and could not.** It read
`[part="toolbar"]:has(> slot:not(:has(*)))`, which is two faults at once:
`:has()` may not be nested inside `:has()`, so the selector failed to parse
and the whole rule was discarded; and `slot:not(:has(*))` is as true of a
filled slot as of an empty one, because assigned nodes are not a slot's DOM
children. Both verified in a browser. A table with no toolbar paid the gap
above the grid for one that was not there.

members.name: markRegion
members.description:
One region, hidden when its slot holds nothing and nothing of ours fills it.

`hidden` beside the `data-empty` mirror: `data-empty` is the hook the styled
sheet reads, and this tier ships no sheet, so an empty region left in the box
tree would be a gap a headless consumer cannot close without knowing to look
for it. The styled rule stays too, because that sheet sets `display` on these
parts and therefore outranks the UA's `[hidden]` one.

members.name: handleSlotChange
members.description: Columns arrive from the light DOM, which changes no property here.

members.name: rowIndex
members.description:
A row's place in the whole result, counting the header as row 1.

**The number describes the result and not the window**, which is the whole
reason a virtualized or paged grid needs `aria-rowindex` at all: a screen
reader on page three should hear row 41, and a grid whose indices restart at
every page tells a reader the result is twenty rows long however many it has.

members.name: handleHeadClick
members.description: A click on a sortable heading.

members.name: handleHeadKey
members.description: The same on Enter and Space, since a heading that sorts is a control.

members.name: handleNavigate
members.description:
The composed pagination's request, relayed as this element's own.

Stopped rather than allowed to bubble, because two `helix-navigate` events
for one click would reach a consumer's handler twice: the pagination's, and
this element's after it. The one that leaves carries this element's page
bounds rather than the inner component's.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.description:
The frame is the field rather than the input, so the trigger sits inside the
same box as the text and the focus ring is drawn once around the whole
control. The trigger is a mark within that box rather than a button beside it:
a second frame inside the first is two controls where a reader sees one.

The calendar is the real `helix-date-picker`, in a panel with no border of its
own. A surface over the page is told apart by its shadow and by what it
covers, and a line around it as well reads as a box drawn around something
already separate.

Height comes from the region, like every other control: `data-density` on
whatever holds it.
