members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the dialog.

members.name: persistent
members.description:
Whether Escape can close it.

Off for a dialog that must be answered. It does not disable the close
control a consumer slots in: refusing to be dismissed is not the same as
refusing to be closed, and a dialog with no way out at all is a trap.

Escape *and* a press on the backdrop, which it now genuinely means. The
sentence said both for a long time while nothing listened for a backdrop
press, so it promised a behavior a consumer would have written their
markup around; the fix then was to narrow the sentence, and the fix now is
to build the half that was missing.

A persistent dialog does not ignore that press. It answers it: see
`refuse`, which is the only way a dialog that will not be dismissed can say
so at the moment a reader asks.

members.name: commands
members.default: new CommandController(this, { commands: { '--close': () => this.close(), '--show': () => this.show(), '--toggle': () => this.toggleOpen(), }, })

members.name: closedBy
members.description:
Which close requests the browser answers on its own.

`<dialog closedby>`, forwarded, and safe to forward because every path it
opens still comes back through this element: a close request fires `cancel`
first, `handleCancel` prevents it, and `requestOpen` decides. So
`closedby="any"` gains light dismiss without giving up the refusal, which is
the property this component exists to keep.

Absent by default, which is the platform's `auto` and this library's rule
that a resting value is an attribute's absence.

members.name: returnValue
members.description:
What the dialog closed with, the way `<dialog>` reports it.

**The whole point of a `<dialog>` returning a value is lost behind a shadow
boundary**, which is where this one is: the platform's contract is
`close(value)` then read `returnValue`, and a consumer could do neither
because `querySelector` does not reach the element. A confirmation asking
which button was pressed is the ordinary case and had no answer.

Held here as well as on the element, so a value set before the first render
survives to it and a consumer reading one back gets what they wrote.

members.name: returned
members.description: What a value set before the element existed is kept in.

members.name: dialog
members.description: The native dialog, or nothing where there is no DOM to hold one.

members.name: show
members.description: Moves focus into the dialog and makes the rest of the page inert.

members.name: close
members.description:
Asks to close, which a consumer may refuse.

Takes what the dialog closed with, the way `<dialog>.close(value)` does, so
the button that dismissed it can say which one it was. Set before the
request rather than after, because a `close` listener reads `returnValue`
and would otherwise read the previous one.

Not set where the request is refused, since nothing closed and a value
saying it did would outlive the refusal.

members.name: handleCancel
members.description:
Escape, intercepted so it is a request rather than an act.

The native `cancel` event fires before the dialog closes, so preventing it
leaves the dialog open and lets `requestOpen` decide. Without this a reader
pressing Escape would close a dialog its consumer had said was open, and
the two would disagree until something else moved.

members.name: handleClose
members.description:
A close that happened anyway, reflected back.

`<form method="dialog">` closes the dialog directly and there is no event
to prevent. Rather than fight it, the state follows: the dialog is shut, so
saying otherwise would be a lie the next `showModal()` would trip over.

members.name: openWhenSlotted
members.description: Opens once anything slotted has had its first render. See `updated`.

members.name: handleBackdrop
members.description:
A press on the backdrop, which lands on the dialog element itself.

**The target alone is not enough here, where it is for `Drawer`.** A modal
`<dialog>` attributes backdrop clicks to itself, which is the usual trick,
and this panel also carries `--dialog-inset` of padding: a press in that
padding has the same target as a press on the backdrop, so the trick alone
closes a dialog when a reader clicks just inside its own edge. The drawer
escapes that because its panel is flush against the window and its content
fills it. So the point is compared against the panel's box.

members.name: refuse
members.description:
Says no to a dismissal, by moving.

A persistent dialog that ignores a press on the backdrop is
indistinguishable from one that did not notice, and a reader's next move is
to press again harder. A short swell and settle is the smallest thing that
reads as "I heard you, and no": it is the same gesture a native alert makes
on macOS and the one every reader has already been taught.

An attribute for the length of the animation rather than a class, cleared
on `animationend`, so the styled tier decides what refusing looks like and
this decides only when it happens. Removed first so a second press
restarts it: without that, pressing twice does nothing the second time,
which is the impression the whole thing exists to avoid.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

attributes.description:

is what the mirror has always been for.

same twenty-four.

The ring starts at twelve o'clock, which is a rotation applied here rather
than arithmetic done below: where a reader expects the first slice to begin
is a fact about the picture, not about the numbers.

still reads as a ring with a gap rather than as a broken arc.

to agree: the outer edge is `r + width / 2`, so setting one in CSS and
deriving the other in markup gives a drawing that is wrong in both. Measured
with the hook still in place, every ring came out twelve units thick whatever
its `hole`, so a pie was a small ring with a hole in it and `large` was drawn
larger than the default.

**The styled tier, so the tooltip this renders is the styled one.**

`tag()` builds a child's tag name from this prefix, and the base declares
`helix-headless-`. Every other styled component that renders a child
overrides it; the three charts that draw a tooltip did not, so a
`helix-bar-chart` on a page put a `helix-headless-tooltip` in its shadow
root: the behavior with none of the surface. What showed was the browser's
own popover defaults, a white 1.5px border, square corners, `0.25em` of
padding and the page's font size, which is why the reading bubble looked
like no other tooltip on the site.

Measured before the fix: the chart's bubble computed
`border: 1.5px solid rgb(255, 255, 255)`, `border-radius: 0px`,
`padding: 3.5px`, `font-size: 14px`. The masthead's, a `helix-tooltip`,
had the component's own `none`, `radii-sm`, `2xs xs` and `text-xs`.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How much ink the slices claim.

`solid` is the resting arrangement and selects nothing: a slice at full
strength is what the base rule already draws. `subtle` is the ring as a wash
of its own colors, still readable and no longer the loudest thing beside the
number it is explaining. `outlined` keeps the slice and fades it toward the
page, leaving a boundary in the series' own color, which is the same trade
`BarChart` makes on a column.

**This took three values on 25 Aug 2026, and the note it replaces argued it
could not.** That note was right about the mark: a slice is a stroke on a
ring, the edge *is* the mark, and there is nothing within it to fade. It
concluded that `outlined` would mean drawing slices as filled paths instead
of arcs, and called that changing what a donut is to satisfy a word.

What it did not weigh is that the two can both be there. The arc still draws
the slice and still carries the animation, and a closed path traces the same
wedge beside it for anything that needs a boundary. Nothing about the donut
changed; something was added next to it. See `renderEdge` on the tier below
for why the dash could not simply be replaced.

slices.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the ring is made of.

`glass` lets the page read through the slices, for a chart sitting on a
surface that is itself translucent: a glass card with an opaque ring on it is
the two-designs-sharing-a-window failure a material policy exists to stop.
The track keeps its fill, a see-through groove being a missing one.

The strength is the theme's, scaled by `--helix-material-opacity`.

**This paints a mark rather than a ground, and the axis still reads the
same way.** On a surface the points are how much of the page shows through;
on a series they are how much ink the mark has, and the order is the same:
`glass` admits most, `frosted` admits less, absent is opaque. The two
factors, 0.62 and 0.88, carry the relationship the surface tokens carry
between `material-translucent` and `material-translucent-strong`, so a
chart and a card mean the same thing by the word.

members.name: source
members.description: Resolves `for` and re-renders when the table behind it changes.

members.name: pointer
members.description:
Which reading a pointer is nearest, for a tooltip to sit on.

Public for the same reason `series` and `named` are: a protected member
cannot be cast onto across unrelated classes, so it would be invisible to
every chart that needs it. Reading where a pointer is resting is a fair
thing to ask a chart anyway.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

members.name: series
members.description: The columns of the table, one series each, or none if there is no table.

members.name: named
members.description:
What to call the drawing, the consumer's word or the table's own.

The fallback is the reason this is shared rather than copied: a caption is
already written, already the right words, and already the thing a reader
of the table sees. A chart that made the consumer say it twice would be
asking for the second one to drift.

members.name: sourceRows
members.description:
Every row of the table, with each cell's text as well as its number.

This is where a tooltip's content comes from, and it is deliberately not
`series`. A chart draws numbers; a reader resting a pointer on one wants
what the table says, which is `$128k` and not `128000`, and often wants
the column beside it that nothing plotted at all.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this paragraph.** It
is the source table's rows, and `rows` on a chart is a name a chart
wants for itself: `helix-heatmap` takes `rows="7"` to mean a calendar
week, and declaring that against a base class whose `rows` is a `Row[]`
getter is a type error at best. The same fault `MixinCollection` had,
where a slot counter called `rows` would have shared one field with a
consumer's data property. Name the member for what it holds rather than
for the shortest word available.

members.name: readings
members.description: How many readings there are, which is what the pointer maps onto.

members.name: hole
members.description:
How much is left open in the middle.

Absent is a ring with room for a total in it. `small` and `large` move the
hole without moving the outer edge, so a chart keeps its footprint.

**`none` is a pie**, and it is the same drawing rather than another one:
the radius follows the thickness, so the inner edge reaching the center is
what closing the hole means. A pie reads less accurately than a ring, angle
being harder to judge than length, but it is not *misleading* the way a bar
measured from anything but zero is, which is why this is a value here and
the bar chart's baseline is not a property at all.

**Geometry rather than a CSS hook, and it had to move.** This was
`--donut-chart-thickness`, and the dash arithmetic needs the circumference,
which needs the radius: reading a custom property means `getComputedStyle`,
which is client-only, so a server would have drawn a different ring than
the client. A plot's proportions are markup for the same reason `curve` is.

members.name: sweep
members.description:
How much of the circle the whole occupies.

Absent is the full turn. `half` is a semi-donut: the same shares spread
over a half circle that opens downward, which is the shape a dashboard
uses when the ring sits above a figure and the space below it is doing
something else.

**A second property rather than another `hole` value**, because the two are
different axes and can both be true: `hole` is radial and says how thick
the band is, this is angular and says how far round it goes. A `half`
`none` is a semi-pie and is a real thing to want.

**Not a gauge**, and the distinction is worth stating because this row was
first filed as one. A gauge is one value against a range, which is a
different data shape entirely and is `Meter`, whose `round` example already
draws the reading as a ring. This divides a whole into parts and then
declines to use the bottom half of the circle.

Reflected, because the stylesheet has three things to say about it: the
rotation that puts the first slice at nine o'clock, the aspect ratio of a
box that is no longer square, and where the middle sits once the bottom of
the circle is not drawn.

members.name: span
members.description: The fraction of the circle the shares are spread over.

members.name: thickness
members.description: How thick the ring is drawn, in the drawing's own units.

members.name: radius
members.description: The ring's radius, which follows its thickness so the outer edge holds.

members.name: renderPlot
members.description:
The ring itself, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

`aria-hidden`, because the table it was read from is the readable version
and a screen reader hearing both hears the same numbers twice.

members.name: frame
members.description:
The view box, cropped to what is actually drawn.

A full turn uses the square. A half arc uses the band from the top of the
ring down to the center line, plus the half stroke its flat ends hang
below that, and cropping to it is the difference between a semi-donut and a
semi-donut with an empty quarter of the box under it. The outer edge is
`EDGE` from the center whatever the thickness, which is what makes this two
numbers rather than a measurement.

members.name: renderSegment
members.description: One slice, as a dash the length of its share.

members.name: renderEdge
members.description:
The same slice again, as a shape with an inside.

**A stroked arc has no boundary to draw, which is why this exists.** The
segment above is a dash on a circle: the mark *is* the edge, so there is
nothing for an outline to trace and nothing within it to fade. Anything
wanting those two separately needs the slice as a closed path, and this is
it: the outer arc, a step inward, the inner arc back, closed.

**Rendered always and painted only sometimes**, which is what keeps this on
this tier. Whether a boundary is drawn is a styled question and the answer
lives in a stylesheet; whether the geometry a boundary would need exists at
all is structural, and a component cannot conjure a shape from CSS. So the
path is here for every donut and is `fill: none; stroke: none` until
something asks for it.

**Not a replacement for the dash, which was the first plan.** The dash
carries three jobs and only one of them is the shape: a share growing is a
`stroke-dasharray` interpolating with no reflow, and `@starting-style` on
that same property is the whole reason the ring sweeps in rather than
appearing. A `d` cannot do either. CSS interpolates one only between paths
of identical command structure, and the large-arc flag flips the moment a
slice crosses a half turn, so a growing slice would pop partway through the
transition it was meant to smooth. Both animations stay on the dash and this
path follows it.

The turn to twelve o'clock is arithmetic here rather than the rotation the
stylesheet gives the circles. That rule uses `transform-box: fill-box`, so
it spins each element about its own bounding box, which is the ring's center
for a circle and is not for a sector.

members.name: renderTooltip
members.description:
What a pointer resting on a slice shows.

Placed in the middle rather than along an axis, a ring having none, and the
middle is where a reader is already looking: the hole usually holds a
total, so a tooltip over it replaces one figure with the one being asked
about rather than covering something else.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

members.name: material
members.description:
Whether the panel is glass rather than opaque.

**The same pair `Card` and `App Header` draw**, and one attribute for the
same reason: a backdrop filter behind an opaque ground filters nothing and a
translucent ground with no filter is a tint, so a consumer says what it
wants rather than assembling it out of two hooks.

A drawer is the case where the pair earns the most, because there is already
something behind it worth seeing: the page it covers, under its own scrim.

Absent is opaque, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default,
so the stylesheet only describes the departure.

**`transparent` is where this one stops, and that is the statement 270
asks for rather than an omission.** A panel that floats over arbitrary page
content is only readable because it has a ground; dropping it does not make
a lighter drawer, it makes an unreadable one. `frosted` and `glass` are the
two honest points here.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-open` or
`helix-before-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the
element opens or closes itself, whether or not a consumer declared
`open`: a declared property is a seed and a correction, and a consumer
who wants the decision for themselves refuses it and assigns their own.
See 294.

members.name: announceToggle
members.description:
Says the state moved, under the platform's own name and in its shape.

**`<details>` fires `toggle` and a popover fires `toggle`, and sixteen

the overlap is ten that would have announced twice. What `toggle` reports

putting a panel on the screen.

consumer arriving from `<details>` reads the same two words. Not
cancelable: the before events are the request, and a second cancelable

members.name: modal
members.description:
Whether the drawer blocks the page behind it.

Turning this off removes the focus trap and the scrim together, because
they are one decision: a panel that traps focus without covering the page
strands the reader, and one that covers without trapping lets them tab
behind the cover.

lost its focus trap because a consumer forgot a word would be worse than an
attribute on the host, and nothing selects on it: the scrim is rendered or
not, rather than shown or hidden by CSS.

members.name: closedBy
members.description:

opens still comes back through this element: a close request fires `cancel`
first, `handleCancel` prevents it, and `requestOpen` decides. So
`closedby="any"` gains light dismiss without giving up the refusal, which is
the property this component exists to keep.

that a resting value is an attribute's absence.

members.name: returnValue
members.description:

boundary**, which is where this one is: `querySelector` does not reach the
element, so a consumer could neither set the value nor read it back. A
drawer asking which of its actions dismissed it is the ordinary case and had
no answer.

call, because this component has no such method: it is driven by `open`
alone, and `Dialog`'s `close()` is the one that takes the value directly.

Held here as well as on the element, so a value set before the first render
survives to it and a consumer reading one back gets what they wrote.

members.name: returned
members.description: What a value set before the element existed is kept in.

members.name: panel
members.description: The panel, which is a real `<dialog>`.

members.name: handleCancel
members.description:

the consumer's state still said open: the bug that makes a modal impossible
to reopen. `Dialog` intercepts it for the same reason.

members.name: handleClose
members.description: A close that happened anyway is reflected back rather than argued with.

members.name: handleBackdrop
members.description:
A press on the backdrop, which lands on the dialog element itself.

The panel fills only part of the dialog's box, so a press beside it hits
the dialog and not a child. A native `<dialog>` does not close on that, and
it is the gesture that most obviously means close.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

attributes.name: material
attributes.description:
Whether the panel is glass rather than opaque.

**The same pair `Card` and `App Header` draw**, and one attribute for the
same reason: a backdrop filter behind an opaque ground filters nothing and a
translucent ground with no filter is a tint, so a consumer says what it
wants rather than assembling it out of two hooks.

A drawer is the case where the pair earns the most, because there is already
something behind it worth seeing: the page it covers, under its own scrim.

Absent is opaque, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default,
so the stylesheet only describes the departure.

**`transparent` is where this one stops, and that is the statement 270
asks for rather than an omission.** A panel that floats over arbitrary page
content is only readable because it has a ground; dropping it does not make
a lighter drawer, it makes an unreadable one. `frosted` and `glass` are the
two honest points here.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all

opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing

back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there

members.name: slotRows
members.description:
How many there were, the last time anyone looked.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this comment.**
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time claim and the runtime field is
whatever it is named, so a subclass declaring `@property() rows` for the
data a consumer hands it would share one field with this counter: the
slot count would overwrite the consumer's array on every `updated`, and
`hasRows` would read the array's length as a slot count. Nothing would
throw. `helix-data-table` takes exactly that property, which is what
found this before it happened.

members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: placeTabStop
members.description:

Every row rendered at `-1`, so nothing in the region was tab-reachable and
the keyboard could not get in at all without a pointer first. One row holds
the stop and the arrows move within, which is the roving pattern the
toolbar uses and the one a `menu` wants.

in replaces the rows outright, and the stop has to land on rows that are
actually showing.

row is read before going back rather than after: a reader who drills in and
comes straight out should be on the row they pressed, not at the top of a
list they have already read.

members.name: mark

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: accept
members.description: Which files the picker offers, as a native `accept` list.

members.name: multiple
members.description: Whether more than one file can be chosen.

members.name: capture
members.description: Which camera or microphone a mobile picker should offer, if any.

members.name: triggerLabel
members.description: What the trigger reads, where nothing is slotted into it.

members.name: locale
members.description:
Language tag the sizes are written in.

Absent uses the runtime's own.

members.name: removeLabel
members.description: What the control removing one file is called, per file.

members.name: dropping
members.description:
Whether something is being dragged over the field.

State rather than a property: it is a fact about a gesture in progress and
nothing a consumer sets. It reaches the stylesheet as `data-dropping` on an
element in this shadow root, never on the host, which is markup a consumer
rendered.

members.name: files
members.description:
The files chosen, which is the element's own and never assigned.

Read from the input rather than mirrored into a field. The input is what
the picker filled and what a form submits, so a copy here could only ever
disagree with it.

members.name: control
members.description:
The input, or nothing where there is no tree to ask.

The guard is for the server, whose element shim carries attributes but not
traversal: `render` reads `files`, `files` reads this, and an unguarded
`querySelector` threw before a single character of markup came out. Nothing
is lost by answering `null` there, because a file only ever arrives through
a reader and a server has never met one.

members.name: clear
members.description:
Takes every file back out.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: toggleState

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:

and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a

it takes the one nobody wanted.

`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches

specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice

the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for

still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:

so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on

makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.description:

so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and

say about it. A timestamp takes the family, size and color of the text around

members.description:
The timestamp, as anything `Date` parses.

An ISO string is what an API sends and what `<time datetime>` takes, so it
is the shape that needs no translation at either end. Left unset this
renders nothing rather than the epoch, which is what parsing an empty string
would give.

browser may use either.

members.description:

members.name: applyTemplate
members.description:
Writes the track list into the shadow root's own stylesheet.

Into a `<style>` rather than onto `this.style`, and the difference is
hydration. An inline style on the host is an attribute the element gives
itself once it upgrades, so a React consumer's server markup does not have
it and hydration reports a mismatch it will not patch up. The shadow root
is not part of the tree React hydrates, so a rule written there is free.

The element is filled imperatively because Lit refuses expressions inside
`<style>`: it is an invalid binding location and throws while rendering
rather than at build time. Hence a static, empty element in the template
and its `textContent` set here.

It sets a custom property rather than the track list itself. A shadow
root's adopted stylesheets cascade *after* its own `<style>` elements, and
`static styles` is adopted, so a `grid-template-columns` here lost to the
one in the stylesheet and every `min` grid came out a single column. The
stylesheet only ever reads `--_grid-template`, so there is nothing to
lose against.

The consequence is that a server-rendered grid falls back to the
stylesheet's single column until it upgrades. That is why `columns` is also
expressed as plain CSS below: the fixed-count case, which can be enumerated,
needs no JavaScript at all, and only `min` depends on this.

reaches a five step ramp of one hue, which is the only thing a reader can
compare two cells by. Both are hooks, so a page may answer differently.
