members.name: gap
members.description:
The first guess at what this sheet draws, before it has been measured.

**Not a contract any more, and it was a bad one.** `fits()` works against a
measured width and a cell size it has to be told, and being told by hand
meant these sat at the base tier's 8 and 2 against a sheet drawing 12 and 4:
the arithmetic believed a cell cost 10 pixels where it cost 16, so a ninety
day strip drew 940 pixels of cells into a 592 pixel box at 640 and 540 into
342 at 390, overflowing the document both times while `visible` reported 59
and 34. The number a summary is told to trust was the number that was wrong.

The strip is read back now, so nothing has to be kept in step and
`--heatmap-cell-width` on its own is enough. These two remain because a
measurement arrives one frame after the first paint, and a first paint from
numbers that match the sheet is one that does not move.

members.name: minCell
members.description: The drawn cell width, for the reason `gap` is the drawn gap. `0.75rem` at the root font size.

members.name: source
members.description: Resolves `for` and re-renders when the table behind it changes.

members.name: pointer
members.description:
Which reading a pointer is nearest, for a tooltip to sit on.

Public for the same reason `series` and `named` are: a protected member
cannot be cast onto across unrelated classes, so it would be invisible to
every chart that needs it. Reading where a pointer is resting is a fair
thing to ask a chart anyway.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

members.name: series
members.description: The columns of the table, one series each, or none if there is no table.

members.name: named
members.description:
What to call the drawing, the consumer's word or the table's own.

The fallback is the reason this is shared rather than copied: a caption is
already written, already the right words, and already the thing a reader
of the table sees. A chart that made the consumer say it twice would be
asking for the second one to drift.

members.name: sourceRows
members.description:
Every row of the table, with each cell's text as well as its number.

This is where a tooltip's content comes from, and it is deliberately not
`series`. A chart draws numbers; a reader resting a pointer on one wants
what the table says, which is `$128k` and not `128000`, and often wants
the column beside it that nothing plotted at all.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this paragraph.** It
is the source table's rows, and `rows` on a chart is a name a chart
wants for itself: `helix-heatmap` takes `rows="7"` to mean a calendar
week, and declaring that against a base class whose `rows` is a `Row[]`
getter is a type error at best. The same fault `MixinCollection` had,
where a slot counter called `rows` would have shared one field with a
consumer's data property. Name the member for what it holds rather than
for the shortest word available.

members.name: readings
members.description: How many readings there are, which is what the pointer maps onto.

members.name: rows
members.description:
How many rows the strip has.

`1` is a status strip and `7` is a calendar week, which are the two readings
this covers. Cells fill down the column and then across, which is what a
calendar heatmap does: a week is a column, so the strip reads left to right
in weeks and top to bottom in days.

members.name: thresholds
members.description:
Lower bounds for the tone buckets, in the order the tones are given.

`thresholds="1 3 6 9"` with `tones="1 2 3 4"` puts 1 and 2 in the ramp's
first step, 3 to 5 in the second, 6 to 8 in the third, and 9 upward in the
fourth. A value below the first bound gets no tone at all: an empty day in a
contribution graph is a day with nothing in it, and painting it as the
lowest bucket claims a reading that does not exist.

members.name: tones
members.description:
Tone per bucket, in the same order as `thresholds`.

A name, resolved as `--heatmap-tone-<name>` by whichever tier answers.
**`"1"` through `"5"` are a ramp and everything else is a category**, which
is the distinction a heatmap lives or dies on: magnitude has to be one hue
getting louder, because a reader compares two cells by weight and cannot
compare two hues at all. This shipped demonstrating the opposite,
`tones="surface info accent success primary"` for a commit count, and five
unrelated hues for five amounts is confetti with no order in it.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: Shown when the table has no readings in it.

members.name: visible
members.description:
How many cells are actually drawn.

**This is the number a summary has to agree with**, and the reason it is
published at all: a consumer's own summary is their markup and this element
cannot rewrite it, so the only honest arrangement is to hand over the count
and say when it changed.

**A plain getter, and the attribute is written in `updated`, because
`@property({ reflect: true })` on a getter with no setter reflects once and
then goes stale.** Lit reflects a property that is in `changedProperties`,
and nothing puts a derived getter there after the first update: the
attribute would be right on load and wrong from the first resize, which is
the exact failure the count exists to prevent, arriving through the
mechanism meant to prevent it.

members.name: width
members.description:
The width last measured, or nothing before the first measurement.

Undefined rather than zero, because the two mean different things and the
difference is a whole strip: unmeasured has to show everything, since a
first paint that shows one cell and then expands is a flicker on every load.

members.name: metrics
members.description:
The cell and gap the strip is drawing, in pixels, once it has been read.

**The arithmetic's inputs are a stylesheet's decisions, so the honest way to
learn them is to ask the stylesheet.** A cell's size is a length that only
the cascade can resolve: it may be a `rem` against a root font size, a
percentage of a container, or whatever a container query chose this frame.
Every one of those is invisible to a number typed into an attribute, and
each of `--heatmap-cell-width`, `--heatmap-cell-height` and `--heatmap-gap`
added one more way for the two to drift apart silently.

Reading it back is not styling and does not breach the tier: this asks what
was decided rather than deciding, which is the same direction as the facts
this component writes out as custom properties, run backwards.

members.name: hovered
members.description:
Which drawn cell the pointer is on, as an index into `drawn`, or -1 for
none.

members.name: points

type.text: Array<{ label: string; tone?: string | undefined; value: number }>

members.description:
Every reading in the table, oldest first, as the table is written.

**Not `readings`, which the mixin already has and which means a count.**
Two members of the same name meaning a number and an array is the kind of
collision that type-checks in one direction and reads wrong in both.

members.name: rowCount
members.description:
`rows` as a usable count, which is not always what the attribute says.

One place rather than two: the fit arithmetic and the grid template both
need it, and a `rows="0"` or a `rows="2.5"` that reached one of them and not
the other would draw a strip whose columns and whose capacity disagreed.

members.name: cellPx
members.description:
The cell width the arithmetic should plan around, in pixels.

The attribute wins where a consumer wrote one, because that is what writing
it is for; otherwise what the strip draws, and the declared default only
until the first measurement lands.

members.name: gapPx
members.description: The gap the arithmetic should plan around, on the same terms as `cellPx`.

members.name: room
members.description: How many cells the container has room for, as a whole number of columns.

members.name: measure
members.description:
Reads back the cell and the gap the strip resolved.

`gridAutoColumns` and `columnGap` rather than a cell's own box, and the
difference matters on the frame it matters: a cell exists only once some
have been drawn, and how many are drawn is what this is measuring *for*.
Asking the track instead breaks the circle, since a track is sized whether
or not anything sits in it. Neither property forces layout, so this stays a
style read on every update rather than a reflow.

Anything that does not parse to a positive number leaves the estimate alone:
`columnGap` computes to `normal` where no gap is set, and a track given a
keyword or a `repeat()` has no single width to report. A wrong number here
is worse than no number, because it is the one the count is published from.

members.name: drawn

type.text: Array<{ label: string; tone?: string | undefined; value: number }>

members.description:
The readings actually drawn, newest kept.

The tail rather than the head: a status strip that drops the newest days to
keep the oldest is answering a question nobody asked.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on the footer whether any of its three slots holds anything.

**The stylesheet used to ask, and could not.** It read
`[part="footer"]:not(:has(slot:has(*)))`, which is two faults at once:
`:has()` may not be nested inside `:has()`, so the selector failed to parse
and the rule was discarded whole; and a slot's assigned nodes are not its
DOM children, so `slot:has(*)` reports fallback content rather than the
fill, and would have been false either way. Both verified in a browser. A
heatmap with no legend and no summary still reserved the row for one.

members.name: markRegion
members.description:
One region, hidden when its slot holds nothing and nothing of ours fills it.

`hidden` beside the `data-empty` mirror: `data-empty` is the hook the styled
sheet reads, and this tier ships no sheet, so an empty region left in the box
tree would be a gap a headless consumer cannot close without knowing to look
for it. The styled rule stays too, because that sheet sets `display` on these
parts and therefore outranks the UA's `[hidden]` one.

members.name: renderTooltip
members.description:
The bubble over the cell a pointer is resting on.

**One tooltip that moves, which is what every other chart here does and is
the thing the `title` attribute was kept to avoid.** The note this replaces
read that ninety `helix-tooltip` elements was the cost of a real one, and
that was never the shape: Bar Chart, Line Chart and Donut Chart each render
a single anchor against an invisible mark and move the mark, so the count is
one however many readings there are. `drawTooltip` is their shared markup
and this is the fourth caller.

What it buys over the native one is the row rather than the reading.
`sourceRows` carries every column of the table including the ones nothing
was plotted from, so a cell reads "11 Jun 2026 / Uptime 81.2% / Note Partial
outage" where `title` could only ever say the two values this component
happens to hold. It is also styleable, appears at once rather than after the
platform's second of delay, and cannot be truncated by the window edge.

The mark is placed in pixels rather than in percent, which is the one thing
this does differently from its siblings: they divide a plot into equal
slots, and a strip's cells are a fixed size with a fixed gap inside a box
that is usually wider, so a percentage of the box lands between cells. The
pitch is `cell + gap` and both are measured.

members.name: onPointerOver
members.description:
Which drawn cell the pointer is over, or -1.

`pointerover` on the strip rather than a listener per cell: the event
bubbles, so one handler covers however many cells there are, and unlike
`mouseover` it is delivered for a pen and for the touch that follows a long
press.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: A strip of cells coloured by how each one went: uptime, contributions, activity.

examples.description: Thirty days of uptime, each cell coloured by how that day went.
Cells with nothing between them, for a reading that never stopped.
Ten weeks of commits, bucketed into five levels rather than a gradient.
A range with no readings in it, which is not the same as a range of empty ones.
A measurement, not a proposal: the grid says how many cells it can show.
Half hours of one day, drawn tall and narrow the way a status page draws them.
The same readings at three cell sizes, set with one custom property.

attributes.name: for
attributes.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

attributes.name: rows
attributes.description:
How many rows the strip has.

`1` is a status strip and `7` is a calendar week, which are the two readings
this covers. Cells fill down the column and then across, which is what a
calendar heatmap does: a week is a column, so the strip reads left to right
in weeks and top to bottom in days.

attributes.name: thresholds
attributes.description:
Lower bounds for the tone buckets, in the order the tones are given.

`thresholds="1 3 6 9"` with `tones="1 2 3 4"` puts 1 and 2 in the ramp's
first step, 3 to 5 in the second, 6 to 8 in the third, and 9 upward in the
fourth. A value below the first bound gets no tone at all: an empty day in a
contribution graph is a day with nothing in it, and painting it as the
lowest bucket claims a reading that does not exist.

attributes.name: tones
attributes.description:
Tone per bucket, in the same order as `thresholds`.

A name, resolved as `--heatmap-tone-<name>` by whichever tier answers.
**`"1"` through `"5"` are a ramp and everything else is a category**, which
is the distinction a heatmap lives or dies on: magnitude has to be one hue
getting louder, because a reader compares two cells by weight and cannot
compare two hues at all. This shipped demonstrating the opposite,
`tones="surface info accent success primary"` for a commit count, and five
unrelated hues for five amounts is confetti with no order in it.

attributes.name: min-cell
attributes.description:
The smallest a cell may get before the strip draws fewer of them, in CSS pixels.

**Set this only to overrule what the strip actually draws.** The arithmetic
needs a width in pixels and the width is a length the stylesheet resolves,
so for as long as this was the only answer it was a promise the consumer had
to keep by hand: it sat at 8 against a sheet drawing 12, the arithmetic
believed a cell cost 10 pixels where it cost 16, and a ninety day strip ran
940 pixels wide out of a 592 pixel box while `visible` reported 59. The one
number a summary is told to trust was the number that was wrong.

The strip is measured now, so `--heatmap-cell-width` and `--heatmap-gap` are
enough on their own and these two are the estimate used until the first
measurement lands. Writing the attribute pins the value and stops the
measurement being consulted, which is what a container query or a transition
on the cell size wants, where what is drawn this frame is not what the
arithmetic should plan around.

Zero turns the dropping off altogether, which is right for a strip in a
container that cannot get narrow.

attributes.name: gap
attributes.description:
Space between cells, in CSS pixels, for the same reason `min-cell` is a
number.

attributes.name: empty-text
attributes.description: Shown when the table has no readings in it.

events.description: Fired when the number of cells drawn changes, carrying that number.
events.name: helix-resize

declarations.description:
Top-level rather than `Button.Icon`, because a namespace means composition:
`Card.Header` is part of a card, and an icon-only button is not part of a
button. It is a button with different content and a different shape, which
makes it its own component.

`label` is not optional in practice. An icon-only control with no accessible
name is announced as "button" and nothing else, which is the single most
common way a toolbar becomes unusable without sight.
declarations.name: HelixIconButton

cssProperties.description: Corner radius of the control, which a group flattens through `--button-radii-start` and `--button-radii-end`.
cssProperties.name: --icon-button-radii

cssProperties.description: What it casts, where it is raised off the page.
cssProperties.name: --icon-button-shadow

cssProperties.description: Edge length of the control.
cssProperties.name: --icon-button-size

cssParts.description: The inner button or anchor.
cssParts.name: button

slots.description: The icon.
Content after the label.
slots.name: end

slots.description: Content before the label, usually an icon.
slots.name: start

members.name: shape
members.description:
The outline it is cut to, which is an axis of its own and not a value on one.

`emphasis` says how filled it is and `tone` says what it means; neither of
them says what shape it is, and folding a shape into either would put a
control's outline in the same word as its color. A rounded square is the
resting one because that is what a control in a row of controls should be.

`circle` is the floating action button, and it is the reason this exists: a
round, raised, primary control holding the one action a screen is for. It is
a shape rather than a component, because a component would re-declare
`emphasis`, `tone`, `label` and the size around a control that already has
them, and because the same shape is wanted by an avatar's overlay, a media
control and a map's own buttons. Where it sits is the page's business: see
`data-dock` in the base layer.

members.name: raised
members.description:
Whether it is raised off the page it sits on.

Separate from `shape`, because they are separate facts: a docked control is
raised whatever its outline, and a circle inside a toolbar is not raised at
all. Shadow rather than a border, since what is under a floating control is
the page and a line drawn on the page is not the same as being above it.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How filled it is drawn.

**This was `appearance`, and the docstring above it always said what it
really was.** "How filled it is drawn", sitting beside `tone`, "What it
means": the axis was named correctly in prose and filed under the word
four axes shared. A Card's `outlined` says where a surface ends and this
one says how much ink a control claims, and one word cannot keep saying
both. `check:axes` holds the vocabulary now.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it, and undefaulted because
it reflects: a reflected property with a default writes its attribute
onto every host anybody renders. The resting treatment is the attribute's
absence, which each control names for itself, `outlined` on `Button` and
`ghost` on `IconButton`.

members.name: tone
members.description:
What it means.

Three and an accent, not the full status set. A tag reports a state and a
button performs an action: a success button and a warning button are not
things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page where the color
of a control means nothing in particular. `accent` is the second
emphasis, a rotation off the brand seed rather than a color of its own,
so it stays in relation when somebody rethemes.

members.name: type
members.description: What activating the button does to its form.

members.name: value
members.description:
What this button submits under its own `name`, the way a native submitter does.

**Reported for exactly the submission this button starts and not otherwise.**
A native submit button contributes `name=value` only when it is the one
that submitted, and every other button on the form contributes nothing. A
form-associated element reporting a value continuously would contribute on
every submission whoever started it, which is a different feature wearing
the same name, so `submit` below sets it, submits, and clears it inside one
synchronous call.

`CopyButton` has a `value` of its own meaning the text to put on the
clipboard, which is not this and is why it is declared there rather than
inherited.

members.name: formAction
members.description:
Where this button's submission goes, overriding the form's own.

**The five `form*` overrides work by writing the form and putting it back**,
which is the only mechanism available and is closer to the platform than it
sounds. `requestSubmit(submitter)` is how a native submitter carries these,
and it refuses ours twice over: the inner `<button>` is `type="button"` so
it is not a submit button, and it sits in this shadow root so its form owner
is not the consumer's form. Both throw. So the submission is started with no
submitter and the overrides are applied to the form for the duration of it.

The whole submit algorithm runs synchronously inside `requestSubmit()`, so
the window is one call and a `finally` closes it whether or not a listener
refused. What a `submit` handler observes during that window is the form a
native submitter would have given it, which is the point.

members.name: formEnctype
members.description: How the submission is encoded, overriding the form's own.

members.name: formMethod
members.description: Which HTTP method the submission uses, overriding the form's own.

members.name: formNoValidate
members.description: Whether this submission skips the form's validation.

members.name: formTarget
members.description: Which browsing context the response lands in, overriding the form's own.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

members.name: command
members.description:
What to send when the button is activated, and what to send it to.

The platform's invoker attributes, forwarded onto the inner `<button>`
rather than left on the host: only a real button is recognized as an
invoker, so `commandfor` written on a custom element resolves nothing and
the trigger silently does nothing at all. A wrapper has to hand them down,
the same way `label` becomes `aria-label` in there.

```html
<helix-button commandfor="confirm" command="--show">Delete…</helix-button>
```

`commandFor` spells its attribute out, because Lit lowercases a property
name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

members.name: commandFor
members.description: The id of the element the command is sent to.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Moves focus to the inner control, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: focusable
members.description:
Whether the button holds its group's tab stop.

A toolbar keeps one tab stop across its children, and the obvious way to do
that is to write `tabindex` onto each of them. That is a change to markup
the consumer rendered, so a React consumer's hydration reports it and does
not patch it up. A parent sets this property instead, which writes nothing,
and the stop lands on the inner control inside the shadow root.

No attribute, because it is coordination between elements rather than
anything a consumer sets.

members.name: expanded
members.description:
Whether this button is a disclosure trigger, and whether its panel is open.

**Set by whatever owns the panel, and a property rather than an attribute
for the reason `Menu` already states about its items**: an attribute
written onto a consumer's element after it upgrades is a hydration mismatch
waiting to happen. Measured 28 Aug 2026 against React 19.2.8, server markup
hydrated with the definitions loaded either side of `hydrateRoot`:
`Megamenu` and `SpeedDial` wrote `aria-expanded` onto the slotted trigger
and React reported "some attributes of the server rendered HTML didn't
match the client properties. This won't be patched up" in both orders;
`Popover` and `Menu`, which write nothing, were clean in both.

**A property crosses that gap because React never looks at one.** It diffs
the attributes it rendered, and this one is `attribute: false`, so the state
travels to the inner `<button>` and lands inside a shadow root React does
not own and cannot compare. The consumer's own element is left exactly as
they served it, which is what `Popover`'s note asks for, and the reader is
still told what the control does, which is what `SpeedDial`'s note asks
for. See #322.

`undefined` renders nothing at all, so a button that is not a trigger
carries no `aria-expanded`: the resting state is the attribute's absence,
which is the rule every reflected property here follows.

A consumer who wants to say this statically writes `aria-expanded` on the
host instead, which `AriaForwardController` carries to the same place.

members.name: submit
members.description:
Submits the form as this button, for the length of one call.

Everything a native submitter carries is written onto the form, the
submission is started, and everything is put back. See `formAction` for why
`requestSubmit(submitter)` is not available to a control inside a shadow
root.

`novalidate` is in the same list rather than reached by `form.submit()`,
which looks like the shortcut and is not: `submit()` skips the `submit`
event as well as the validation, so a consumer's handler would stop running
the moment somebody wrote `formnovalidate`. Turning the flag on and calling
`requestSubmit()` skips the validation alone, which is what the attribute
means.

members.name: commandForElement
members.description:
The element this button's command is sent to, resolved.

The platform's own accessor, and this element had the resolution and kept
it to itself: `linkCommand` writes the target onto the inner `<button>`,
where a consumer cannot reach it, and `commandFor` answers with an id
rather than an element. Writing assigns the inner control directly, which
is what an invoker without an id in the same tree needs.

members.name: linkCommand
members.description:
Points the inner button at the command's target, by reference.

**The attribute cannot do this and it fails silently.** `commandfor` is an
IDREF, and an IDREF resolves inside the tree it is written in: forwarded
onto a button in this shadow root it looks for the id *here*, finds
nothing, and the trigger does nothing at all. Measured before this existed:
the button clicked, no `command` event was dispatched, and there was
nothing anywhere to say why.

`commandForElement` takes an element instead, and an element reference
resolves outward: a node in a shadow root may point at one in the document.

members.name: commandTarget
members.description:

inside somebody else's shadow root finds a target in that same root and not

members.name: sendCommand
members.description:
Sends the `command` event where the browser will not.

Invoker commands are recent, and where they are missing `linkCommand` set a
property that does not exist and returned, so the button did nothing at all
when clicked. Silently: the markup was right, the component was right, and
every `command` in the library was inert at once with no error to find. A
design system cannot ship an example that depends on a feature failing that
quietly.

exactly one event and this sends none. Doing both would open a dialog and
immediately toggle it shut again, which is a worse bug than the one this
fixes and would only appear on the browsers that work.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that

source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per

members.name: internals
members.description:

attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:

bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the

itself before React reached the node.

other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:

an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: shape
attributes.description:
The outline it is cut to, which is an axis of its own and not a value on one.

`emphasis` says how filled it is and `tone` says what it means; neither of
them says what shape it is, and folding a shape into either would put a
control's outline in the same word as its color. A rounded square is the
resting one because that is what a control in a row of controls should be.

`circle` is the floating action button, and it is the reason this exists: a
round, raised, primary control holding the one action a screen is for. It is
a shape rather than a component, because a component would re-declare
`emphasis`, `tone`, `label` and the size around a control that already has
them, and because the same shape is wanted by an avatar's overlay, a media
control and a map's own buttons. Where it sits is the page's business: see
`data-dock` in the base layer.

attributes.name: raised
attributes.description:
Whether it is raised off the page it sits on.

Separate from `shape`, because they are separate facts: a docked control is
raised whatever its outline, and a circle inside a toolbar is not raised at
all. Shadow rather than a border, since what is under a floating control is
the page and a line drawn on the page is not the same as being above it.

attributes.name: emphasis
attributes.description:
How filled it is drawn.

**This was `appearance`, and the docstring above it always said what it
really was.** "How filled it is drawn", sitting beside `tone`, "What it
means": the axis was named correctly in prose and filed under the word
four axes shared. A Card's `outlined` says where a surface ends and this
one says how much ink a control claims, and one word cannot keep saying
both. `check:axes` holds the vocabulary now.

Reflected because the stylesheet selects on it, and undefaulted because
it reflects: a reflected property with a default writes its attribute
onto every host anybody renders. The resting treatment is the attribute's
absence, which each control names for itself, `outlined` on `Button` and
`ghost` on `IconButton`.

attributes.name: tone
attributes.description:
What it means.

Three and an accent, not the full status set. A tag reports a state and a
button performs an action: a success button and a warning button are not
things anybody writes, and offering them invites a page where the color
of a control means nothing in particular. `accent` is the second
emphasis, a rotation off the brand seed rather than a color of its own,
so it stays in relation when somebody rethemes.

attributes.name: type
attributes.description: What activating the button does to its form.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What this button submits under its own `name`, the way a native submitter does.

**Reported for exactly the submission this button starts and not otherwise.**
A native submit button contributes `name=value` only when it is the one
that submitted, and every other button on the form contributes nothing. A
form-associated element reporting a value continuously would contribute on
every submission whoever started it, which is a different feature wearing
the same name, so `submit` below sets it, submits, and clears it inside one
synchronous call.

`CopyButton` has a `value` of its own meaning the text to put on the
clipboard, which is not this and is why it is declared there rather than
inherited.

attributes.name: formaction
attributes.description:
Where this button's submission goes, overriding the form's own.

**The five `form*` overrides work by writing the form and putting it back**,
which is the only mechanism available and is closer to the platform than it
sounds. `requestSubmit(submitter)` is how a native submitter carries these,
and it refuses ours twice over: the inner `<button>` is `type="button"` so
it is not a submit button, and it sits in this shadow root so its form owner
is not the consumer's form. Both throw. So the submission is started with no
submitter and the overrides are applied to the form for the duration of it.

The whole submit algorithm runs synchronously inside `requestSubmit()`, so
the window is one call and a `finally` closes it whether or not a listener
refused. What a `submit` handler observes during that window is the form a
native submitter would have given it, which is the point.

attributes.name: formenctype
attributes.description: How the submission is encoded, overriding the form's own.

attributes.name: formmethod
attributes.description: Which HTTP method the submission uses, overriding the form's own.

attributes.name: formnovalidate
attributes.description: Whether this submission skips the form's validation.

attributes.name: formtarget
attributes.description: Which browsing context the response lands in, overriding the form's own.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
Accessible name, for a button whose content is not text.

Lives here rather than only on `IconButton` so the two share one render.
An icon-only button without it is a control a screen reader announces as
"button" and nothing else.

attributes.description:


name to derive one rather than dash-casing it, and what a consumer writes
is the platform's `commandfor`.

`lazy` by default, which is the opposite of the platform's, because a
picture worth putting in a component is usually below the fold and the one
that is not is the exception worth writing down.

members.name: srcset
members.description: The candidate widths, passed through to the picture.

members.name: sizes
members.description: How much of the line it will take, passed through to the picture.

members.name: fetchPriority
members.description:
How urgently to fetch it, for the one picture that is the page.

The hero of a page is usually its largest contentful paint, and the fix is
two attributes rather than one: `loading="eager"` stops it waiting for the
viewport, and this stops it queueing behind everything else the parser
found first. Left alone the browser decides, which is right for the other
ninety-nine pictures.

members.name: decoding
members.description:
Whether the browser may decode off the main thread.

**The template hardcoded `async` and a consumer could not reach it**, which
is worse than the property being absent: the decision was taken on their
behalf and nothing said so. `async` is still the resting value and still
right for a picture in a page, and `sync` is what a consumer reaches for
when the picture is about to be composited with something else and a tear
would show.

members.name: crossOrigin
members.description:
How the picture is fetched across origins, which decides whether a canvas
can read it.

members.name: referrerPolicy
members.description: How much of the referring URL to send with the request.

members.name: status
members.description:
Whether the picture is on its way, here, or never coming.

Read-only to a consumer: it is a report rather than a setting.

**Mirrored to `data-status`, and not reflected as `status`.** It is element
state, so reflecting it puts the element's own bookkeeping into the markup
a consumer rendered: React reads the attribute appearing at upgrade as a
hydration mismatch, and a serialized `<helix-image status="loaded">` pasted
back declares that a picture has arrived which this element has never
fetched. The `data-` name is the library's answer to both, being a
different name a re-parse cannot mistake for a declaration, and it is what
`data-closed` on `Toast.Item` already does, and `AppHeader` did until its
own moved to `:state(scrolled)` for the hydration reason recorded there.
A picture arrives after somebody fetched it, which puts this on the safe
side of hydration: a fact that can be true on the *first* update mirrors to
a custom state instead, which is what `:state(open)` and `:state(checked)`
became on 27 Aug 2026 for exactly that reason.

`loading` writes nothing, because it is where every image starts and the
resting state of a mirror is the attribute's absence.

members.name: answered
members.description: Which `src` the current status belongs to, so a new one starts over.

members.name: announce
members.description: Says so under the platform's own name, because the platform's cannot escape. `load` and `error` on an `` neither bubble nor compose, so the ones fired inside this shadow root reach nobody outside it. A consumer had a reflected attribute and a `MutationObserver` and nothing else. Re-emitting from the host is what `relayNativeEvent` is for, and it is what `Avatar` already did for the same pair on the same element. **These were `helix-load` and `helix-error`, and the rename is the fix.** The argument for a prefix is a collision with a native name, and there was none to collide with here: the native events cannot reach a consumer at all. So the prefix bought nothing and cost the two spellings this library had for one idea, `Avatar` relaying `load` while `Image` invented one. See 294 and 295. **Not bubbling, and that is not a small point.** The retired events were `bubbles: true, composed: true` deliberately, so a gallery could count its pictures with one listener. A bubbling relay of `load` reaches nothing in React: `load` is in react-dom's `nonDelegatedEvents`, so there is no root listener to catch it, and React attaches a direct one for `` and never for a custom element. `bindReactHandler` binds exactly the non-bubbling ones, so matching the native propagation is what makes `onLoad` work at all. A gallery does here what it already does for ``, which is listen in the capture phase or listen per picture.

members.name: settle
members.description:
Catches the picture that was already there.

A cached image can finish loading before this element has a listener on it,
and then `load` never fires and the placeholder stays up over a picture that
is sitting right behind it. `complete` is the platform's own answer to that
question, and `naturalWidth` separates a decoded picture from one that
carries no pixels, which `complete` reports as finished either way.

**It can only ever conclude success.** A picture that has not been attempted
looks exactly like one that failed: `complete` is true and `naturalWidth` is
zero for both, and a DOM that never fetches anything reports that for every
image it has. Deciding `error` here called every picture broken the moment
it rendered. Failure has an event of its own and that event is reliable, so
this is only here to catch the success that happened too early to hear.

members.name: image
members.description: The picture's own state, under the platform's own names. The `` is inside this shadow root, so a consumer asking how big the picture turned out to be, or whether it is already there, had nowhere to ask: `querySelector` does not cross a shadow boundary. `status` answers a narrower question and answers it in this library's words, which is the right report for the three states this element draws and is not a substitute for the numbers. `naturalWidth` and `naturalHeight` are the case worth having: they are how a consumer sizes a lightbox or works out an aspect ratio, and they exist nowhere else on the page.

members.name: complete
members.description: Whether the picture has finished arriving, however it went.

members.name: currentSrc
members.description: Which candidate the browser actually chose out of `srcset`.

members.name: naturalHeight
members.description: The picture's own height in pixels, and zero until it has arrived.

members.name: naturalWidth
members.description: The picture's own width in pixels, and zero until it has arrived.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: rounded
attributes.description:
Whether the corners are cut.

A boolean rather than a radius, because the radius is a token and the
question a consumer is answering is whether this picture is a card's
surface or a page's. `--image-radius` moves it for the case that is
neither.

Empty is a real answer and means decoration. Omitting the attribute is not

declarations.description:
The frame is the field rather than the input, so anything slotted at either
end sits inside the same box as the text and the focus ring is drawn once,
around the whole control, instead of around a smaller box within it.

The input itself is the native one, stripped rather than replaced, so the
caret, the selection, the autofill, and the keyboard a phone chooses are all

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

helix-input

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description:
Whether a reader edits this continuously, which decides the native name.

**It used to pick between `helix-input` and `helix-change`**, which was
one mechanism under two names and said *phase* where it meant
*granularity*. The request event is `helix-before-change` whatever the
answer; this decides which native event announces the result, `input`
while a reader is editing against `change` when they are done, which is
the distinction the platform already draws. See 294.

Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says
otherwise.

members.name: announceNatively
members.description:
Announces the applied value under the platform's own name.

**After `apply`, never before**, which is the whole reason this is
separate from the request event: a native handler reads
`event.target.value`, and it has to be the value that was just applied.

**Both, for a discrete control, because that is what the platform does.**
A native `<select>` sends `input` and then `change` from one choice: the
value moved, and the reader is also done. A continuous control announces
`input` here and relays `change` from its inner control when the reader
is done, so the pair keeps the platform's timings rather than reporting a
commit on every keystroke.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the control updates
itself, whether or not a consumer declared `value`: a declared property
is a seed and a correction, the way `<input value>` is, and a consumer
who wants the change for themselves refuses it and assigns their own.
See 294.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: autocomplete
members.description:
What the browser may autofill here, as one of the platform's own tokens.

Empty leaves the attribute off, which is the browser's default. Set it to
a token like `email` or `bday` to ask for autofill, or to `off` to refuse.

members.name: placeholder
members.description:
Shown while the field is empty.

Not a label: it goes when typing starts.

members.name: readOnly
members.description:
Whether the field refuses input while still submitting its value.

**`readonly`, which is the platform's spelling, and it was `read-only`
until 28 Aug 2026.** A camelCase property needs an explicit `attribute`
and the library had been answering that question two ways: thirteen
attributes kept the name HTML uses (`crossorigin`, `maxlength`,
`formnovalidate`, `dirname` and the rest) and five dash-cased a word the
platform writes as one. `readonly` was the only one on both lists, this
spelling on `Rating` and `read-only` on the eight other fields, so one
library shipped both and each was inert on the other's families.

The cost of the dash-cased form is the one this repository keeps writing
down about attributes: nothing warns. `<helix-input readonly>` is what
anybody who has written HTML types, it parsed to no property at all, and
the field stayed editable with no error anywhere. Measured before the
rename: `readOnly` came back `false`.

Taken now for the reason [#213](../../../../../docs/19-queue.md) gives
about the part it renamed for the same kind of reason: there is no
`helix-v` tag, so no consumer is holding the old spelling, and this is free
today and a deprecation after the first release.
`check:attribute-names` holds it from here.

members.name: type
members.description:
What the field accepts, which decides the keyboard and the validation.

**Not reflected**, and it was. Reflection exists so a selector can reach a
value, and no stylesheet in this repository selects on `type`: what it did
instead was write `type="text"` onto every `<helix-input>` ever rendered,
an attribute no consumer's markup had. That is precisely the fault `Button`
had with `href`, `target` and `rel`, written up in the area rules as the
reason the rule exists, and this was the last property in the library still
doing it. Audited: ten reflected attributes have no selector anywhere, and
this is the only one of them with a value that puts itself on the host.

Nothing reads it from the attribute either. The real `<input>` inside takes
it as a property binding, which is what makes the keyboard and the
validation follow.

members.name: clearable
members.description:
Whether the field offers a button that empties it.

Shown only while there is something to clear, because a control that does
nothing is worse than no control: a reader who presses it and sees no
change has to work out whether the field was already empty or the button
is broken.

members.name: clearLabel

members.name: revealed

members.name: effectiveType
members.description:

members.name: shadowRootOptions

members.name: selectionDirection
members.description:

members.name: selectionEnd
members.description: Where the selection ends, as an offset into the value.

members.name: selectionStart
members.description: Where the selection starts, as an offset into the value.

members.name: setSelectionRange
members.description:

members.name: handleInput
members.description:

consumer that refuses the change has to see the field returned to what the
element still holds. Otherwise the text on screen and the value the form
would submit disagree, which is the one thing a controlled field must never
do.

members.name: handleClear
members.description:

about to disappear: a reader who cleared a field is going to type in it,
and focus resting on a control that is being removed lands on the body.

Through `requestValue` like every other change, so a consumer who owns the
value hears about it and decides, and a canceled clear leaves the text
where it was.

members.name: handleChange
members.description: Relayed, because `change` does not cross a shadow boundary on its own.

members.name: sync

members.name: select

members.name: releaseCaret
members.description:

members.name: pattern
members.description:

were set on the real input, and no such properties existed: a consumer
following that sentence wrote an attribute on the host, it reached no input,
and the field constrained nothing while looking as though it did.

members.description: Fewest characters the value may have.

members.name: maxLength
members.description: Most characters the value may have.

members.name: formAssociated
