members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: placement
members.description:
Where the legend sits and which way its entries run.

Absent is a wrapping row, which is what sits under a chart. `start` and
`end` stack the entries in a column, for a legend beside one.

**This says which way the entries run and not where the element is**, which
is the honest limit of a component that is a sibling of the chart rather
than part of it. A legend cannot place itself relative to something it is
not inside, so the consumer still puts it above, below or beside; this
makes it lay out correctly once it is there, which was the part that
previously took a custom property nobody would guess at.

The alternative was a `legend` slot on every chart, so a chart could place
its own. That is worse: it makes the legend's position a fact about the
chart, so two charts sharing one legend becomes impossible, and it puts a
list inside a drawing that is `aria-hidden`.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How much ink the swatches claim.

**The same axis as the chart's, with the same values, because a legend that
does not match its chart is worse than no legend.** A key whose swatches are
solid while the columns they key are outlined tells a reader the two are
different kinds of fact, which is the exact thing `outlined` on a chart
exists to say. `outlined` is the series color as an edge over a fill faded
toward the page, `subtle` is that edge over a wash, and absent is the filled
patch, per the rule that a reflected property takes no default.

**The legend declares it rather than reading it off the chart, and that is a
decision rather than a shortcut.** A legend has no reference to a chart: it
points at a *table* through `for`, which is what lets two charts share one,
and the chart points at the same table independently. Giving it a chart to
read would make a list of names depend on a drawing it is deliberately not
part of, and would still not answer the per-series case, where `outlined` is
a set of names rather than one value. Two attributes carrying the same word
is the honest cost of the legend being a sibling.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the swatches are made of.

`glass` thins whatever emphasis drew, the way it does on a column, so a
legend beside a glass chart is in the same substance as the chart. Scaled by
`--helix-material-opacity`, so a theme that is more see-through everywhere is
more see-through here.

**This paints a mark rather than a ground, and the axis still reads the
same way.** On a surface the points are how much of the page shows through;
on a series they are how much ink the mark has, and the order is the same:
`glass` admits most, `frosted` admits less, absent is opaque. The two
factors, 0.62 and 0.88, carry the relationship the surface tokens carry
between `material-translucent` and `material-translucent-strong`, so a
chart and a card mean the same thing by the word.

**`transparent` is where this one stops.** A mark with no ink is not a
material choice, it is an absent series, and a chart says that by not
having the datum rather than by painting it invisibly. See 270.

members.name: outlined
members.description:
Which entries are drawn as an outline rather than a fill, by name.

Space or comma separated and matched against the names this legend is
showing, which are the same names the chart matches its own `outlined`
against, since both read one table. So a chart and its key say the same
thing the same way: `outlined="Forecast"` on both.

members.name: subtle
members.description:
Which entries are drawn as a wash of their color, by name.

Matched as `outlined` is.

members.name: glass
members.description:
Which entries are glass rather than solid, by name.

Matched as `outlined` is.

members.name: entries
members.description:
Which way to read the table.

Absent is `series`, one entry per data column. `categories` reads one entry
per body row instead, for a donut, whose slices are the rows.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the table to take the names from.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a legend inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: names
members.description:
The names, in the order the chart will draw them.

`protected` rather than private because the styled tier has to match a
per-series treatment against them, the way `BarChart` matches `outlined` and
`subtle` against the headings its table gives. A legend keys a chart, so the
two answer the same question about the same series, and the tier that paints
cannot do that without knowing which entry is which.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: tier
members.description:
**The styled tier, so the tooltip this renders is the styled one.**

`tag()` builds a child's tag name from this prefix, and the base declares
`helix-headless-`. Every other styled component that renders a child
overrides it; the three charts that draw a tooltip did not, so a
`helix-bar-chart` on a page put a `helix-headless-tooltip` in its shadow
root: the behavior with none of the surface. What showed was the browser's
own popover defaults, a white 1.5px border, square corners, `0.25em` of
padding and the page's font size, which is why the reading bubble looked
like no other tooltip on the site.

Measured before the fix: the chart's bubble computed
`border: 1.5px solid rgb(255, 255, 255)`, `border-radius: 0px`,
`padding: 3.5px`, `font-size: 14px`. The masthead's, a `helix-tooltip`,
had the component's own `none`, `radii-sm`, `2xs xs` and `text-xs`.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How much ink the lines claim.

`subtle` mixes each series toward the page, so a chart that is context stays
legible without competing. Toward the page rather than translucent, because a
translucent line takes its color from whatever it crosses, which on a chart
with several is the whole risk.

`outlined` thins the wash and leaves the line at full weight, so the boundary
carries the reading, which is the trade `BarChart` makes on a column. `solid`
takes the wash to full strength and the fill carries it instead.

**This refused `outlined` until 25 Aug 2026, and `area` was the reason
given**: on a column `outlined` is the edge without the loud fill, the line
chart's version of that is the line without its wash, and `area` already says
exactly that. `area` is unchanged and still says it. What the argument
conflated is existence with weight: `area` decides whether a wash is drawn,
which is structural and belongs to the tier below, and emphasis decides which
of the two marks is carrying the reading. Both ends need a wash present and
neither can summon one.

`ghost` would be a chart with no lines.

members.name: material
members.description:
What the lines are made of.

`glass` lets the gridlines read through them, which is what translucency is
for on a chart rather than decoration.

On the lines and not the wash: the wash is already scaled by
`--helix-material-opacity` whatever this says, being a wash by nature, and
scaling it twice would compound the policy against itself.

**This paints a mark rather than a ground, and the axis still reads the
same way.** On a surface the points are how much of the page shows through;
on a series they are how much ink the mark has, and the order is the same:
`glass` admits most, `frosted` admits less, absent is opaque. The two
factors, 0.62 and 0.88, carry the relationship the surface tokens carry
between `material-translucent` and `material-translucent-strong`, so a
chart and a card mean the same thing by the word.

**`transparent` is where this one stops.** A mark with no ink is not a
material choice, it is an absent series, and a chart says that by not
having the datum rather than by painting it invisibly. See 270.

members.name: source
members.description: Resolves `for` and re-renders when the table behind it changes.

members.name: pointer
members.description:
Which reading a pointer is nearest, for a tooltip to sit on.

Public for the same reason `series` and `named` are: a protected member
cannot be cast onto across unrelated classes, so it would be invisible to
every chart that needs it. Reading where a pointer is resting is a fair
thing to ask a chart anyway.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the table to read.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a chart inside another component's
shadow root names a table in that root rather than in the document. A
`<table>` or anything built from grid roles, including `helix-table`.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
The drawing's name, for a pointer resting on it.

Absent falls back to the table's own caption, which is usually the right
words and is already written.

members.name: series
members.description: The columns of the table, one series each, or none if there is no table.

members.name: named
members.description:
What to call the drawing, the consumer's word or the table's own.

The fallback is the reason this is shared rather than copied: a caption is
already written, already the right words, and already the thing a reader
of the table sees. A chart that made the consumer say it twice would be
asking for the second one to drift.

members.name: sourceRows
members.description:
Every row of the table, with each cell's text as well as its number.

This is where a tooltip's content comes from, and it is deliberately not
`series`. A chart draws numbers; a reader resting a pointer on one wants
what the table says, which is `$128k` and not `128000`, and often wants
the column beside it that nothing plotted at all.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this paragraph.** It
is the source table's rows, and `rows` on a chart is a name a chart
wants for itself: `helix-heatmap` takes `rows="7"` to mean a calendar
week, and declaring that against a base class whose `rows` is a `Row[]`
getter is a type error at best. The same fault `MixinCollection` had,
where a slot counter called `rows` would have shared one field with a
consumer's data property. Name the member for what it holds rather than
for the shortest word available.

members.name: readings
members.description: How many readings there are, which is what the pointer maps onto.

members.name: area
members.description:

ground it should feel like a quantity against is the case for this.

bounded. The interpolation is monotone cubic, so it never leaves the band

have, and within that bound the smoothed line is the easier one to follow

reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto every host
anybody renders, including the ones nobody configured.

consumer wrote, and caught that the first time. The default therefore lives
where the path is built, as `curve ?? 'smooth'`.

than to where the data starts, so two charts over different ranges rule at
the same levels. `category` rules the axis they are *arranged* on, one
through each reading, which is what lets a point be traced down to its
label across a wide chart. `both` draws both.

Written out, the attribute a consumer reaches for first should be the grid
they meant, and a typo should fall back to the useful half rather than to

indistinguishable from the attribute being absent, which is the one thing
a reader cannot debug.

and reach no reader through the table.

members.name: rulesValue
members.description: Whether the levels are ruled, which is every value but `category`.

members.name: rulesCategory
members.description: Whether each reading is ruled, which only two values ask for.

members.name: zero
members.description:
Whether zero is forced into the range.

Absent measures from the data's own extent, which is what a line is for.
Set it where the distance from nothing is the point rather than the shape,
and accept that a series which never approaches zero becomes a flat rule
near the top of the box.

members.name: range
members.description: The domain every series is drawn against, which the tooltip also needs.

members.name: terminus
members.description:
The shape of the mark on each series' last reading.

Absent is a dot, and absent rather than defaulted because a reflecting
property with a default writes its attribute onto a host the consumer
rendered, which React reports as a hydration mismatch.

shares an x-axis and therefore ends at the same reading. That column is the
useful thing: it is where a reader looks for "and what is it now", which is
the question a sparkline's single mark answers too.

shape rather than for where it finished. The shapes come from

the set is identical wherever one appears.

line ends at the reading, which is the hole's center, so the `<svg>` is
masked with one disc per series and every stroke stops at its own ring's

layers; a single `mask-image` would only ever cut the last one.

members.name: ends

type.text: Array<{ index: number; x: number; y: number }>

members.description:
Where each series ends, as percentages of the drawing's own box.

Percentages rather than user units, for the reason the mark is a `<span>`
rather than a `<circle>`: `preserveAspectRatio="none"` stretches the
coordinate space, so a length in there means two different things depending
on how wide the consumer made the chart. The host's box stretches nothing.

members.name: renderPlot
members.description:
The lines themselves, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

`aria-hidden`, because the table it was read from is the readable version
and a screen reader hearing both hears the same numbers twice.

members.name: renderGridlines
members.description:
The grid, behind everything, or nothing at all.

Drawn first so a series is never cut by a rule, and before the baseline so
that where the two coincide the baseline wins: zero is a fact about the
data and a gridline is a ruler, and the reader should see the fact.

members.name: renderBand
members.description:
The slot the pointer is resting in, drawn behind the drawing.

A band and not a second rule. The guide says exactly where the reading is
and the band says which share of the width belongs to it, which is what a
reader is actually pointing at: the catchment is a slot wide, so a pointer
a few pixels off the line is still asking about that reading, and without
the band nothing on screen says so.

The same slot arithmetic the pointer controller resolves with, so the lit
region and the region that answers are the same region by construction
rather than by two files agreeing.

members.name: renderGuide
members.description:
A rule down the reading the tooltip is about.

Without it the tooltip is a box of numbers floating over a drawing, and a
reader has to match its heading against the row of names to find out which
column it means. The rule is the whole of what connects the two, and it
matters most on a line, where there is no marker under the pointer to
stand in for one.

Drawn before the series so a line is never cut by it.

members.name: renderTermini

type.text: Array<{ index: number; x: number; y: number }>

members.description:
The marks, as elements beside the drawing rather than shapes inside it.

A seam of its own, so a tier or a consumer's subclass can draw them
differently without reimplementing the plot.

members.name: renderSeries
members.description: One series, its wash first so the line is drawn over its own fill.

members.name: renderLabels
members.description:
The reading names, as HTML beside the drawing rather than inside it.

Inside, they would scale with the box, for the reason the class doc gives.

members.name: renderTooltip
members.description:
What a pointer resting on a reading shows.

A seam over `drawTooltip`, which holds the markup every chart shares. The
usual reason to override is arrangement: every cell of the row is already
there, including the columns nothing was plotted from.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: emphasis
attributes.description:

legible without competing. Toward the page rather than translucent, because a
translucent line takes its color from whatever it crosses, which on a chart
with several is the whole risk.

`outlined` thins the wash and leaves the line at full weight, so the boundary
carries the reading, which is the trade `BarChart` makes on a column. `solid`
takes the wash to full strength and the fill carries it instead.

given**: on a column `outlined` is the edge without the loud fill, the line

conflated is existence with weight: `area` decides whether a wash is drawn,

members.name: renderRail
members.description:
The rail cell, which this tier can afford because it has a sheet.

An element rather than `[part="row"]::before`, which could hold the same
counter. Generated content can only ever be a string, and this cell is the
one place a row's ordinal lives, so a consumer replacing it with a state
mark or a step glyph wants somewhere to put it. It is also a name: a part is
in `custom-elements.json` and a pseudo-element on another part is not, and a
hook nobody can find is a hook nobody uses.

Always rendered, because a row cannot know whether its list asked for a
rail, and drawn `display: none` until the list says so. *Absent* and not
*empty*: an empty box is free to layout and is not free to the native
marker, which aligns to the first line box it can see. Measured against the
same tree without it, every row and label sat on the identical pixel and 178
pixels of the markers on a plain ordered list moved, which is a retaken
baseline for a feature that list is not using.

members.name: href
members.description:
Where the row goes, and nothing when it goes nowhere.

Empty rather than optional, and unset by default: a list is not always a
list of links, and an empty `href` written onto every row would be a link
to the current page on every row a consumer never asked to be one.

members.name: target
members.description: Where the link opens, for the rare row that leaves the site.

members.name: rel
members.description:
What the link declares about where it goes. The consumer's decision rather
than one derived from `target`, for the reason `Tree.Item` gives.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: divided
members.description: Whether a rule sits between rows.

members.name: marker
members.description:
Where the marker sits.

On the styled tier because it is decoration, which is the other half of the
argument `kind` makes on the headless one: *that* a list is numbered is a
fact about the content, and *where the numbers are drawn* is not. A railed
ordered list and a plain one say the same thing about their rows.

- unset draws the platform's marker beside the row, which is what a list of
  short rows wants.
- `rail` draws the ordinal in a track of its own at the start edge of the
  block, so the numbers read as a column and every row's text begins at one
  measure. This is how a numbered argument is set: a claim per item, prose
  under it, and the numbering carried down the left rather than tucked
  against the words.

A rail replaces the marker rather than joining it, so it applies to
`unordered` too, where it numbers what a bullet did not.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the set.

members.name: kind
members.description:
What kind of list this is, which is a fact about the content.

On the headless tier because it is meaning rather than decoration, the same
argument `severity` makes on `Callout`. A numbered list is numbered because
the order carries information; a bulleted one is bulleted because the items
are a set and the order does not. That distinction is the reader's, and it
has to survive with the stylesheet turned off.

- `default` is a run of rows and takes no marker. It is what a list of
  settings or files is: neither ordered nor a set to be counted.
- `ordered` numbers them, for steps.
- `unordered` bullets them, for a set.
- `description` pairs each row's label with its supporting text as a term
  and what the term means.

**`description` reuses the row's existing slots rather than inventing a
  second kind of row.** A term and its description is exactly the label and
  the supporting text `List.Item` already has, so the kind changes how the
  pair is drawn and nothing about what a consumer writes. A separate
  `List.Term` element would be a second row shape for one attribute's sake.

members.name: type
members.description:
Which markers an ordered list draws, in `<ol type>`'s own five values.

Reflected, because this is one of the things a stylesheet selects on and
the styled tier maps each to a `list-style-type`. The platform's spellings
rather than the CSS ones, so `<helix-list kind="ordered" type="i">` is what
a consumer would have written on an `<ol>`.

**`start` and `reversed` are both absent and neither can be done here.**
This renders no `<ol>`: the rows are slotted and numbered by the CSS
`list-item` counter, and that counter is not author-resettable. Measured in
Chrome 148, `counter-reset: list-item 4` moves nothing on a `<div>`, on a
`<ul>`, or even on a real `<ol>`, while `<ol start="5">` does and a *named*
counter with explicit `::before` content does. So the markers would have to
be rebuilt out of generated content to gain a start, which is a different
component. `type` is only `list-style-type` and works.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.description:

equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything

the list rather than the host, so a filter that empties it leaves a box with
