members.name: offset
members.description:
How far below the top of the window a heading counts as reached, in pixels.

The reading line. A page with a sticky masthead sets this to its height, or
a little more: without it the current section changes as a heading slides
under the chrome rather than as it reaches the top of what can be seen.

members.name: behavior
members.description:
How a click on one of these links travels to its section.

The platform's own vocabulary, because this is the platform's own option:
`auto` defers to whatever `scroll-behavior` the page has set on its scroll
container, which is the honest default and means an outline changes nothing
a consumer did not ask it to. `smooth` slides, `instant` jumps.

**`auto` is also the only value that leaves the navigation to the browser.**
A fragment link does four things: it scrolls, it writes the hash, it pushes
a history entry, and it moves the sequential focus point so the next Tab
continues from the heading rather than from the link. Choosing a behavior
means intercepting the click, and an interception that does only the first
of those is a keyboard reader stranded in the contents list. So the other
three are done by hand here, and only when there is a reason to take over.

`smooth` becomes `instant` under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. That is
read at the click rather than cached, because a reader can change it while
the page is open and this is the only motion in the component that
JavaScript rather than CSS decides.

members.name: current
members.description:
The id of the section being read, or empty before anything is measured.

Read-only, and a getter rather than a property for that reason: it is
derived from where the page is scrolled to, so a consumer setting it would
be overwritten by the next thing that crossed the reading line. Every other
writable property in this library that a component also writes is state a
consumer can own; this one cannot be, and saying so with the type is better
than saying it in a sentence nobody reads.

members.name: reading
members.description: What `current` reports, which only `mark` writes.

members.name: links
members.description: The links, in document order. Empty on the server, which has no tree.

members.name: sections
members.description: What each link points at, paired with the link, skipping anything missing.

members.name: mark
members.description:
Works out which section is being read, and marks its link.

Positional rather than a reading of what intersects, for the reason above.
The comparison is against `offset` and not zero, so the reading line is
wherever the page says the top of the readable area is.

members.name: markTo
members.description: Where the destination is set, whether measured or asked for.

members.name: atEnd
members.description:
Whether the page has no more scroll left.

`Math.ceil` and a pixel of slack, because a fractional device pixel ratio
leaves the position a hair under the height at the very bottom and an exact
comparison never fires.

**All three numbers off the same element**, which this did not do: it added
`scrollY` and `innerHeight`, both of the window, and compared them against
`documentElement.scrollHeight`. Those are one coordinate system only while
the viewport is what scrolls, and the body takes that job the moment it
becomes a scroll container. Measured on a page whose body is
`overflow: clip visible`, which is a pair CSS resolves by making the
`visible` axis `auto`: `documentElement.scrollTop` read 1126 at the bottom
of the page and `window.scrollY` read 240, so a contents rail never learned
it had reached the end and its last item stayed unreachable. That page is
this library's own base layer.

`clientHeight` rather than `innerHeight` for the same reason, and because it
is the one that excludes a scrollbar, which is what `scrollHeight` is
measured against.

members.name: frame
members.description: The frame a mark is already scheduled for, so a scroll asks for one.

members.name: landing
members.description: Where a click said to go, while the page is still on its way there.

members.name: landed
members.description: The guard behind `scrollend`, in case it never comes.

members.name: handleScroll
members.description:
The two things an `IntersectionObserver` cannot see, and one listener for
both.

This component's own note said the observer keeps the marker honest without
a scroll listener. It was wrong twice.

*At the bottom*, arriving at the end of a page changes no intersection: a
short last section is fully visible long before the final pixel, so its
ratio reached 1 and stopped moving. Nothing fires for the scroll that ends
the page.

*And at the end of a smooth scroll*, which is the one that showed up in
use. Clicking a link in the contents list scrolled to the section and left
the mark where it was. Measured on the shipped example: after clicking
`#usage` the heading sat at 72px, exactly the reading line, and `current`
was still `install`. The observer fires several times during the travel and
the last of them lands a frame or two before the final position, where the
heading has not crossed yet, and no callback follows for the rest of the
way.

There was a listener already, added for the first of those, and it compared
two numbers and marked only when the answer *changed*. That was too clever
by half: it fixed the bottom and could not fix the settle. Marking once per
animation frame while a scroll is happening covers both and every other case
of the same shape, and the cost is what `mark()` costs, a `getBoundingClientRect`
per section on frames a reader is already scrolling through. Passive, and
coalesced to one call per frame however many events arrive.

members.name: reach
members.description:
Gives every section the same reading line the marker uses.

`offset` described where the top of the readable area is and was read by
exactly one thing, the marker. Click a link and the browser put the heading
against the very top of the window, underneath the sticky masthead whose
height the consumer had just finished measuring for us. So the component
knew about the chrome when deciding what you were reading and forgot about
it when taking you somewhere, which is the same number meaning two things.

`scroll-margin-block-start` rather than an interception, because it is the
property the platform provides for exactly this and the UA honours it on
ordinary fragment navigation, on `scrollIntoView`, and on a browser
restoring a position. Nothing has to be taken over to get it.

Written onto the consumer's element, like `aria-current` above and for the
same reason: it is derived from a property describing the page's chrome,
so no server rendered it and there is nothing to disagree with. Cleared
rather than set to `0px` when there is no offset, so the common case leaves
no attribute at all.

members.name: handleClick
members.description:
Takes a link's click, but only where `auto` would not have done the job.

Left the platform's wherever it can be: a modified click is a new tab or a
download and none of this applies, a click something else has already
handled is not ours, and `auto` is the whole point of `auto`.

members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches every section, and re-marks whenever any of them crosses anything.

The thresholds are what make the trigger frequent enough: an observer fires
on entering and leaving, and a long section scrolled slowly crosses neither
for a long time. Asking for a callback at each quarter of visibility is
cheap and keeps the marker honest without a scroll listener.

members.name: handleSlotChange
members.description:
The set changed: watch it, and measure it.

Both, for the reason the tab strip records: the host renders before its
links have anything to point at, so the first measurement finds nothing,
and without a second one at `slotchange` the mark stays unplaced for the
life of the page.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: Links to the headings on this page, marking the one being read.

examples.description: Headings on a page, with the one in view marked as the page scrolls.
The section being read, announced as the page scrolls past it.
The same outline, scrolling smoothly and stopping clear of a sticky header.

slots.description: The links, as anchors with fragment hrefs.

cssParts.description: The mark that travels to the section being read.
cssParts.name: indicator

cssParts.description: The navigation landmark.
cssParts.name: nav

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the navigation.

attributes.name: offset
attributes.description:
How far below the top of the window a heading counts as reached, in pixels.

The reading line. A page with a sticky masthead sets this to its height, or
a little more: without it the current section changes as a heading slides
under the chrome rather than as it reaches the top of what can be seen.

attributes.name: behavior
attributes.description:
How a click on one of these links travels to its section.

The platform's own vocabulary, because this is the platform's own option:
`auto` defers to whatever `scroll-behavior` the page has set on its scroll
container, which is the honest default and means an outline changes nothing
a consumer did not ask it to. `smooth` slides, `instant` jumps.

**`auto` is also the only value that leaves the navigation to the browser.**
A fragment link does four things: it scrolls, it writes the hash, it pushes
a history entry, and it moves the sequential focus point so the next Tab
continues from the heading rather than from the link. Choosing a behavior
means intercepting the click, and an interception that does only the first
of those is a keyboard reader stranded in the contents list. So the other
three are done by hand here, and only when there is a reason to take over.

`smooth` becomes `instant` under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`. That is
read at the click rather than cached, because a reader can change it while
the page is open and this is the only motion in the component that
JavaScript rather than CSS decides.

events.description: The section being read has changed, carrying its id as the value. Cancelable: refusing it takes the decision and nothing moves.
events.name: helix-before-activate

declarations.description:
One box for every control in the row, arrows and numbers alike, so the run has
a single rhythm and the steps sit at the numbers' height rather than between
them. Square, because a page number is one or two characters and a box sized
to the widest would leave the short ones swimming; `min-inline-size` rather
than a fixed one, so page 100 grows instead of overflowing.

Figures are tabular throughout. A page number is the one thing here that
changes under the pointer, and proportional digits make the whole row shuffle
as it does.

The current page is a raised chip rather than a brand fill, which is the
treatment `Tabs` gives its selected tab. Brand on a page number claims more
than the state deserves: it is not a choice the reader made about anything,
it is where they happen to be standing, and a row of gray numbers with one
blue one reads as the blue one being an action.

Selected on `aria-current` rather than on a second attribute saying the same
thing: the state is already in the accessibility tree, and a `data-current`
beside it would be two places to keep in step.

The gap takes the same box as everything else in the row and only sits back a
shade in color. It is a control, so it answers hover and focus like one; it
is a way through rather than a destination, so it does not compete.

members.name: pages
members.description:
How many pages there are in total.

Clamped to at least one wherever it is read, so a result that has not
loaded yet renders a single page rather than an empty control that then
appears and pushes the layout down.

Left unset where `total` and `page-size` are both given, since the two of
them already say it. A fallback rather than an override: writing this wins,
so there is never a question of which of two sources is current.

members.name: total
members.description:
How many items there are across every page.

What `pages` falls back to together with `page-size`. Unset is the common
case, where a consumer knows the page total and not the item total.

Nothing is rendered from it. `Pagination.Summary` is what reads a total out
to a reader, and takes its own.

members.name: pageSize
members.description:
How many items are on a page.

Only arithmetic: this does not slice anything, because the component never
sees the items. It is what turns `total` into a page count, and nothing
else.

members.name: ends
members.description:
Whether to offer a jump to the first and last pages.

Off by default. The gaps already reach any page in a few presses and the
last page is one of the two the run always shows, so on a short set these
are two more controls for a move already on screen. They earn their place
where the reader is deep in a long result and "back to the start" is the
move they actually want.

Not reflected. It adds two elements rather than changing how any of them
look, so no rule selects on it, and the house rule is that reflection
exists for selectors: an unread reflected attribute is one more thing
written onto a host at upgrade that a server's output never had.

members.name: page
members.description:
The page on show, one-based.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the calendar's `month`. Reading gives
the page on show; writing declares it the consumer's, and `default-page`
seeds one the element owns.

**Clamped on the way out, because "the page on show" is what it says it
gives.** It returned whatever had been written, so `default-page="99"` on a
ten-page result rendered page 10, marked page 10 with `aria-current`, and
reported 99. A consumer syncing their query from this read a page that does
not exist while the control in front of them said otherwise. Not a
far-fetched value: it is a bookmarked link after the result shrank.

Rounded here too, so `2.7` reads as the 2 it renders.

members.name: defaultPage
members.description: Page to open on, where nothing declared one.

members.name: siblings
members.description: How many pages to show either side of the current one.

members.name: boundaries
members.description: How many pages to show at each end, whatever the current one is.

members.name: href
members.description:
Address for a page, with `{page}` standing in for its number.

Absent renders buttons. Present renders links, which is what a paged result
with its own URL should be: a crawler follows them, a middle click opens
one, and the back button works without the consumer wiring anything.

members.name: compact
members.description:
Where the numbers are replaced by a reading of the two.

A different structure rather than a different look, which is why it is
here: the run of pages is gone and a single status line stands in its
place. This is the shape a narrow screen wants, and the only shape possible
where the total is large enough that no window over it is useful.

Not reflected, for the reason `ends` is not: it decides what renders, so
nothing has to select on it.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.

members.name: locale
members.description:
Locale for the page numbers. Absent uses the runtime's own.

The same property the calendar takes, doing the same job one layer down:
the templates make the *words* the consumer's, and this makes the *numbers*
theirs. A page number is a number like any other, so `1234` is `1,234` in
`en-US`, `1.234` in `de-DE` and `١٢٣٤` in `ar-EG`, and a component that
lets a consumer translate "Page {page} of {pages}" and then prints Latin
digits into it has done half the job.

Not applied to `href`. That one is machine-facing, and `?page=1,234` is a
different address from `?page=1234`.

members.name: pageLabel
members.description: Accessible name for one page, with `{page}` and `{pages}` filled in.

members.name: statusLabel
members.description:
The reading shown in `compact`, with `{page}` and `{pages}` filled in.

The word went: it read "Page 7 of 24" and the landmark it sits in is
already named "Pagination", so the noun was said twice to a screen reader
and took a third of the width from a control whose whole reason for
existing is that the row is narrow. The numbers are the reading.

members.name: previousLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the control that moves back.

members.name: nextLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the control that moves forward.

members.name: firstLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the control that jumps to the first page.

members.name: lastLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the control that jumps to the last page.

members.name: gapLabel
members.description: Accessible name for a gap, with `{page}` filled in as where it goes.

members.name: announcement
members.description:
What the live region says, and nothing until the page has moved once.

`pageLabel` rather than a template of its own, so the announcement is the
same sentence the control the reader just pressed already carried, and
there is not a ninth string to translate for the sake of one of them.

members.name: announced
members.description: The page last announced, so the first render announces nothing.

members.name: pageState
members.description: The page on show, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: numbers
members.description: Held across every component asking for the same locale.

members.name: count
members.description:
How many pages, clamped once, so every reader agrees on it.

`pages` first, because writing it is the explicit answer. Then `total` over
`pageSize`, which is the same fact stated the other way round and is what a
consumer holding a result set already has. Then one, so a result that has
not loaded renders a single page rather than an empty control that appears
later and pushes the layout down.

members.name: current
members.description: The page on show. `page` does the clamping now; this is the older name.

members.name: slots
members.description:
Which pages to show, and where the runs break.

`most` is the number of slots the control holds at its widest: both
boundaries, the run around the current page, and a gap on each side. Below
that there is nothing to hide, and the whole range is shown.

Above it, the two gaps are decided independently, and a gap standing over
exactly one page is not drawn: `boundaries + 2` is the first page whose
predecessor is not a boundary, so a run starting there is contiguous with
what precedes it. Where one side has no gap the run on that side extends to
`most` slots, which is what holds the width still.

members.name: request
members.description:
Asks to move, and reports whether the request stood.

Announced before it is applied, so `preventDefault()` is a refusal and
nothing moves. In controlled mode nothing is written whatever the answer:
the consumer holds the page and this is the element telling them a reader
asked for another one.

members.name: go
members.description:
The click handler, which is also what stops a link from following itself.

A refused change has to refuse the navigation with it, or a router that
cancels the event still loses the document underneath it. `preventDefault`
on a button's click does nothing and costs nothing, so this is one handler
for both shapes rather than two that have to stay in step.

members.name: renderPage
members.description:
One page, as a link or a button.

`aria-current="page"` is what says which one you are on, and it stays a
control rather than becoming text: a reader who tabs into the run and finds
the current page missing from it has lost the only landmark in the row.

members.name: renderGap
members.description:
A gap, which is a control and not a mark.

**It goes to the middle of what it hides**, and the label says so. That is
the binary-search step, so an arbitrary page in a set of any size is a
handful of presses: 128 pages is `1 … 96 97 98 … 128`, and the leading gap
lands on 48, whose gaps land on 24 and 88, and so on. A jump of a fixed size
would need forty presses on that set.

**A menu over these pages was the other idea and it does not survive the
arithmetic.** The run a gap covers is unbounded by construction: two pages
on a twelve-page set, ninety-four on a hundred-and-twenty-eight-page one. A
menu is pleasant at the first and is a scroll of ninety-four items at the
second, which is worse than the ellipsis it replaced, and there is no total
at which it stops being possible. It would also make `Pagination` depend on
`Menu` and `Popover` for a case a button already covers.

So it is announced rather than hidden, which is the change from when it was
a decoration: a control a reader can reach has to be in the tree, and the
label naming its destination is the whole affordance.

members.name: step
members.description:
Everything a step needs, computed once, so the markup below is only markup.

Split out because the part name has to be a literal. `check:parts` reads
`part="name"` out of the source, so a computed one is a part the tooling
cannot see: nothing pairs it with its `@csspart` and a later rename takes
the promise silently. With four controls and two shapes each that is eight
literals, and eight copies of the arithmetic behind them would be the
actual duplication. This is the arithmetic, written once.

members.name: renderFirst
members.description:
The four controls, inert at the end each points at.

Inert rather than absent: a control that disappears at the first page takes
the row's width with it and moves everything else under the pointer. In
link mode the inert one is an `<a>` with no `href`, which is not a link and
is not focusable, and is the platform's own way of saying there is nowhere
to go.

**Each glyph is a slot fallback, and each method is a seam**, which answer
two different people: the slot is how a page swaps a caret for its own icon
set, and `protected` is how the tier above swaps all four without
reimplementing a template that renders eight controls across two shapes.
`Select` and `Listbox` carry the same pairing on one mark each.

**Four slot names rather than one**, even though the four controls draw
from the same shared `mark` part. A single `<slot name="icon">` is assigned
once and the other three occurrences of it get nothing, so a consumer
replacing the caret would silently lose three of their four marks.

members.name: renderLive
members.description:
The region that says the page moved.

Always rendered and empty until it has something to say. A live region
populated at the moment it enters the document announces itself on arrival,
which for a component that upgrades on load is every page load.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition

Pages as real links, so each is a URL a reader can keep.
How many numbers show either side of the current page.

attributes.name: pages
attributes.description:
How many pages there are in total.

Clamped to at least one wherever it is read, so a result that has not
loaded yet renders a single page rather than an empty control that then
appears and pushes the layout down.

Left unset where `total` and `page-size` are both given, since the two of
them already say it. A fallback rather than an override: writing this wins,
so there is never a question of which of two sources is current.

attributes.name: total
attributes.description:
How many items there are across every page.

What `pages` falls back to together with `page-size`. Unset is the common
case, where a consumer knows the page total and not the item total.

Nothing is rendered from it. `Pagination.Summary` is what reads a total out
to a reader, and takes its own.

attributes.name: page-size
attributes.description:
How many items are on a page.

Only arithmetic: this does not slice anything, because the component never
sees the items. It is what turns `total` into a page count, and nothing
else.

attributes.name: ends
attributes.description:
Whether to offer a jump to the first and last pages.

Off by default. The gaps already reach any page in a few presses and the
last page is one of the two the run always shows, so on a short set these
are two more controls for a move already on screen. They earn their place
where the reader is deep in a long result and "back to the start" is the
move they actually want.

Not reflected. It adds two elements rather than changing how any of them
look, so no rule selects on it, and the house rule is that reflection
exists for selectors: an unread reflected attribute is one more thing
written onto a host at upgrade that a server's output never had.

attributes.name: page
attributes.description:
The page on show, one-based.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the calendar's `month`. Reading gives
the page on show; writing declares it the consumer's, and `default-page`
seeds one the element owns.

**Clamped on the way out, because "the page on show" is what it says it
gives.** It returned whatever had been written, so `default-page="99"` on a
ten-page result rendered page 10, marked page 10 with `aria-current`, and
reported 99. A consumer syncing their query from this read a page that does
not exist while the control in front of them said otherwise. Not a
far-fetched value: it is a bookmarked link after the result shrank.

Rounded here too, so `2.7` reads as the 2 it renders.

attributes.name: default-page
attributes.description: Page to open on, where nothing declared one.

attributes.name: siblings
attributes.description: How many pages to show either side of the current one.

attributes.name: boundaries
attributes.description: How many pages to show at each end, whatever the current one is.

attributes.name: href
attributes.description:
Address for a page, with `{page}` standing in for its number.

Absent renders buttons. Present renders links, which is what a paged result
with its own URL should be: a crawler follows them, a middle click opens
one, and the back button works without the consumer wiring anything.

attributes.name: compact
attributes.description:
Where the numbers are replaced by a reading of the two.

A different structure rather than a different look, which is why it is
here: the run of pages is gone and a single status line stands in its
place. This is the shape a narrow screen wants, and the only shape possible
where the total is large enough that no window over it is useful.

Not reflected, for the reason `ends` is not: it decides what renders, so
nothing has to select on it.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the navigation landmark.

attributes.name: locale
attributes.description:
Locale for the page numbers. Absent uses the runtime's own.

The same property the calendar takes, doing the same job one layer down:
the templates make the *words* the consumer's, and this makes the *numbers*
theirs. A page number is a number like any other, so `1234` is `1,234` in
`en-US`, `1.234` in `de-DE` and `١٢٣٤` in `ar-EG`, and a component that
lets a consumer translate "Page {page} of {pages}" and then prints Latin
digits into it has done half the job.

Not applied to `href`. That one is machine-facing, and `?page=1,234` is a
different address from `?page=1234`.

attributes.name: page-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for one page, with `{page}` and `{pages}` filled in.

attributes.name: status-label
attributes.description:
The reading shown in `compact`, with `{page}` and `{pages}` filled in.

The word went: it read "Page 7 of 24" and the landmark it sits in is
already named "Pagination", so the noun was said twice to a screen reader
and took a third of the width from a control whose whole reason for
existing is that the row is narrow. The numbers are the reading.

attributes.name: previous-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the control that moves back.

attributes.name: next-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the control that moves forward.

attributes.name: first-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the control that jumps to the first page.

attributes.name: last-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the control that jumps to the last page.

attributes.name: gap-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for a gap, with `{page}` filled in as where it goes.

events.description: Fired before the page changes, and cancelable. The only way to refuse one.

word differently.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: Reads out which items of how many are on show.

attributes.name: page
attributes.description: The page on show, one-based.

attributes.name: page-size
attributes.description: How many items are on a page.

attributes.name: total
attributes.description: How many items there are across every page.

attributes.name: format
attributes.description:
The reading, with `{from}`, `{to}` and `{total}` filled in.

A template rather than a prefix and a suffix, because word order is not
universal: `format="{total} 件中 {from}-{to} 件"` is one attribute here and
three concatenations anywhere else.

**`format`, not `label`, and the difference is worth the rename.** `label`
across this library means the accessible name of a thing that has one:
`Pagination.label` names the landmark and `Pagination.Size.label` is the
words beside the control. This is neither. It is the whole visible content
of the element, so calling it `label` put one word on three jobs inside one
family. The root's templates are `pageLabel`, `statusLabel` and `gapLabel`,
which each label something; this labels nothing, it *is* the thing.

attributes.name: locale
attributes.description:
Locale for the numbers.

Absent uses the runtime's own.

declarations.description:
Square boxes at the control height with real space between them, which is the
whole picture: a code is read as separate characters, and boxes shoulder to
shoulder read as one field with lines drawn in it.

The focus ring is on the box the reader is in rather than around the row. A
code is entered one character at a time and the boxes exist to say which one
is next, so a ring around all six would answer the question the component is
for.

Figures are tabular, so a 1 takes the room an 8 does and the row does not
breathe as a code is typed into it.
declarations.name: HelixPinInput

cssProperties.description: Space between one box and the next.
cssProperties.name: --pin-input-gap

cssParts.description: One box.
cssParts.name: cell

cssParts.description: The row of boxes.
cssParts.name: field

cssParts.description: What is wrong with it.
cssParts.name: feedback

cssParts.description: Help under the boxes, while nothing is wrong.
cssParts.name: hint

cssParts.description: The question, over the boxes.
cssParts.name: label

members.name: defaultValue
members.description: The value the markup declared, which is where a reset returns to.

members.name: value
members.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

helix-input

members.name: valueState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it.

members.name: announcesInput
members.description:
Whether a reader edits this continuously, which decides the native name.

**It used to pick between `helix-input` and `helix-change`**, which was
one mechanism under two names and said *phase* where it meant
*granularity*. The request event is `helix-before-change` whatever the
answer; this decides which native event announces the result, `input`
while a reader is editing against `change` when they are done, which is
the distinction the platform already draws. See 294.

Discrete by default: only a control the reader edits continuously says
otherwise.

members.name: announceNatively
members.description:
Announces the applied value under the platform's own name.

**After `apply`, never before**, which is the whole reason this is
separate from the request event: a native handler reads
`event.target.value`, and it has to be the value that was just applied.

**Both, for a discrete control, because that is what the platform does.**
A native `<select>` sends `input` and then `change` from one choice: the
value moved, and the reader is also done. A continuous control announces
`input` here and relays `change` from its inner control when the reader
is done, so the pair keeps the platform's timings rather than reporting a
commit on every keystroke.

members.name: requestValue
members.description:
Requests a new value, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-change` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the control updates
itself, whether or not a consumer declared `value`: a declared property
is a seed and a correction, the way `<input value>` is, and a consumer
who wants the change for themselves refuses it and assigns their own.
See 294.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description:
Returns the control to the value its markup declared.

Both halves are dropped, the consumer's and the control's, because a
reset means the form is as it was served. Clearing only the internal one
would leave a control that had been written to stuck at that value.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the value when the browser brings a form back.

Falling back to `defaultValue` rather than to empty, because a restore
with no state is a form the browser has nothing recorded for, which is
the same situation as a fresh one.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: autocomplete
members.description:
What the browser may autofill, reaching the first cell only.

`one-time-code` is why this defaults to anything at all: it is the token
that lets a phone offer the code out of a message. Later cells stay `off`
for the reason in the class comment above, that six cells each offering
the same code is one offer made six times.

members.name: length
members.description: How many characters the code has.

members.name: type
members.description:
What a box accepts, which decides the keyboard a phone offers.

`numeric` and `alphanumeric` also refuse anything else on the way in,
because a code that is digits is digits: letting a letter into a box a
reader cannot submit is a mistake they have to find and undo themselves.
`text` refuses nothing and only trims, so it is the mode for a code with a
hyphen in it.

**`alphanumeric` is ASCII letters and digits**, which is narrower than the
word is in general and is the right narrowness here. A code of this kind
comes off a keypad, an SMS or an authenticator, and none of them emit `é`;
a filter that accepted it would let through a character the service on the
other end is going to reject. A consumer whose codes really do carry
marked letters wants `text`, which judges nothing.

**Not reflected**, and it was until this component's own server spec caught
it: nothing selects on it, so all reflection did was write `type="numeric"`
onto every `<helix-pin-input>` ever rendered, an attribute no consumer's
markup had. That is the fault `Input`'s own `type` had and the reason the
area rules carry the sentence "reflect only what CSS selects on". The real
inputs take it as a binding, which is what makes the keyboard follow.

members.name: mask
members.description: Whether the characters are hidden, the way a password is.

members.name: placeholder
members.description:
What an empty box shows, usually a single dot.

The platform's own placeholder, on each cell, rather than a character
drawn behind the field: it clears the moment anything is typed, it is
already excluded from the accessible value, and it works the same under
`mask`, where the cell is a password input and a hand-drawn glyph would
have to know that.

Empty by default, because a row of boxes already reads as a row of boxes
and a dot in each is a choice about how much the field should announce
itself before anybody has touched it.

members.name: readOnly
members.description: Whether the boxes refuse input while still submitting their value.

members.name: cellLabel
members.description: Accessible name for one box, with `{index}` and `{length}` filled in.

members.name: shadowRootOptions
members.description: Focus is delegated, so the host is never the focus target.

members.name: count
members.description: How many boxes there are, clamped once so every reader agrees.

members.name: characters
members.description: The code as characters, padded to the row so every box has one to show.

members.name: clean
members.description: Everything this box would accept, with the rest dropped.

members.name: write
members.description:
Writes a run of characters from one box onward.

The single path for typing, pasting and autofill alike, because they are
the same act at different lengths and splitting them is how the three
disagree about trimming, about the cursor, and about what happens at the
end.

members.name: paint
members.description:
Puts the value back into the boxes.

The cells are uncontrolled between renders, because Lit will not rewrite an
input's `.value` when the bound string has not changed, and a refused
keystroke leaves the box holding a character the element rejected. This is
the same put-back `Input` does with `restoreValue`, once per box.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
The keys that move between boxes, and the one that clears backwards.

Backspace in an empty box goes back and clears the one it lands in, which
is what makes a code correctable without the reader hunting for the box
they meant. In a full box it does what it always does and is left alone.

members.name: committed
members.description:
The code as it stood at the last commit, so a blur that changed nothing
says nothing.

**The last commit, and not the value the reader arrived on**, which is what
the platform compares against. Taking that reading means recognizing the
arrival, and this component moves focus itself on every character, so the
`focus` it would be reading is mostly one it caused: telling those apart
rests entirely on `relatedTarget`, on an event the element dispatched to
itself. The last commit rests on nothing, and it is the value the event
would carry anyway.

They agree everywhere a reader is involved, including the case the platform
is careful about: typing a character and deleting it again leaves the code
where it was, so neither reading commits. They part only when a script
assigns while the field is unfocused, where this commits on the way out and
the platform does not, having taken its baseline after the assignment.
Announcing a value a consumer set themselves is the safe half of that trade.

Seeded in `firstUpdated`, a code in the markup being committed by whoever
wrote it.

members.name: handleFocus
members.description: Selecting on focus, so typing replaces rather than appending.

members.name: handleFocusOut
members.description:
Commits when focus leaves the row, which is the moment every other field in
the library has and this one did not.

`change` is one of the two events `MixinField` reads as "the reader has had
a go at this", so a code that was never completed was never `touched` and
its own `tooShort` message could not show: two boxes of four filled and
tabbed away from was answered with nothing at all. `Input` gets this for
free by relaying its control's own `change`; here the cells each fire one,
none of them means the code is entered, and neither does any single one of
them mean the reader has left.

**Focus leaving the row, and not a cell.** Every character moves focus to
the next box, so a per-cell blur would commit on every keystroke, which is
the fault this exists to fix pointed the other way.

`composed: false`, like the completion above and like the native event this
stands in for. It is dispatched on the host, so a consumer hears it.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports the code and a verdict on it.

members.name: focus
members.description: Puts the caret in the first empty box, which is where a reader resumes.

members.name: clear
members.description: Empties every box and returns to the first.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description:
What the control holds now, and what its form submits.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real value whichever mode the
control is in, so `input.value` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what
`<helix-input value="x">` says too, and matches what a controlled input
means in React: the value is theirs and the control waits to be told.
`default-value` is how markup seeds one it does not want to own.

The same shape as the other three mixins, which is the point of them
being four of a kind rather than four of three kinds.

helix-input

attributes.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

attributes.name: feedback
attributes.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

attributes.name: required
attributes.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

attributes.name: autocomplete
attributes.description:
What the browser may autofill, reaching the first cell only.

`one-time-code` is why this defaults to anything at all: it is the token
that lets a phone offer the code out of a message. Later cells stay `off`
for the reason in the class comment above, that six cells each offering
the same code is one offer made six times.

attributes.name: length
attributes.description: How many characters the code has.

attributes.name: type
attributes.description:
What a box accepts, which decides the keyboard a phone offers.

`numeric` and `alphanumeric` also refuse anything else on the way in,
because a code that is digits is digits: letting a letter into a box a
reader cannot submit is a mistake they have to find and undo themselves.
`text` refuses nothing and only trims, so it is the mode for a code with a
hyphen in it.

**`alphanumeric` is ASCII letters and digits**, which is narrower than the
word is in general and is the right narrowness here. A code of this kind
comes off a keypad, an SMS or an authenticator, and none of them emit `é`;
a filter that accepted it would let through a character the service on the
other end is going to reject. A consumer whose codes really do carry
marked letters wants `text`, which judges nothing.

**Not reflected**, and it was until this component's own server spec caught
it: nothing selects on it, so all reflection did was write `type="numeric"`
onto every `<helix-pin-input>` ever rendered, an attribute no consumer's
markup had. That is the fault `Input`'s own `type` had and the reason the
area rules carry the sentence "reflect only what CSS selects on". The real
inputs take it as a binding, which is what makes the keyboard follow.

attributes.name: mask
attributes.description: Whether the characters are hidden, the way a password is.

attributes.name: placeholder
attributes.description:
What an empty box shows, usually a single dot.

The platform's own placeholder, on each cell, rather than a character
drawn behind the field: it clears the moment anything is typed, it is
already excluded from the accessible value, and it works the same under
`mask`, where the cell is a password input and a hand-drawn glyph would
have to know that.

Empty by default, because a row of boxes already reads as a row of boxes
and a dot in each is a choice about how much the field should announce
itself before anybody has touched it.

attributes.name: readonly
attributes.description: Whether the boxes refuse input while still submitting their value.

attributes.name: cell-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for one box, with `{index}` and `{length}` filled in.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

attributes.name: name
attributes.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.description:
How the panel separates itself from what it floats over.

One of the axis's four values, which is all this surface has meaning for: a
floating panel keeps its lift by default, `ThemeIntent.separation.floating`
refusing `space` for the reason it refuses it everywhere, that a panel over
content nobody can predict has to be readable.
