members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How much ink the drawing claims.

`subtle` mixes the drawing toward the page. The case is a table where one row
is being read and the rest are context.

It moves the host's `color`, which is what every mark here is drawn in: the
line strokes it, both gradient stops take it so the wash is the line's own
color, and the terminus fills it. So one declaration quietens all of them,
and a consumer's `--sparkline-color` is quietened rather than replaced.

**The other two follow whichever plot is drawn**, because a sparkline is
three marks behind one property and the difference between a boundary and a
fill does not exist until you know which. A `bar` plot answers like
`BarChart`, an `area` or `line` plot like `LineChart`. `solid` on bars is the
resting column and selects nothing.

**`outlined` was refused here until 25 Aug 2026**, on the grounds that it
needs a fill to remove and this is a stroke. That is true of the line and not
of the other two plots, which is what the argument missed: a bar has an area
and an area plot is one.

`ghost` is still an empty cell, and there is still no `material`. Glass
exists so what is behind a mark reads through it, and at the size a sparkline
draws there is nothing behind it a reader could resolve.

members.name: weight
members.description:
How heavy the line is drawn.

Absent is the weight a sparkline is usually drawn at. `thin` suits one set
in a table row among many; `thick` suits one standing on its own, where a
hairline reads as an accident.

Three steps rather than a number, because `--sparkline-width` is already
the number and an attribute earns its place by being the thing a consumer
reaches for without reading the stylesheet. The hook stays for anything the
three do not cover.

members.name: terminus
members.description:
The shape of the mark on the last reading.

Absent is a dot, which is how a line is usually ended, and absent rather
than defaulted because a reflecting property with a default writes its
attribute onto a host the consumer rendered, which React reports as a
hydration mismatch.

`none` lets the line stop on its own, which suits a series read as a shape
rather than for where it finished. `ring` lets the ground through, for a
chart drawn over something busy. `triangle` points along the axis and reads
as "and onward" rather than as a second claim about the data.

A `bar` plot draws none of them: the last column already is the last
reading, and a mark on top of it would say the same thing twice.

The shapes come from `helix/styled/src/shared/chart/terminus.css`, shared with
`LineChart`, so the set is the same wherever a line ends. `ring` is the
one that asks anything of the drawing: the disc it leaves open is masked out
of the `<svg>`, so the line stops at the ring's inner edge rather than
running on to the reading at its center, and the middle shows whatever the
chart is drawn over rather than a guess at it.

members.name: plot
members.description:
What the readings are drawn as.

Absent is a line, `area` is a line with the region beneath it washed, and
`bar` is a column per reading.

**A bar plot measures from zero and the other two measure from the data's
own range**, which is the one way the plots are not interchangeable. A line
says where the readings sit relative to each other, so a scale over their
extent uses the whole box and claims nothing about absolute size. A bar's
length *is* the value, so any baseline but zero makes the lengths
proportional to nothing.

**Which is a reason to prefer a line for readings in a narrow band far from
zero.** Seven values between 1,102 and 1,408 drawn as columns from zero are
seven columns of nearly the same height, and that is the true picture: they
*are* nearly the same. The same readings as a line fill the box and show
the movement, because a line is only ever claiming a shape.

**Absent is `area`**, which is the departure from the rule that a resting
arrangement is the plainest thing. At the size a sparkline is actually
drawn, a hairline in a wide box is mostly box: the wash under it is what
gives the shape a body and lets a reader see it at a glance rather than
hunting for it, which is the entire job. `line` is the bare stroke for
anywhere the fill would be noise, several of them in one box for instance.

This tier rather than the one above: a plot type is geometry and geometry
is markup, the same reason `curve` lives here.

members.name: curve
members.description:
How the line gets from one reading to the next.

**`smooth` is the resting curve.** *Changed 21 Aug 2026, reversing the
argument this comment used to make.* It read that joining the readings
claims nothing in between and is the default for that reason, which is true
and is why `straight` still exists: a straight segment asserts nothing about
the values between two readings, and a curve invents them.

What settles it the other way is that the invention is bounded. The
interpolation is monotone cubic, so it never leaves the band the data sets
and never introduces a peak or a trough the series does not have. Within
that bound the smoothed line is the easier one to follow across a long
series, which is what the drawing is for. `straight` becomes the claim a
consumer makes deliberately rather than the one they get by saying nothing.

**The property stays optional and the default lives in the render.** A
reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto every host
anybody renders, including the ones nobody configured, which the SSR specs
assert against. So the resting state is still the attribute's absence, and
`curve ?? 'smooth'` is what reads it.

`step` claims the opposite of both, that a reading holds until the next.
Bars ignore it, having no between to interpolate.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of a table to read instead, when there is one behind the line.

The first column of numbers is the series drawn. This wins over `values`,
because a table is the readable representation and a list of numbers in an
attribute is not.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: label
members.description:
What the line says, in a sentence.

"Sessions rose from 1,240 to 1,318 and fell to 1,102 over fourteen days" is
the accessible representation of a sparkline, and a list of the fourteen
numbers is not. Absent, the drawing is hidden from a screen reader rather
than announced without a name.

members.name: values
members.description:
The numbers, separated by whitespace or by commas.

Both separators, so `values="1240 1318"` and an array assigned to the
property both work: assigning `[1240, 1318]` stringifies to `1240,1318`,

attributes.name: emphasis
attributes.description:
How much ink the drawing claims.

`subtle` mixes the drawing toward the page. The case is a table where one row
is being read and the rest are context.

It moves the host's `color`, which is what every mark here is drawn in: the
line strokes it, both gradient stops take it so the wash is the line's own
color, and the terminus fills it. So one declaration quietens all of them,
and a consumer's `--sparkline-color` is quietened rather than replaced.

**The other two follow whichever plot is drawn**, because a sparkline is
three marks behind one property and the difference between a boundary and a
fill does not exist until you know which. A `bar` plot answers like
`BarChart`, an `area` or `line` plot like `LineChart`. `solid` on bars is the
resting column and selects nothing.

**`outlined` was refused here until 25 Aug 2026**, on the grounds that it
needs a fill to remove and this is a stroke. That is true of the line and not
of the other two plots, which is what the argument missed: a bar has an area
and an area plot is one.

`ghost` is still an empty cell, and there is still no `material`. Glass
exists so what is behind a mark reads through it, and at the size a sparkline
draws there is nothing behind it a reader could resolve.

attributes.name: weight
attributes.description:
How heavy the line is drawn.

Absent is the weight a sparkline is usually drawn at. `thin` suits one set
in a table row among many; `thick` suits one standing on its own, where a
hairline reads as an accident.

Three steps rather than a number, because `--sparkline-width` is already
the number and an attribute earns its place by being the thing a consumer
reaches for without reading the stylesheet. The hook stays for anything the
three do not cover.

attributes.name: terminus
attributes.description:
The shape of the mark on the last reading.

Absent is a dot, which is how a line is usually ended, and absent rather
than defaulted because a reflecting property with a default writes its
attribute onto a host the consumer rendered, which React reports as a
hydration mismatch.

`none` lets the line stop on its own, which suits a series read as a shape
rather than for where it finished. `ring` lets the ground through, for a
chart drawn over something busy. `triangle` points along the axis and reads
as "and onward" rather than as a second claim about the data.

A `bar` plot draws none of them: the last column already is the last
reading, and a mark on top of it would say the same thing twice.

The shapes come from `helix/styled/src/shared/chart/terminus.css`, shared with
`LineChart`, so the set is the same wherever a line ends. `ring` is the
one that asks anything of the drawing: the disc it leaves open is masked out
of the `<svg>`, so the line stops at the ring's inner edge rather than
running on to the reading at its center, and the middle shows whatever the
chart is drawn over rather than a guess at it.

attributes.name: plot
attributes.description:
What the readings are drawn as.

Absent is a line, `area` is a line with the region beneath it washed, and
`bar` is a column per reading.

**A bar plot measures from zero and the other two measure from the data's
own range**, which is the one way the plots are not interchangeable. A line
says where the readings sit relative to each other, so a scale over their
extent uses the whole box and claims nothing about absolute size. A bar's
length *is* the value, so any baseline but zero makes the lengths
proportional to nothing.

**Which is a reason to prefer a line for readings in a narrow band far from
zero.** Seven values between 1,102 and 1,408 drawn as columns from zero are
seven columns of nearly the same height, and that is the true picture: they
*are* nearly the same. The same readings as a line fill the box and show
the movement, because a line is only ever claiming a shape.

**Absent is `area`**, which is the departure from the rule that a resting
arrangement is the plainest thing. At the size a sparkline is actually
drawn, a hairline in a wide box is mostly box: the wash under it is what
gives the shape a body and lets a reader see it at a glance rather than
hunting for it, which is the entire job. `line` is the bare stroke for
anywhere the fill would be noise, several of them in one box for instance.

This tier rather than the one above: a plot type is geometry and geometry
is markup, the same reason `curve` lives here.

attributes.name: curve
attributes.description:
How the line gets from one reading to the next.

**`smooth` is the resting curve.** *Changed 21 Aug 2026, reversing the
argument this comment used to make.* It read that joining the readings
claims nothing in between and is the default for that reason, which is true
and is why `straight` still exists: a straight segment asserts nothing about
the values between two readings, and a curve invents them.

What settles it the other way is that the invention is bounded. The
interpolation is monotone cubic, so it never leaves the band the data sets
and never introduces a peak or a trough the series does not have. Within
that bound the smoothed line is the easier one to follow across a long
series, which is what the drawing is for. `straight` becomes the claim a
consumer makes deliberately rather than the one they get by saying nothing.

**The property stays optional and the default lives in the render.** A
reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto every host
anybody renders, including the ones nobody configured, which the SSR specs
assert against. So the resting state is still the attribute's absence, and
`curve ?? 'smooth'` is what reads it.

`step` claims the opposite of both, that a reading holds until the next.
Bars ignore it, having no between to interpolate.

attributes.name: for
attributes.description:
The id of a table to read instead, when there is one behind the line.

The first column of numbers is the series drawn. This wins over `values`,
because a table is the readable representation and a list of numbers in an
attribute is not.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, the way
`Tooltip.for` does, so it does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description:
What the line says, in a sentence.

"Sessions rose from 1,240 to 1,318 and fell to 1,102 over fourteen days" is
the accessible representation of a sparkline, and a list of the fourteen
numbers is not. Absent, the drawing is hidden from a screen reader rather
than announced without a name.

attributes.name: values
attributes.description:
The numbers, separated by whitespace or by commas.

Both separators, so `values="1240 1318"` and an array assigned to the
property both work: assigning `[1240, 1318]` stringifies to `1240,1318`,
and a string is what survives React's hydration where an array property
does not.

declarations.summary: A line with no axes, for the shape of a series beside the number it belongs to.

examples.description: The same seven days as bars, as a line and as an area.
The same seven readings drawn three ways, and each says something different about what happened between them.
Each weight against each plot, since a boundary and a fill mean different things per shape.
The same line taken from a table instead, for the sparkline that has one behind it. The table is clipped and still read.
All twenty-four series colours on identical readings: eight hues in three tones, as a line and as a wash.
One series drawn four ways: a line, a wash under it, columns, and a thin line for a row among many.
Five ways to end a line. The shapes are shared with every other chart that draws one.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-open` or
`helix-before-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the
element opens or closes itself, whether or not a consumer declared
`open`: a declared property is a seed and a correction, and a consumer
who wants the decision for themselves refuses it and assigns their own.
See 294.

members.name: announceToggle
members.description:
Says the state moved, under the platform's own name and in its shape.

**`<details>` fires `toggle` and a popover fires `toggle`, and sixteen
families here fired neither.** Two of them render a real `<dialog>` and
ten show a `popover="manual"` panel, so the browser was already firing
something on an element inside a shadow root, where `toggle` neither
bubbles nor composes and so reaches nobody. The rest, the disclosures,
have no native element to fire anything at all: `AccordionItem` and
`TreeItem` are `aria-expanded` and `hidden` written by hand, which is
`<details>`'s job done manually.

**From here rather than from `PopoverController`, which had it first.**
The controller covers eleven families and the mixin covers sixteen, and
the overlap is ten that would have announced twice. What `toggle` reports
is the *state*, and the state is this mixin's; the controller is a way of
putting a panel on the screen.

**`newState` and `oldState`, because that is the platform's shape**, so a
consumer arriving from `<details>` reads the same two words. Not
cancelable: the before events are the request, and a second cancelable
event for one transition is two answers to one question.

members.description:
Which way the actions fan out. They move if that side does not fit.

Up by default, because the control this hangs off is usually docked to the

members.name: trigger
members.description: Whatever the consumer slotted, or the button rendered in its place.

members.name: items
members.description: The actions, which are this element's own rows and nothing else slotted.

members.name: close
members.description: Shuts it and puts the reader back on the trigger.

members.name: announce
members.description:
Tells a slotted trigger what it is doing, since it cannot know.

The fallback button is rendered by this element and says so in its own
template. A trigger the consumer slotted is their markup, and the state it
needs to announce is state only this element holds: without this, the
arrangement this component recommends, an icon button slotted as the
trigger, is a control that opens a menu and never says it has one. A
consumer who has to mirror `open` back onto their own trigger is a consumer
who will forget, and the failure is silent to everyone who can see the
screen.

**Every word of that survives; the mechanism does not.** This wrote
`aria-expanded` and `aria-haspopup` onto the consumer's element with
`setAttribute`, and measured against React 19.2.8 that is a hydration
mismatch React reports and does not patch up. `tellDisclosure` carries the
argument and the measurement: the state travels as a property now, into the
trigger's own shadow root, where React neither looks nor compares.

`aria-haspopup` goes with it rather than being written separately. It is a
constant, so it could stay an attribute without changing on every open, and
an attribute the consumer's server never sent is a mismatch whether or not
it moves afterwards: that was measured too, both load orders. A trigger that
says it is expanded is already saying it has something to expand.

members.name: renderTrigger
members.description:
The control that opens it, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

**This is the case the tier rule blocks and a render method unblocks.** A
bare `<button>` is what the headless tier can write: it must not reach for
`helix-button`, which lives a tier above and would make `headless` depend
on `web`. So the base draws the plain control and a tier that has buttons
of its own overrides this to use one, which is the whole shape #76 exists
for. Written inline the only way to change it was to reimplement the
template, panel and all.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

A fan of actions that opens, and one of them chosen.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

declarations.description:
The divider is a line to look at and a box to hit, and they are different
sizes. Drawn at the border's own width it is a one pixel pointer target, which
is the fault every hand-rolled splitter has; the line is a border and the
target is the box around it.

It lights on hover before it is touched, because a hairline says nothing about
being movable, and the whole target lights rather than the line, so the thing
that answers the pointer is the thing that changed.

Both panes scroll and both have their minimum size taken off them. A flex
item's floor is its content, so a pane holding anything scrollable would
otherwise refuse to go below it: the divider would stop at a width nobody
asked for and nothing would say why.

The corner where a nested splitter crosses is twice the divider's target,
because it is aimed at as a point rather than a line. It draws nothing of its
own: the `move` cursor already says what it is, at the moment a reader is on
it. A ring on focus is the exception, since with nothing drawn there would
otherwise be no way to see where the keyboard is.

A divider stays lit for as long as it is moving, which `:hover` cannot say on
its own: a drag captures the pointer, and a corner moves the nested divider
while the reader is nowhere near it. It goes primary while it moves rather
than merely darker, because hover is a question and a drag is an answer, and
because a corner moving two dividers at once needs the pair to read as one
gesture.

members.name: variant
members.description:
Whether the divider carries a grip.

- `line` is the divider alone, for a splitter the reader already knows is
  one: an editor, a mail client, anything they open every day.
- `grip` adds a short capsule beside the line, for the first encounter. A
  hairline between two panels is a border until something says otherwise,
  and at rest the only thing saying otherwise is a cursor that appears once
  the pointer is already on it.

`grip` rather than `handle`, which this component has already spent on the
corner: that is a box the reader grabs, and this is a mark that says the
line can be grabbed. The grip adds no hit area of its own.

Both are writable, so a generated page can say which it means rather than
relying on the absence of an attribute.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the panes are laid out.

`horizontal` is side by side with an upright divider between them, and
`aria-orientation` on that divider is therefore `vertical`: a separator's
orientation is the direction it is *drawn* in, not the axis it moves along,
so the two words are opposite each other here on purpose. The code had this
right and the sentence beside it said the reverse.

Unset is horizontal and stays unset, so a reflected default cannot appear on
a host whose server output never had it.

**`auto` lays the panes out along whichever axis the splitter has room for**,
stacking them once its own inline size falls under `STACK_BELOW`. It is a
value rather than a default because turning a splitter is not a style
change: the drag axis, the arrow keys and `aria-orientation` all turn with
it, so a CSS-only version would look stacked and behave side by side, with
the keyboard moving the wrong way and the accessibility tree saying
something untrue. Everything here reads `vertical` rather than this
property, which is what makes one getter enough to turn all three together.

**Its own width and not the viewport**, per the responsiveness policy in
`.claude/rules/helix.md`: a splitter in a 300px panel of a 1400px window has
no room for two panes side by side, and a media query would hand it the
desktop branch. A `ResizeObserver` on the host asks the only question that
has an honest answer.

members.name: position
members.description:
Where the divider sits, as a percentage of the whole.

Reading gives where it is; writing declares it the consumer's, and
`default-position` seeds one this element owns. The same accessor pair
`Pagination.page` and the calendar's `month` carry.

members.name: defaultPosition
members.description: Where the divider starts, where nothing declared it.

members.name: collapsed
members.description:
Which pane is shut, if either.

The same accessor pair as `position`, and deliberately a second state
rather than a reading of the first. A pane shut by dragging the divider to
the edge and a pane shut on purpose look identical in geometry and are not
the same thing: only the second knows where to go back to. Kept apart, the
open position is simply the one collapsing never overwrote, so restoring
needs no memory of its own.

It overrides `min` and `max`, which is the point of it. Those keep a sliver
of a pane during a drag; this is the thing that says the sliver can go.

members.name: defaultCollapsed
members.description: Which pane starts shut, where nothing declared it.

members.name: collapsedSize
members.description:
How much of a shut pane is still shown, as a percentage.

Zero by default, which is a pane fully gone. A tab strip or a title bar
that should survive its own collapse says how much of itself to keep, and
only whoever put it there knows that, which is the same reason `min` is a
consumer's to set.

members.name: min
members.description:
Nearest the divider may come to the start.

A bare number is a percentage, which is what this always took. A CSS length
is resolved against the splitter's own box along its axis, so `min="15rem"`
means fifteen rem of pane whatever the container is doing.

**The length is the one that holds.** A percentage minimum does not: twenty
per cent is 280px in a 1400px splitter and 100px in a 500px one, and the
number a consumer picked was almost certainly about how much text fits
rather than about a ratio. The pane that a percentage protects at desk
width is squeezed past reading at half of it.

**It does not fight `collapsed`.** Collapse overrides `min` and `max`, as
the class docstring says, so a pane can still be shut and reopened. What a
minimum forbids is the space between shut and usable: a pane wide enough to
be there and too narrow to read is the state nobody wants and every drag
passes through.

members.name: max
members.description: Nearest it may come to the end, on the same terms as `min`.

members.name: toPercent
members.description:
Either kind of bound as a percentage of the box.

Measured rather than cached: a length is only meaningful against the size
the splitter is right now, and the drag that asks is already reading layout.
Falls back where there is nothing to measure, which is the server and an
element that is not displayed, so `aria-valuemin` is a number either way.

members.name: minPercent
members.description: `min` as a percentage, whichever way it was written.

members.name: maxPercent
members.description: `max` as a percentage, whichever way it was written.

members.name: step
members.description: How far one arrow press moves it, as a percentage.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the divider.

members.name: cornerLabel
members.description: Accessible name for the handle where two dividers cross.

members.name: positionState
members.description: The position, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: collapsedState
members.description: The collapse, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: opened
members.description:
Where the divider was before the gesture that may be about to shut it.

A drag writes a position on every pointer move, so by the time it reaches
the edge the number it started from is gone. Taken once, on the press, and
written back if the gesture ends shut, so the pane opens to where it was
rather than to the edge it was dragged against.

members.name: reached
members.description:
Where the gesture has moved to, whether or not it was applied. See `move`.

`@state`, because the divider is drawn from it while a drag is under way.

members.name: showing
members.description:
The position to draw, which is not always the position to report.

A controlled splitter applies nothing, so `position` holds still for the
whole gesture and the divider stayed where it was until the pointer came up
and the consumer answered: it jumped to the end rather than following the
hand. Reported as resizing that was not seamless and did not work as it had.

So a drag draws itself. The number is not announced until it settles, which
is the rule that has not changed, and the consumer's answer takes over the
moment they give one. It is what the sandbox did for itself before it used
this component: write the size on every pointer move, tell anyone once.

members.name: dragging
members.description:
Whether this divider is being moved right now, by anything.

`:hover` is not enough on its own. A drag holds the pointer through capture
and a fast one leaves the eight pixel target behind, and a corner moves a
divider the pointer is nowhere near: the nested one, while the reader is on
the crossing. Both are dividers that are moving and should say so.

A `data-` attribute on an element in this shadow root, never on the host.

members.name: crossings
members.description:
Nested splitters that cross this one, and how far along they cross it.

Written by the child, not found by the parent: a parent cannot poll for a
child that has not upgraded, so the child announces itself once it has. The
number is the child's own `position`, which is also its offset along this
divider, because the child fills the pane and the pane spans this splitter
end to end on the axis the divider runs.

Not `@state`, because the array is mutated in place. `cross` and `uncross`
request the update themselves.

members.name: outer
members.description: The splitter this one is nested in, once it has found it.

members.name: crossedAt
members.description: The last position announced upward, so an unchanged one costs nothing.

members.name: cornerOrigin
members.description: The two boxes a corner drag is measured against, taken once.

members.name: origin
members.description:
The host's box, measured once when a drag starts.

Measuring per move is a forced layout on every pointer event, in the middle
of a gesture whose whole job is to stay ahead of the pointer. Nothing about
it moves while the divider does.

members.name: moveTo
members.description:
Moves the divider, and optionally says so.

Public because a corner on a nested splitter has to drive the one it is
nested in, and that is the whole of what it needs: the pair are not
otherwise coupled and neither reads the other's state. `settled` is false
for each step of a drag and true once, at the end, for the reason a drag
announces once: only the position it ends at is a preference.

members.name: sliver
members.description: The collapsed size, held inside the range a percentage can be.

members.name: flush
members.description:
Whether the divider is against an edge with nothing beside it.

Geometry, not state, which is the second answer here: it asked whether the
pane was `collapsed`, and a divider driven to the edge by a consumer setting
`position` is just as flush and drew a line anyway. What the stylesheet
needs to know is whether there is a pane on both sides, and that is a fact
about where the divider is however it got there.

Still not the same question as `collapsed`: a pane shut to a sliver has a
boundary worth drawing, and one shut to nothing has the container's own edge
there instead.

members.name: clamp
members.description: Pulled between the bounds, which are the ends unless a consumer moved them.

members.name: stacked
members.description: Whether `auto` has resolved to stacked, which only the observer sets.

members.name: sizes
members.description: Watches this element's own width while `auto` is what it was asked for.

members.name: watchWidth
members.description:
Starts or stops watching, according to what the axis was asked to be.

Called from `firstUpdated` and from `updated`, so a consumer switching to
`auto` after mount is observed and one switching away stops being: an
observer left running would keep writing `stacked` that nothing reads, and
a splitter told `horizontal` has been given its answer already.

members.name: vertical
members.description:
Public because a nested splitter compares axes with the one it is in.

The one place the axis is decided, which is why `auto` costs a single line
here rather than a pass over seventeen readers: the drag, the arrow keys and
`aria-orientation` all ask this and all turn together.

members.name: move
members.description:
Asks to move, and applies it where the position is this element's to move.

Not announced per step: `helix-before-resize` is the settling, below. A drag that
announced every position would be asking a consumer to record a hundred
decisions to keep one.

members.name: settle
members.description:
Says the arrangement has settled, so a consumer can keep it.

Through the audited path, so a consumer who owns `position` is told what was
asked for and decides, and one who does not has already had it applied.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
The keys a separator answers.

One axis, the one the divider actually travels along, plus `Home` and `End`
for its bounds. The other two arrows are left alone and the page scrolls
under them as it would anywhere else.

*Corrected 18 Aug 2026. This said "both axes, always", on the reasoning
`KeyboardNavigationController` uses for a set of items: a reader who guesses
the wrong arrow gets nothing. The code has never done it, and measuring the
three tab stops of a nested pair is what turned that up, so the prose was
describing a decision nobody implemented.*

*Leaving it as one axis, because nesting is what settles it. Taking all four
would mean `ArrowLeft` moving a horizontal divider up and down, which is not
a reader being helped past a guess, it is an arrow that does not go the way
it points. And the guess it was protecting against is answered better by the
corner: there, all four arrows are live and each moves the divider it points
along, which is the only place in a splitter where a second axis means
anything.*

members.name: reset
members.description: Puts the divider back where the markup put it.

members.name: handleCornerDoubleClick
members.description:
Both of them, because the corner moves both.

It needs its own handler now. Inside the separator this came free by
bubbling, and moving the corner out to sit against the host for the stacking
reason took the double click with it: the divider reset and the crossing
did not. Reported.

members.name: cross
members.description:
Records that a nested splitter crosses this one at `at` percent along it.

Public because it is the whole of the channel between the two, and it runs
one way: the child tells the parent where it is, and the parent draws the
corner and drives them both. Nothing is read back, so neither has to know
anything about the other's state.

members.name: uncross
members.description: Forgets a nested splitter that has left the tree. See `cross`.

members.name: findOuter
members.description:
Announces this splitter to the one it is nested in, if they cross.

Client only. The server has no tree to walk, and a parent that has not
upgraded has no `orientation` to compare against, so this waits for
`firstUpdated`. That is what the corner is allowed to be: an affordance
rather than content, absent from the served markup and appearing at
hydration, with two working dividers in the meantime.

`parentElement` first, so a splitter does not find itself.

**By identity rather than by tag, which `closestInstance` exists for and
counts this file in its own documentation.** It matched
`'helix-splitter, helix-headless-splitter'`, and only `@fusion.dev/helix` registers
the first of those: a headless package naming a styled one by string. Under
any third tag, which is exactly what subclassing a headless element is for and
what `helix/styled` itself does, the lookup returned null and a nested
splitter had no corner, with no error anywhere.

It also crosses shadow boundaries, which `closest` does not: a splitter
slotted into another component's shadow root has a `parentNode` chain
ending at a `ShadowRoot`, and nesting through a slot is the ordinary case
for anything composable.

members.name: handleCornerMove
members.description: Both axes at once, each measured against the splitter that owns it.

members.name: handleCornerKeydown

The corner takes every arrow, each moving the splitter whose axis it points

members.name: leaveSeparator
members.description:
Keeps a gesture on the corner to itself.

The corner was a child of the separator first, and every one of its events
bubbled there, so the separator started its own drag from the same press.
That is worse than moving twice: the separator calls `setPointerCapture`,
which retargets every later pointer event to *it*, so the corner's
`pointerup` never arrived, its origin was never cleared, and it went on
resizing with no button held. Reported as resizing without a press.

The corner is a sibling now, for the stacking reason in the stylesheet, so
nothing reaches the separator by bubbling. This stays because the fix should
not depend on where the element happens to sit, and `preventDefault` is
still needed either way: a drag across a pane would otherwise select the
text under it.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: variant
attributes.description:
Whether the divider carries a grip.

- `line` is the divider alone, for a splitter the reader already knows is
  one: an editor, a mail client, anything they open every day.
- `grip` adds a short capsule beside the line, for the first encounter. A
  hairline between two panels is a border until something says otherwise,
  and at rest the only thing saying otherwise is a cursor that appears once
  the pointer is already on it.

`grip` rather than `handle`, which this component has already spent on the
corner: that is a box the reader grabs, and this is a mark that says the
line can be grabbed. The grip adds no hit area of its own.

Both are writable, so a generated page can say which it means rather than
relying on the absence of an attribute.

attributes.name: orientation
attributes.description:
Which way the panes are laid out.

`horizontal` is side by side with an upright divider between them, and
`aria-orientation` on that divider is therefore `vertical`: a separator's
orientation is the direction it is *drawn* in, not the axis it moves along,
so the two words are opposite each other here on purpose. The code had this
right and the sentence beside it said the reverse.

Unset is horizontal and stays unset, so a reflected default cannot appear on
a host whose server output never had it.

**`auto` lays the panes out along whichever axis the splitter has room for**,
stacking them once its own inline size falls under `STACK_BELOW`. It is a
value rather than a default because turning a splitter is not a style
change: the drag axis, the arrow keys and `aria-orientation` all turn with
it, so a CSS-only version would look stacked and behave side by side, with
the keyboard moving the wrong way and the accessibility tree saying
something untrue. Everything here reads `vertical` rather than this
property, which is what makes one getter enough to turn all three together.

**Its own width and not the viewport**, per the responsiveness policy in
`.claude/rules/helix.md`: a splitter in a 300px panel of a 1400px window has
no room for two panes side by side, and a media query would hand it the
desktop branch. A `ResizeObserver` on the host asks the only question that
has an honest answer.

attributes.name: position
attributes.description:
Where the divider sits, as a percentage of the whole.

Reading gives where it is; writing declares it the consumer's, and
`default-position` seeds one this element owns. The same accessor pair
`Pagination.page` and the calendar's `month` carry.

attributes.name: default-position
attributes.description: Where the divider starts, where nothing declared it.

attributes.name: collapsed
attributes.description:
Which pane is shut, if either.

The same accessor pair as `position`, and deliberately a second state
rather than a reading of the first. A pane shut by dragging the divider to
the edge and a pane shut on purpose look identical in geometry and are not
the same thing: only the second knows where to go back to. Kept apart, the
open position is simply the one collapsing never overwrote, so restoring
needs no memory of its own.

It overrides `min` and `max`, which is the point of it. Those keep a sliver
of a pane during a drag; this is the thing that says the sliver can go.

attributes.name: default-collapsed
attributes.description: Which pane starts shut, where nothing declared it.

attributes.name: collapsed-size
attributes.description:
How much of a shut pane is still shown, as a percentage.

Zero by default, which is a pane fully gone. A tab strip or a title bar
that should survive its own collapse says how much of itself to keep, and
only whoever put it there knows that, which is the same reason `min` is a
consumer's to set.

attributes.name: min
attributes.description:
Nearest the divider may come to the start.

A bare number is a percentage, which is what this always took. A CSS length
is resolved against the splitter's own box along its axis, so `min="15rem"`
means fifteen rem of pane whatever the container is doing.

**The length is the one that holds.** A percentage minimum does not: twenty
per cent is 280px in a 1400px splitter and 100px in a 500px one, and the
number a consumer picked was almost certainly about how much text fits
rather than about a ratio. The pane that a percentage protects at desk
width is squeezed past reading at half of it.

**It does not fight `collapsed`.** Collapse overrides `min` and `max`, as
the class docstring says, so a pane can still be shut and reopened. What a
minimum forbids is the space between shut and usable: a pane wide enough to
be there and too narrow to read is the state nobody wants and every drag
passes through.

attributes.name: max
attributes.description: Nearest it may come to the end, on the same terms as `min`.

attributes.name: step
attributes.description: How far one arrow press moves it, as a percentage.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the divider.

attributes.name: corner-label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the handle where two dividers cross.

A divider the page owns, answering the event and assigning `position` and `collapsed`.
One gesture, two facts, and each says which one it is.
A divider with a visible grip rather than a bare rule.
A splitter inside a pane of another, which is how a workbench is built.
Panes stacked, with the divider between them.
The arrangement an editor uses: a tree, a document and a panel.

members.name: direction
members.description:
Which way the label and the value are arranged.

Absent is a column, the label over the number, which is how a figure is read
on a dashboard: the words say what is coming and the number answers.
`column-reverse` puts the number first, which is right where the number is
the headline and the label is a caption under it.

The row directions set them side by side, for a figure in a line of text or
a narrow strip where a stacked pair would be two lines of almost nothing.

A property rather than a `helix-flex` around it, because the unit has to
stay on the value's baseline whichever way the pair goes, and only this
element knows which of its children the unit belongs to.

**Optional rather than defaulted to `column`, which is not a style
preference.** A reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto
the host the moment the element upgrades, and the host is markup the
consumer rendered: React compares what it rendered against what is there and
reports a hydration mismatch. The absent attribute is the column, which the
stylesheet reads as the base case. The existing server spec caught this,
being the one that asserts the host carries nothing nobody wrote.

a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

attributes.name: direction
attributes.description:
Which way the label and the value are arranged.

Absent is a column, the label over the number, which is how a figure is read
on a dashboard: the words say what is coming and the number answers.
`column-reverse` puts the number first, which is right where the number is
the headline and the label is a caption under it.

The row directions set them side by side, for a figure in a line of text or
a narrow strip where a stacked pair would be two lines of almost nothing.

stay on the value's baseline whichever way the pair goes, and only this
element knows which of its children the unit belongs to.

preference.** A reflecting property with a default writes its attribute onto
the host the moment the element upgrades, and the host is markup the
consumer rendered: React compares what it rendered against what is there and
reports a hydration mismatch. The absent attribute is the column, which the
stylesheet reads as the base case. The existing server spec caught this,
being the one that asserts the host carries nothing nobody wrote.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description:
Initial item for uncontrolled use.

Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-activate` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back. Nobody refusing means the set updates itself,
whether or not a consumer declared `active`, a declared property being a
seed and a correction. See 294.

members.name: announceActivated
members.description:
Says the current child moved, once it has.

**This was the only one of the four mixins with no notification**, and the
event class said so deliberately: no native word means "a set chose a
different member", so borrowing `change` would be a lie about what moved.
That half still holds, and is why the pair is `helix-activate`. What did
not follow is that a set should therefore announce nothing.

The cost is the one 294 fixed for values and left here. A consumer who
only wants to know which child is current had one channel and it fires
*before* `apply`, so `currentTarget.active` is the previous value inside
the handler and `detail.value` is a proposal another listener may refuse.
Measured across the four families taking this: `Tabs` and `Tree` looked
covered because `helix-select` bubbles up from a child, which fires when an
item is *chosen* and not when `active` is assigned, and `Steps` and
`Video Playlist` announced nothing at all.

**After `apply`, which is the whole reason it is a second event**, so the
state is on the element by the time a handler reads it. Not cancelable:
the decision was taken by the event before this one, and two refusable
events for one transition are two answers to one question. See #325.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: label
members.description:
Accessible name for the sequence.

A list of stages is a landmark a reader arrives at out of order, so it
needs a name of its own rather than borrowing the heading above it.

members.name: orientation
members.description:
Which way the steps run.

Absent is a row, which is what a form header wants, with each name under
its mark: beside them there is a word in the rule's path and the line would
be struck through it. `vertical` stacks them, names beside their marks,
which is the shape with room under a step for what the stage holds.

Each axis has one arrangement rather than a second property offering both
in both. Of those four combinations three are ones nobody should pick, and
a property whose job is mostly to be left alone is a property that mostly
catches people out.

members.name: variant
members.description:
What each step is marked with.

Absent is the state itself: a check where a stage is done, a target where
the reader is, an empty ring ahead of them. Three marks that need no
legend, which a number does: "3" says where a stage sits in the order and
nothing about whether it is finished.

`numeric` is the older convention and is still the right one where the
order is the point, a form that says "step 3 of 5" beside it, or a sequence
a reader is told to come back to by number.

members.name: steps
members.description: The steps, in the order the consumer wrote them.

members.name: sync
members.description:
Puts `active` on whichever step owns it.

Returns without touching anything where nothing has set `active`, which is
the case a server renders: the steps' own `current` is the state then, and
overwriting it on hydration is exactly the flash this design exists to
avoid.

`current` only. `complete` is the consumer's on each step, because a reader
who steps back has finished more stages than they are standing in front of.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:

members.name: complete
members.description: Whether the reader has finished this stage.

members.name: current
members.description: Whether this is the stage the reader is in.

members.description: Whether the reader may go to this stage.

members.name: select

members.name: renderMarker
members.description:
The mark this stage's state calls for.

`complete` first, so a stage a reader has stepped back into keeps its check
rather than losing it to the target: they did finish it, and the name and
the rule below still say which one is open.

**Three shapes, and the reader can tell them apart with the color off.**
An outline circle for a stage nobody has reached, the same circle with a
center for the one they are standing on, a bare check for one that is done.
The first two are one shape filling in, which is the progression, and the
check is the only mark that leaves the family because finishing is the only
state that is not a position in the sequence.

What went was the coin around the check: a filled disc carrying a check
beside a filled disc carrying a ring put two of the three inside the same
container, and left hue doing most of the work of telling them apart.

The bare check is `Timeline`'s, deliberately: the two components report the
same kind of thing, a sequence with marks down it, and a check floating on
a hairline in one beside a check inside a green coin in the other was two
answers to one question. Timeline's rings came off the same day.

out, without reimplementing the whole template to do any of them. The tag is
interpolated rather than written, so `tier` resolves it: this renders the
headless element, and a styled subclass that sets `tier` renders the styled one
from the same template.

declarations.description:
A thumb traveling in a groove, which is the one place in the library color
is used to say "on". A checkbox does not, because a tick is legible on its
own; a switch has no mark, so the fill is the whole of what distinguishes the
two states and there is nothing else for it to be.

The input itself is the hit target and is drawn as the track, stretched over
it and invisible, so the press, the focus and the label forwarding are all
the platform's while the picture is ours.

**Its height is `--helix-size-switch`, which is one step above the
checkbox's** at every density rather than the same as it. A checkbox is a box
with a mark in it; a switch is a track with a thumb inside it, and at the
checkbox's height the thumb has two pixels of groove around it and the whole
control reads as a small dash. The width follows the height, so setting
`--switch-height` widens it too and the proportion is not something a
consumer has to keep.
