members.name: checked
members.description:
Whether the control is checked.

One property rather than two. Reading gives the real state whichever
mode the control is in; writing hands ownership to the consumer, which
is what the attribute in `<helix-checkbox checked>` does as well. The
same shape all four of these mixins have, for the reason given on
`MixinControllerOpen.open`.

Not reflected: the attribute is the consumer's input and stays as they
wrote it, and `:state(checked)` carries the resolved state for
stylesheets.

members.name: defaultChecked
members.description: Initial checked state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: checkedState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: requestChecked
members.description:
Requests a checked change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the
`helix-before-toggle` is a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the element updates itself, whether or not a consumer
declared the property: a declared property is a seed and a correction,
the way `<input value>` is, and a consumer who wants the change for
themselves refuses it and assigns their own. See 294.

members.name: toggleChecked
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: formStateRestoreCallback
members.description:
Restores the control when the browser brings a form back.

Hand-written on the checkbox and nowhere else, so `Switch`, the mixin's
only other consumer, had no restore at all: a reader who navigated away
and came back to a restored form found their switch flipped off. The
mixin owns `checked`, so the mixin owns putting it back.

Through `checked` rather than the private state, so a controlled consumer
is asked the same way every other change asks.

members.name: resetChecked
members.description:
Drops the uncontrolled state, so the control reads `defaultChecked`
again.

A form reset has to return a control to what its markup declared, and
clearing `checked` alone only leaves controlled mode. The value the
element has been keeping lives here, so this is where it is dropped.

members.name: hint
members.description: Help under the control, shown while there is nothing wrong.

members.name: feedback
members.description: What is wrong, in the reader's words rather than the browser's.

members.name: label
members.description: The accessible name, and the fallback for the `label` slot.

members.name: required
members.description: Whether the form refuses to submit without it.

members.name: touched
members.description:
Whether the reader has had a go at the field yet.

This was `:user-invalid`, which is the platform's own answer to "is this
field wrong *yet*" and is the right idea. It does not work here, and the
reason is structural rather than a browser bug: `:user-invalid` tracks
interaction with the element it is on, and nobody interacts with this
element. The reader types into an `<input>` inside its shadow root, so
the host's interaction flag is never set and the selector never matches.
Measured after submitting an invalid required field and again after
editing one and leaving it: false both times, while `:invalid` matched
both times.

So the moments are listened for instead, and both of them demonstrably
reach the host: `invalid` when a form is submitted with this control
failing, and `change` when the reader has edited and committed. Focus
alone is deliberately not one of them. Tabbing past an empty required
field should not be answered with an error.

members.name: validates
members.description:
Whether this element may be asked about its own validity at all.

Reading the static the platform itself reads to decide, rather than
probing: `validity` and `validationMessage` throw `NotSupportedError` on
an element that is not form-associated, and a group whose members each
submit themselves is not. Such a control still shows a message, it just
has to be given one.

members.name: renderGroupLabel
members.description:
A label over a set rather than beside a control.

A plain element and not a `<label for>`, because a group is not a single
control and there is nothing for `for` to point at. What names the group
is `linkHost`, pointing the host's internals at this element.

members.name: renderLabel
members.description:
A label above the control, pointing at it.

A real `<label for>`, so pressing the words focuses the field and the
browser does the forwarding. It resolves because `for` looks within the
same tree, and the control it names is in this shadow root.

**Nothing at all when there is no label**, which is the same rule the
hint and the feedback follow: none of the three is always used, and an
element rendered empty is not free. It still generates a box, so it still
takes a row of the grid and a gap on either side of it, which is a field
that has moved down the page for a label nobody wrote. `nothing` leaves
comment markers rather than a node, so the gap has nothing to sit between.

**`aria-label` names without showing**, and it is forwarded rather than
left where the consumer put it. A custom element has no way to delegate a
label to the control inside it, so an `aria-label` on the host reaches
nothing: measured, the inner input came back with no label and no name of
its own while the attribute sat on the wrapper. What happens instead is
that the label is rendered and clipped, so the name arrives through the
same `<label for>` a visible one does.

This replaced `hide-label`, which was a second attribute to say what the
absence of the first should have said. The rule is now `label` means a
label, `aria-label` means a name, and neither means an unnamed field a
screen reader announces as "edit text"

members.name: renderHint
members.description:
Help under the control, unless something has gone wrong.

The two share a place rather than stacking, so a field is one line of
small text either way and nothing below it moves when the message
changes. What the reader needs at that moment is what is wrong, and a
hint that survives the error it describes is a second line to read before
getting to the one that matters.

members.name: renderFeedback
members.description:
The validation message, in the hint's place.

`role="alert"` rather than a live region on the whole field, so what is
announced is the message and not the label and help along with it.

members.name: linkHost
members.description:
Points the host at its own label and description nodes, for a group.

A control's `<input>` and its hint are both in the shadow root, so a
plain `aria-describedby` resolves between them. A group's host is in the
light DOM and its hint is not, so the IDREF cannot reach and
`element.ariaDescribedByElements` drops the reference outright. Only the
`ElementInternals` form keeps it, measured in Chrome 148: two of two
kept through internals, zero of one through the element.

Client only, and deliberately, because element references need the nodes
to exist and on the server they do not. The name is therefore also set as
a plain string by the component, which a server can write, and the
reference here overrides it wherever a consumer slotted something richer
than a string. A group with only a property for a label reads the same
either way.

members.name: shownFeedback
members.description: What the last render put on screen, so a change can be noticed.

members.name: refreshFeedback
members.description:
Re-reads the platform's verdict, for a control that has just reported one.

Validity changes through `ElementInternals` rather than through a
property, so nothing schedules an update for it. Worse, the order is
against us: this mixin sits above the control in the prototype chain, so
its `updated` runs before the control's own, which is where `setValidity`
is called. Reading the verdict here would always read the previous one,
which is what left a corrected field still showing the error it had
before. So the control says when it has reported, and this schedules the
one further update that needs. It converges because the second pass finds
nothing changed.

members.name: reportRequired
members.description:
Reports "required and empty" and refreshes the message, or clears both.

Seven families had this written out: the same `valueMissing`, the same
anchor lookup, the same `refreshFeedback` under the same comment about
validity moving without a property moving. Seven copies of a five-line
shape is the threshold at which this mixin itself was extracted, and two
of them had already drifted, `checkbox-group` having no validity at all
until yesterday.

What differs between them is exactly two things, so those are the
arguments: whether the control is empty, which only it can say, and the
sentence to say about it, which is different for a box, a switch and a
set. The anchor is looked up here because every one of them anchored on a
rendered part and the browser needs somewhere to point the bubble.

The message is not derived from the control's kind, deliberately. "Tick
this box" and "Choose one" are not the same instruction and a lookup
table would be one more thing to keep in step with the components.

members.name: value
members.description: Value submitted when the switch is on.

members.name: sync
members.description: Reports what the form would submit, and the verdict on it.

members.name: formResetCallback
members.description: Returns the switch to the state its markup declared.

members.name: markEmpty
members.description:
Says on the `label` region whether anything is in it.

An empty region is not free: it is still a flex item, so it still takes the
container's gap. There is no selector that can ask, `slot:empty` being
about a slot's fallback rather than its assigned nodes, so the component
asks and says so, on the region inside this shadow root rather than on the
host: an attribute written onto the host is a change to markup the consumer
rendered, which React reports on hydration and does not patch up.

members.name: formAssociated
members.description: Opts the element into form ownership, labels, and submission.

members.name: disabled
members.description:
Whether the control is non-interactive.

Reflected, because the styled tier selects on it, and mirrored to
`aria-disabled` rather than removing the element from the accessibility
tree, so a screen reader can still announce that the control exists.

The mirror is below and was for a while only a sentence: this paragraph
described it, four components had their own copies of it, and the class
itself did nothing. Here is where it belongs, because here is where
`disabled` is.

members.name: formDisabled
members.description:
Whether an ancestor `<fieldset disabled>` has switched this control off.

The platform tells a form-associated element through `formDisabledCallback`
and nothing here implemented it, so a control inside a disabled fieldset
stayed fully typeable and announced itself as enabled. Measured: a
`helix-input` in one accepted text, reported `disabled` as false, and
carried no `aria-disabled`.

What the platform already did on its own is the submission half. The same
measurement showed the fieldset's controls absent from the form's entry
list and the host matching `:disabled`, so the value never went anywhere.
What was missing is everything a reader can see or touch.

State rather than the `disabled` property. Writing that would reflect an
attribute the consumer's server markup does not have, which React reports
on hydration and does not patch up, and it would also silently overwrite
what the consumer set.

members.name: formDisabledCallback
members.description:
The platform's notice that an ancestor fieldset changed.

**The argument is the effective state, and taking it whole is what latched
every control in the library.** The platform calls this for the element's
own `disabled` as well as for a fieldset, and our own arrives here at the
worst possible moment: reflecting `disabled` to the attribute happens
inside Lit's `update()`, the UA fires this synchronously from that write,
and a reactive write during an update is a change-in-update Lit does not
re-render for. So `formDisabled` ran exactly one update behind forever.

Measured on Slider, logging what `render` saw:

```
set true    disabled true   formDisabled false  isDisabled true
set false   disabled false  formDisabled true   isDisabled true   <- stale
(no third render)
```

The host came out right every time, `disabled` false, `:disabled` not
matching, and the inner control kept the attribute, so a control disabled
once could never be re-enabled. It only shows when something re-enables,
which is the same shape of bug `inheritDisabled` was written for.

Our own half is already in `this.disabled` and `isDisabled` is an or, so
this records only what the fieldset adds. That also removes the write
entirely on the own-disabled path rather than moving it.

The one case this cannot see is a control that is disabled itself *and*
inside a disabled fieldset, whose own `disabled` is then removed: the
effective state does not change, so the platform does not call again, and
the fieldset's hold is not recorded. There is no callback to learn it from
and reading `:disabled` here would answer about the attribute we are in the
middle of removing.

members.name: name
members.description:
Name submitted with the form.

**Reflected, and it is the exception to "reflect only what CSS selects
on".** The platform builds a form's entry list from the `name` *content
attribute*, not from the property, so a control named through the property
submitted under no name at all and was silently dropped. Measured: two
inputs in one form, one named by attribute and one by property, and the
form carried a single entry.

Safe for a React consumer, which is what the rule is protecting: React
renders a custom element's props as attributes on the server, so the name
is already in the markup being hydrated and reflecting it writes what is
there. It is only a change to the markup when a consumer assigns it
imperatively later, and nothing is hydrating by then.

Here rather than on each control, where it was declared eight times and
reflected none of them.

members.name: form
members.description: The form this control belongs to, if any.

members.name: labels
members.description: Labels associated with this control.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: One cell of a table.

attributes.name: header
attributes.description: Whether the cell heads its column.

declarations.description:
Styled as the header cell it is, and it carries the same rule and inset as
the cells beneath it so the heading and its column read as one line down the
table.
declarations.name: HelixTableColumn

members.name: width
members.description:
The track this column takes, as CSS.

A single track value, so anything valid in `grid-template-columns` works:
`16rem`, `auto`, `minmax(0, 2fr)`. Left unset the column shares what is
left over equally, as `minmax(max-content, 1fr)`.

**The floor was `0` and that is what broke a narrow table.** A zero floor
lets a track shrink under its own content, so at 375 the columns were
squeezed to 75px and `eu-central-1` wrapped across lines, which reads as
corrupt data rather than as a table that ran out of room. The zero was
chosen to stop one long value pushing the table past its container, and
that was the right worry with nowhere for the overflow to go.

Somewhere now exists: `@fusion.dev/helix` scrolls the table's own box. So a
long value pushes past the container as the old comment feared, and the
table scrolls instead of the value being destroyed. Measured at 375: tracks
of 192, 89 and 102 against a 343 box, so the table scrolls 384 and the page
does not move.

**`max-content` and not `min-content`, because a hyphen is a wrap
opportunity.** A `min-content` floor still broke `eu-central-1` at its
hyphens, which is the whole of the reported fault. The cost is that a
column of prose asks for its longest paragraph on one line, so a column
holding sentences rather than values wants `width="minmax(0, 1fr)"` to opt
back into wrapping. A headless consumer owns the overflow either way, that
being paint, and gets the honest track list.

members.name: field
members.description:
The key this column reads out of a row.

Dot paths resolve, so `field="owner.name"` reads a nested value: a result
from an API arrives shaped the way the API shaped it, and requiring a flat
row would push a mapping pass onto every consumer.

**It is also the sort and filter identity**, which is why sorting is by
field and not by column index: a reordered or hidden column would otherwise
change what `sort="2:asc"` means, and a sort that means something different
after a column moves is a sort a consumer cannot store in a URL.

Empty on a column that is purely presentational, an actions column say, and
such a column is never sortable however it is marked.

members.name: sortable
members.description:
Whether a reader may reorder the set by this column.

Ignored without a `field`, and silently: a column with nothing to sort by
has no order to offer, and refusing loudly would mean an actions column
carrying `sortable` breaks a table rather than doing nothing.

members.name: align
members.description:
Which edge the values line up against.

`end` is what a column of numbers wants, so digits of the same magnitude sit
above each other. Left unset the cell inherits the table's own alignment,
which is `start` for text in either writing direction.

members.name: cell
members.description:
How to read the cell, where the field alone will not do.

A property and not an attribute, because it is a function. Set it from a Lit
template with `.cell=${...}`, or assign it in script. A column with neither
this nor a `field` renders an empty cell rather than the whole row stringified,
which is the failure mode of guessing.

members.name: compare
members.description:
How to read the value that gets sorted and filtered, where it is not the cell.

**The one that is easy to leave out and expensive to add later.** A cell
showing `2.4 MB` sorts as a string unless something says the underlying value
is a number, so `12 kB` sorts above `2.4 MB` and the column looks broken
while every value in it is right. Left unset this is the field, which is the
correct default: the raw value is what an API sorted by.

members.name: track
members.description: The track this column contributes, resolved.

members.name: canSort
members.description: Whether a reader can actually reorder by this column.

members.name: read
members.description:
The value this column shows for a row.

`cell` first, then the field. An explicit reader that returns `undefined` is
treated as declining rather than as an answer, so a formatter can hand the
default back for the rows it has nothing to say about.

members.name: order
members.description: The value this column sorts and filters by, which is not always what it shows.

members.name: tier

decorating none of it.

cssProperties.description: Track list for the columns.
cssProperties.name: --table-columns

cssProperties.description: The column track list this element worked out from the columns declared in it. Written by the component, read by the sheet that paints: a stylesheet takes it to lay the grid out, and setting it does nothing, because the component writes it inline on the very element that reads it and an inline declaration beats any sheet. `--table-columns` is the one to set.
cssProperties.name: --table-template

cssParts.description: The grid.
cssParts.name: table

cssParts.description: Shown when there are no rows to show.
cssParts.name: empty

cssParts.description: The row the column headings sit in. `display: contents`, so it takes no space.
cssParts.name: head

cssParts.description: Shown while the rows are still on their way.
cssParts.name: loading

slots.description: The table's rows.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the rows are still on their way.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What is said while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: slotCounted
members.description: Whether the rows have been looked at yet.

members.name: slotRows
members.description:
How many there were, the last time anyone looked.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this comment.**
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time claim and the runtime field is
whatever it is named, so a subclass declaring `@property() rows` for the
data a consumer hands it would share one field with this counter: the
slot count would overwrite the consumer's array on every `updated`, and
`hasRows` would read the array's length as a slot count. Nothing would
throw. `helix-data-table` takes exactly that property, which is what
found this before it happened.

members.name: countRows
members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: renderStatus
members.description:
The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: columns
members.description:
Column track list, as CSS. Deprecated: declare columns instead.

Kept for a table that has no `helix-table-column` children, and ignored the
moment it has one. A raw track list is the right shape for the value and
the wrong place for it: the headings and the widths were two halves of one
fact held in two places, and nothing checked that they agreed. Worse, the
value is CSS, so handing it headings by mistake produced an invalid track
list, which a grid ignores in silence: the table collapsed to one column
and said nothing. Columns carry both halves now.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the table.

members.name: tableColumns
members.description: The columns declared as children, in the order they are written.

members.name: template
members.description:
The track list, from the columns if there are any.

Read from the DOM rather than kept, so adding or removing a column needs
nothing else to be told. Falls back to the `columns` string for a table
written before columns existed, and to a single track for one that declares
neither.

members.name: shadowRootOptions

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.

word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug

itself before React reached the node.

other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:

whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description:
Initial item for uncontrolled use.

Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-activate` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back. Nobody refusing means the set updates itself,
whether or not a consumer declared `active`, a declared property being a
seed and a correction. See 294.

members.name: announceActivated
members.description:
Says the current child moved, once it has.

**This was the only one of the four mixins with no notification**, and the
event class said so deliberately: no native word means "a set chose a
different member", so borrowing `change` would be a lie about what moved.
That half still holds, and is why the pair is `helix-activate`. What did
not follow is that a set should therefore announce nothing.

The cost is the one 294 fixed for values and left here. A consumer who
only wants to know which child is current had one channel and it fires
*before* `apply`, so `currentTarget.active` is the previous value inside
the handler and `detail.value` is a proposal another listener may refuse.
Measured across the four families taking this: `Tabs` and `Tree` looked
covered because `helix-select` bubbles up from a child, which fires when an
item is *chosen* and not when `active` is assigned, and `Steps` and
`Video Playlist` announced nothing at all.

**After `apply`, which is the whole reason it is a second event**, so the
state is on the element by the time a handler reads it. Not cancelable:
the decision was taken by the event before this one, and two refusable
events for one transition are two answers to one question. See #325.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: keys
members.default: new KeyboardNavigationController(this, { items: () => this.tabs, origin: 'focus', selects: () => !this.manual, })

members.name: indicator
members.default: new IndicatorController(this, { active: () => this.tabs.find((tab) => tab.selected), indicator: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="indicator"]'), surface: () => this.renderRoot?.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="tabs"]'), })

members.name: variant
members.description:
How the row reads.

Unset is a raised pill on the selected tab with nothing behind the row,
which is what a set sitting inside other chrome wants. `underlined` is a
rule under the row and a thicker one under the selected tab, for a set that
heads a page. `segmented` puts the pill in a framed, sunken track, which
reads as one control rather than as a row.

`segmented` and not `toggle`, which is what this was called. An appearance
value that is another component's name says "it looks like that one", which
a reader can only act on if they already know what that one looks like, and
every other appearance in the library describes itself: `outlined`,
`spaced`, `plain`. This component's own comments called it segmented in
both places it explained itself, which is the name that was doing the work.

`underlined` and not `underline` for the shape of the word rather than the
sense: the two values sit in one list and read as a pair, and `segmented`
is a participle. `outlined` on Accordion is the same word doing the same
job. The example file was already `underlined.html`, which is what a reader
meets first.

Reflected and left unset by default, so the host carries nothing a
consumer's server markup does not already have.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the tab list.

members.name: manual
members.description:
Whether arrowing to a tab also selects it.

Automatic is the default because showing a panel is usually cheap. Set this
where it is not, so a reader arrowing past four tabs does not load four
panels on the way.

members.name: observer
members.description: Watches for anything that moves a tab, since none of it is a property.

members.name: sync
members.description: Pushes the current value down to whichever tab and panel own it.

members.name: measure
members.description: The host's own size, which moves every tab and therefore the mark.

members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches every tab for a change of size.

Called again whenever the set changes, because `tabs` reads `this.children`
and filters on `instanceof`, so it is empty until the tab elements upgrade.
At `firstUpdated` it frequently is empty, and observing nothing is silent.

`observe` is idempotent per element, so re-running this costs nothing and
needs no bookkeeping about which tabs are already watched.

members.name: handleSlotChange
members.description:
The set changed: pair it up, watch it, and measure it.

All three, where this used to be `sync()` alone, and the missing `place()`
is why an indicator could stay unplaced for the life of the page. The order
of events is what does it: the host renders and measures before its tabs
have upgraded, so there is no selected tab to measure and `place` refuses;
the ResizeObserver's one initial callback lands in that same gap; and then
the tabs upgrade, `slotchange` pairs them, nothing measures, and nothing
ever will again, because the host's size never changes.

Invisible in every example, because a tab strip that is only tabs is
exactly as tall as its tabs, so a mark at the top of the strip is a mark on
the tab. It showed up where something gives the strip a height of its own.

The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: A row of tabs and the panel each one shows.

examples.description: Panels behind tabs, with a mark that travels between them.
A strip the page owns, answering the event and assigning `active`.
A move announced before it happens, and one tab that refuses to be moved to.
Arrow keys move between tabs without opening them, so a reader can look before choosing.
The tabs drawn as one segmented control.
A rule under the active tab rather than a filled one.

attributes.name: active
attributes.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

attributes.name: default-active
attributes.description:
Initial item for uncontrolled use.

Ignored once `active` is written.

attributes.name: variant
attributes.description:
How the row reads.

Unset is a raised pill on the selected tab with nothing behind the row,
which is what a set sitting inside other chrome wants. `underlined` is a
rule under the row and a thicker one under the selected tab, for a set that
heads a page. `segmented` puts the pill in a framed, sunken track, which
reads as one control rather than as a row.

`segmented` and not `toggle`, which is what this was called. An appearance
value that is another component's name says "it looks like that one", which
a reader can only act on if they already know what that one looks like, and
every other appearance in the library describes itself: `outlined`,
`spaced`, `plain`. This component's own comments called it segmented in
both places it explained itself, which is the name that was doing the work.

`underlined` and not `underline` for the shape of the word rather than the
sense: the two values sit in one list and read as a pair, and `segmented`
is a participle. `outlined` on Accordion is the same word doing the same
job. The example file was already `underlined.html`, which is what a reader
meets first.

Reflected and left unset by default, so the host carries nothing a
consumer's server markup does not already have.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name for the tab list.

attributes.name: manual
attributes.description:
Whether arrowing to a tab also selects it.

Automatic is the default because showing a panel is usually cheap. Set this
where it is not, so a reader arrowing past four tabs does not load four
panels on the way.

events.description: Fired once the current one has moved, so the element already holds it.
events.name: helix-activate

events.description: Fired before the current tab moves, and cancelable. The only way to refuse one.
events.name: helix-before-activate

events.description: Fired when a tab is chosen. Dispatched by the tab and listened for here, because the root is what a consumer holds. Cancelable: refusing it takes the decision and nothing moves.
events.name: helix-select

declarations.description:
Selection is marked with a rule under the active tab rather than a filled
pill, which keeps the row flat and lets the underline animate between tabs as
a movement instead of two separate fills.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: tone
members.description:
Which status the tag reports.

This was called `appearance`, and it never was one. `tone` is semantic
color, which is what these are and what `helix-text` already calls them.
One axis was wearing the other's name, and the axis it should have held did
not exist.

**Written before there was a registry, and it turned out to be the first
instance of a general fault rather than a local one.** `appearance` was not
a treatment either: it held four different questions across 21 components,
and this file found one of them the hard way. The rest is `check:axes`.

members.name: emphasis
members.description:
How much of the tone the tag wears.

- `subtle` is the default: a wash of the tone with the label in it, for a
  tag that labels something rather than warning about it.
- `solid` fills with the tone and puts the label on top of it, for the one
  that has to be seen first.
- `outlined` is the tone at its edge only, for a dense set where filling
  each of them turns a list into a mosaic.

Independent of `tone` on purpose: an outlined danger tag and a solid danger
tag are both sensible, and until these were two properties you could ask
for neither, because color and fill were welded together. Which is the same
test the whole axis registry answers to, arrived at here first and one
component at a time.

members.name: dismissible
members.description: Whether it offers a control to take it away.

members.name: dismissLabel
members.description:
Accessible name for that control.

`attribute` is spelled out because Lit lowercases a property name to
derive one rather than dash-casing it, so this would otherwise be
reachable only as `dismisslabel`, which nobody would guess and no linter
would catch.

members.name: dismissEvent
members.description:
The event, built and not dispatched.

Reading text is safe here: nothing calls this on a server, because the
only things that do are a press and a timer.

members.name: dismiss
members.description: Announces that it should go, and reports whether the request stood.

declarations.description:
Two properties, and they answer different questions. `as` is the element, which decides the document outline and what a screen reader announces. `variant` is the ramp, which decides size, weight, leading, and tracking together. They are separate because they genuinely come apart: a section's second heading sometimes has to look smaller without lying about the outline, and a `

` sometimes has to read as a caption. They default to matching, so the common case is `as="h2"` and nothing else. The pairing is resolved in CSS rather than by computing an attribute, so the element writes nothing to its own host: `as="h2"` picks up the heading ramp through a selector, and setting `variant` takes the pairing rule out of play. Deriving it in `willUpdate` worked, but it put an attribute on the host that the server's markup did not have, which is a hydration mismatch in every React consumer. **Size, weight, and leading are not properties.** Exposing them separately offers a few hundred combinations of which a handful are right, and every caller then picks one. A ramp is a decision the system already made: the ramp is named, and a page built from it is consistent because there was nothing else to choose. `tone` stays separate, because color carries state rather than typography. Folding it in would mean `caption-danger` and `label-primary` and the rest of cross product, which is the explosion a named ramp exists to prevent.

members.name: as
members.description:
Which element to render.

Decides the outline and the semantics.

members.name: variant
members.description:
Type treatment.

Defaults to the one that matches `as`.

members.name: tone
members.description:
Color role. A separate axis from the type ramp, because color carries
state: folding it in would mean `caption-danger` and the rest of the cross
product.

**`default` is gone, having been styled nowhere.** It matched no rule and
fell through to the inherited ink, so it read as working while saying
nothing, which is the same shape as the `shadow` an example wrote at Video.
The resting case is the absent attribute.

**`muted` and `subtle` are weight rather than meaning and belong on
`emphasis`, which is why this is still off the registry.** Splitting them
out is blocked on the palette rather than on the rename: there is a quiet
step for the neutral ink and none for any other tone, so a muted danger has
nothing to be made of. `primary-subtle` is a tinted *ground* and not a
quiet ink. That is #141's to derive, and until it does, folding the two
halves apart would leave three of the four combinations unsayable.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.
