members.name: material
members.description:
What the bubble is made of.

Absent is the inverse bubble, a dark surface over a light page, which is
what a hint over content the theme cannot know has always been here. `glass`
makes it the page's own translucent ground instead, for a page whose surfaces
are glass, so a hint over a glass header is not the one opaque slab on it.

**It flips the ink and adds an edge, which no other family carrying this axis
has to do.** A card is already the page's surface, so glass swaps one ground
for another; this one starts inverse, and `--helix-material-translucent` is
the page's ground, so taking it without the foreground would put light ink on
a light bubble. An inverse bubble is told from the page by being its
opposite and a glass one has to be told from what is behind it, which is why
the border arrives with the material rather than being there all along.

The strength is the theme's: `--helix-material-translucent` and
`--helix-material-backdrop` are what the policy moves.

**`emphasis` is not here and that is not an omission.** It says how much ink
a *mark* claims, and this is a surface: what varies about a surface is where
it ends, which is `separation`, and a bubble in the top layer with a point on
it has one answer to that. A quiet tooltip is a tooltip that is not shown.

**`transparent` is where this one stops, and that is the statement 270
asks for rather than an omission.** A panel that floats over arbitrary page
content is only readable because it has a ground; dropping it does not make
a lighter tooltip, it makes an unreadable one. `frosted` and `glass` are the
two honest points here.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-open` or
`helix-before-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the
element opens or closes itself, whether or not a consumer declared
`open`: a declared property is a seed and a correction, and a consumer
who wants the decision for themselves refuses it and assigns their own.
See 294.

members.name: announceToggle
members.description:
Says the state moved, under the platform's own name and in its shape.

**`<details>` fires `toggle` and a popover fires `toggle`, and sixteen
families here fired neither.** Two of them render a real `<dialog>` and
ten show a `popover="manual"` panel, so the browser was already firing
something on an element inside a shadow root, where `toggle` neither
bubbles nor composes and so reaches nobody. The rest, the disclosures,
have no native element to fire anything at all: `AccordionItem` and
`TreeItem` are `aria-expanded` and `hidden` written by hand, which is
`<details>`'s job done manually.

**From here rather than from `PopoverController`, which had it first.**
The controller covers eleven families and the mixin covers sixteen, and
the overlap is ten that would have announced twice. What `toggle` reports
is the *state*, and the state is this mixin's; the controller is a way of
putting a panel on the screen.

**`newState` and `oldState`, because that is the platform's shape**, so a
consumer arriving from `<details>` reads the same two words. Not
cancelable: the before events are the request, and a second cancelable
event for one transition is two answers to one question.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: content
members.description:
The text shown in the bubble.

The common case, and the fallback for the `content` slot: slot something
there and it replaces this. Both cannot show at once, which is the point
of using fallback content rather than rendering whichever is present.

members.name: for
members.description:
The id of the element this describes, in this tooltip's own tree.

Set it and the tooltip stops wrapping: it renders no trigger, listens on
the element it names, and points its bubble there. Leave it unset and the
default slot is the trigger, which is the older form.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a tooltip inside another component's
shadow root names an element in that root rather than in the document.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, which is
worth knowing before someone reads the DOM and thinks it did not take.
Measured against React 19.2.8: `for` exists on the prototype, so React sets
`element.for = 'save'` and writes nothing to the markup, where `content`
and `placement`, which are not properties on the class at that moment, come
through as attributes. Both paths reach the same place through Lit, so
nothing is broken by it; a `[for]` selector would find nothing, which is
why this does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

members.name: placement
members.description:
Preferred side.

It moves if that side does not fit.

members.name: offset
members.description:
Space between the trigger and the point of the bubble, in pixels.

**Measured from the point, which is what the arrow being back changed.**
The arrow is drawn half outside the bubble, so a gap measured to the
bubble's edge is a smaller gap to the tip: at the default it left the point
two pixels off the trigger, which reads as touching. The controller is
given this plus however far the arrow actually protrudes, so eight means
eight from whatever is nearest, arrow or edge, and a consumer who changes
it changes the visible gap rather than a number the arrow then eats into.

members.name: within
members.description:
The id of a box to keep the bubble inside, instead of the viewport.

Resolved the way `for` is, so an id in the same tree, which is what lets a
component name a box in its own shadow root. A chart does: its bubble is
centered on a reading, and the first and last readings sit at the ends of
the plot, so half the box hangs past the drawing and, measured on a chart
in a 320px card, three pixels past the card itself.

Clamping is on the cross axis only, which is what makes this safe to point
at a box the bubble genuinely does not fit inside. See `within` on
`FloatingController` for what happens if it is applied to the rest.

members.name: disabled
members.description: Whether the tooltip never shows.

members.name: persist
members.description:
Whether the bubble survives the trigger being used.

**Activation takes a tooltip down, because a hint about what a control will
do is spent once the control has done it.** That is right for a gear that
opens a drawer and wrong for a control whose tooltip *becomes* the answer:
`CopyButton` swaps its content from Copy to Copied on the same click, so the
bubble was being hidden at the exact moment it had something to say. What a
reader saw was a flash, and the confirmation the component had carefully
written was never on screen long enough to read.

So this is not "keep it open", it is "the hint is not spent": set it where
the words change to describe what just happened, and leave it alone
everywhere else. Escape, blur and pointer-leave still close it, because
those are a reader saying they are done rather than a control saying it
worked.

members.name: delay
members.description:
How long the pointer must rest before the bubble appears, in milliseconds.

Without one, sweeping across a row of controls flashes a tooltip for each
of them, which is noise rather than help. Focus opens with no delay: a
keyboard reader arriving on a control has already committed to it.

members.name: delayOut
members.description: How long the bubble stays after the pointer leaves, in milliseconds.

members.name: holds
members.description:
What is currently keeping the bubble up.

The pointer and focus are two holders and they shared one timer with
nothing counting them, so whichever left last won: moving the pointer off a
control that still had keyboard focus scheduled a hide and took the bubble
away from under the reader. The same fault the toast timer had, and the
same answer.

members.name: trigger
members.description:
The element the bubble points at.

The trigger, not the host. The host is `display: contents` so it wraps
without adding a box, and an element that generates no box measures as
nothing at the document origin: the bubble was placed against the corner
of the viewport rather than against the button.

members.name: reposition
members.description:
Places the bubble again, for an anchor that moved without the page moving.

Public because a chart needs it. Its mark walks from reading to reading
while the page holds still, and `autoUpdate` watches scrolling, resizing
and layout shift, none of which is that. Everything else floating here is
anchored to something the page moves, which is why nothing wanted this
until a chart did.

members.name: named
members.description:
The element `for` names, or null.

`getRootNode()` rather than `document`, which is what makes this work inside
another component: an id is unique to a tree, and a tooltip in a shadow root
names an element in that root. Client only, since the server has no tree to
search.

members.name: bubbleLayer
members.default: new PopoverController(this, { anchor: () => this.trigger, arrow: () => this.renderRoot.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="arrow"]'), /* Annotated, because without it the array's element type is inferred from `this`, whose own type depends on this controller, and TypeScript stops at the cycle. */ boundary: (): readonly (Element | null)[] => [this, this.named], /* The declared gap plus the arrow's own reach, so the gap is to the point. * * A square of side `n` rotated forty-five degrees about its own center * reaches `n / sqrt(2)` from that center, and the arrow is placed with its * center on the bubble's edge, so that is exactly how far past the edge the * tip goes. Read from the element rather than assumed, because * `--tooltip-arrow-size` is a hook and a theme may have moved it. * * `offsetWidth` and not `getBoundingClientRect`, which reports the rotated * box and would count the reach twice. Zero while the bubble is closed and * unrendered, which is right: there is nothing to place then either. */ offset: () => { const point = this.renderRoot.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="arrow"]') return this.offset + (point?.offsetWidth ?? 0) / Math.SQRT2 }, onDismiss: () => this.hide(), placement: () => this.placement, surface: () => this.renderRoot.querySelector<HTMLElement>('[part="tooltip"]'), within: () => this.enclosure, })

members.name: enclosure
members.description:
The element `within` names, or null.

Same resolution as `named`, and separate from it because they answer
different questions: one is what the bubble points at and the other is what
it must stay inside, and a component often has one and not the other.

members.name: hasContent
members.description: Whether there is anything to show. Asked of the slot rather than of the property, because either can carry the content. `assignedNodes` without `flatten` answers what the consumer provided and not what the fallback would render, which is exactly the question: a bubble with only fallback and an empty property is empty. Text or an element, because neither alone is the test. An element on its own would count ` ` as something to say, and text on its own would count an icon as nothing, when an icon is the whole point of slotting rather than setting the property. Client only. The server has no assignment to inspect, and nothing calls this there: a tooltip opens in response to a pointer or to focus.

members.name: describedText
members.description:
The bubble's words as a plain string, for naming the host.

The property when it is set, otherwise whatever was slotted, flattened.
Rich content collapses to its text, which is the right answer for a
description: `Save ⌘ S` is what a reader needs, not the markup.

members.name: handleContentChange
members.description:
Re-links the description when what is in the bubble changes.

`updated` alone is not enough: content arriving from the light DOM changes
no property here, so nothing would schedule the update that re-reads it. A
consumer rendering the bubble's content after this upgrades, which is what
a framework does, would leave the trigger describing nothing.

members.name: show
members.description: Shows the bubble, unless there is nothing to show.

members.name: hide
members.description:
Closes the bubble, and cancels a show that had not happened yet.

The timer matters as much as the state: a pointer that arrives and leaves
inside the delay left one queued, and the tooltip appeared over whatever
the reader had moved on to.

members.name: showLater
members.description: Shows after the pointer has rested for `delay`.

members.name: hideLater
members.description: Hides after `delayOut`, so crossing the gap to the bubble does not close it.

members.name: showNow
members.description:
Focus opens the bubble, but only the kind of focus a reader chose.

**A mouse press focuses the button it pressed**, so an unconditional focus
hold meant that after any click the bubble was held up by a reader who was
not asking for it: moving the pointer away released the pointer hold, found
a focus hold still set, and left the tooltip on screen until something else
blurred the control.

It never showed until `persist` arrived, because activation used to clear
every hold and hide, so the click path threw the stale hold away before
anyone could see it. A tooltip that survives its own activation is the first
one to hold that focus long enough to matter.

`:focus-visible` is the platform's own answer to "did they mean it", and a
button does not match it on a mouse press. Keyboard focus still opens with no
delay, which is the case this branch exists for: a reader who tabbed to a
control has already committed to it. Where it does not match there is nothing
to do, the pointer having opened the bubble already if a pointer is involved.

members.name: release
members.description: Hides only once nothing is holding the bubble up.

members.name: handleActivate
members.description:
Activating the trigger closes the bubble, which nothing was doing.

A tooltip is a hint about what a control will do, and once the control has
been used the hint is spent. Nothing else was going to take it down either:
`pointerleave` cannot fire while the pointer is still on the button it just
pressed, and `focusout` does not fire when activation leaves focus where it
was. So a gear that opened a drawer left its own label floating over the
drawer until the reader moved the mouse away.

`click` rather than `pointerdown`, because it is the one event both a mouse
and a keyboard produce: Enter and Space on a focused button raise it, and a
hint that outlived activation for keyboard readers alone would be the same
bug with a smaller audience.

Holds are cleared as well as hiding, the same as Escape. Leaving them set
means the pointer is still recorded as being over the trigger, so the next
`focusout` anywhere releases nothing and the bubble comes back on a
`release` it should have been dropped from.

`persist` opts out entirely, holds included: a tooltip whose content becomes
the confirmation has not spent its hint, it has changed it, and the pointer
really is still over the trigger. See the property.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
Escape closes the bubble from wherever the reader is.

On the document, not on the host, which is where it was: a tooltip opened
by hover has focus somewhere else entirely, so the press never reached this
element and Escape worked only for the one case that needed it least. That
is the case the pattern names, a reader escaping a tooltip obscuring what
is under it, and it was the case that did nothing.

Not stopped from propagating: a tooltip is not what the reader was trying
to escape if it sits inside something else that also closes.

members.name: bound
members.description:
What the pointer and focus listeners are currently on.

Held, rather than recomputed at removal time, because what `for` names can
change: unbinding from wherever the element is *now* leaves a live listener
on wherever it was, and a tooltip that opens from a control it no longer
describes is worse than one that does not open at all.

members.name: bind
members.description:
Puts the listeners on whatever the trigger is.

The host when it wraps, since the trigger is inside it and both `focusin`
and `focusout` bubble. The named element when `for` is set, because then the
host wraps nothing and `pointerenter` does not bubble at all.

Client only, and after the first render: `for` names an element that may not
have upgraded, or existed, when this one connected.

members.name: audited
members.description: Said once per element, however many times it opens.

members.name: auditDescription
members.description:
Checks that the trigger actually points back, and says so once if not.

`for` is only half a link: this element finds the trigger, and the trigger
has to name this element for a screen reader to read the two together. That
second half is the consumer's line to write, deliberately, because writing
it from here means `setAttribute` on markup they server-rendered. So it is
theirs to forget, and a silent accessibility gap is the worst kind: the
tooltip looks completely correct.

On first open rather than on connect, because a framework may render the
attribute after this element upgrades, and because a tooltip that never
opens has described nothing eitherway.

Either attribute counts. WebAwesome uses `aria-labelledby` over
`aria-describedby` on purpose, their reasoning being that some screen
readers want the description on the focusable element itself while a label
reads on first focus regardless, and that is a live enough question that
this should not be the thing to settle it.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: material
attributes.description:
What the bubble is made of.

Absent is the inverse bubble, a dark surface over a light page, which is
what a hint over content the theme cannot know has always been here. `glass`
makes it the page's own translucent ground instead, for a page whose surfaces
are glass, so a hint over a glass header is not the one opaque slab on it.

**It flips the ink and adds an edge, which no other family carrying this axis
has to do.** A card is already the page's surface, so glass swaps one ground
for another; this one starts inverse, and `--helix-material-translucent` is
the page's ground, so taking it without the foreground would put light ink on
a light bubble. An inverse bubble is told from the page by being its
opposite and a glass one has to be told from what is behind it, which is why
the border arrives with the material rather than being there all along.

The strength is the theme's: `--helix-material-translucent` and
`--helix-material-backdrop` are what the policy moves.

**`emphasis` is not here and that is not an omission.** It says how much ink
a *mark* claims, and this is a surface: what varies about a surface is where
it ends, which is `separation`, and a bubble in the top layer with a point on
it has one answer to that. A quiet tooltip is a tooltip that is not shown.

**`transparent` is where this one stops, and that is the statement 270
asks for rather than an omission.** A panel that floats over arbitrary page
content is only readable because it has a ground; dropping it does not make
a lighter tooltip, it makes an unreadable one. `frosted` and `glass` are the
two honest points here.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

attributes.name: default-open
attributes.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

attributes.name: content
attributes.description:
The text shown in the bubble.

The common case, and the fallback for the `content` slot: slot something
there and it replaces this. Both cannot show at once, which is the point
of using fallback content rather than rendering whichever is present.

attributes.name: for
attributes.description:
The id of the element this describes, in this tooltip's own tree.

Set it and the tooltip stops wrapping: it renders no trigger, listens on
the element it names, and points its bubble there. Leave it unset and the
default slot is the trigger, which is the older form.

Resolved through `getRootNode()`, so a tooltip inside another component's
shadow root names an element in that root rather than in the document.

**In React this arrives as a property and not as an attribute**, which is
worth knowing before someone reads the DOM and thinks it did not take.
Measured against React 19.2.8: `for` exists on the prototype, so React sets
`element.for = 'save'` and writes nothing to the markup, where `content`
and `placement`, which are not properties on the class at that moment, come
through as attributes. Both paths reach the same place through Lit, so
nothing is broken by it; a `[for]` selector would find nothing, which is
why this does not reflect and nothing styles on it.

attributes.name: placement
attributes.description:
Preferred side.

It moves if that side does not fit.

attributes.name: offset
attributes.description:
Space between the trigger and the point of the bubble, in pixels.

**Measured from the point, which is what the arrow being back changed.**
The arrow is drawn half outside the bubble, so a gap measured to the
bubble's edge is a smaller gap to the tip: at the default it left the point
two pixels off the trigger, which reads as touching. The controller is
given this plus however far the arrow actually protrudes, so eight means
eight from whatever is nearest, arrow or edge, and a consumer who changes
it changes the visible gap rather than a number the arrow then eats into.

attributes.name: within
attributes.description:
The id of a box to keep the bubble inside, instead of the viewport.

Resolved the way `for` is, so an id in the same tree, which is what lets a
component name a box in its own shadow root. A chart does: its bubble is
centered on a reading, and the first and last readings sit at the ends of
the plot, so half the box hangs past the drawing and, measured on a chart
in a 320px card, three pixels past the card itself.

Clamping is on the cross axis only, which is what makes this safe to point
at a box the bubble genuinely does not fit inside. See `within` on
`FloatingController` for what happens if it is applied to the rest.

attributes.name: disabled
attributes.description: Whether the tooltip never shows.

attributes.name: persist
attributes.description:
Whether the bubble survives the trigger being used.

**Activation takes a tooltip down, because a hint about what a control will
do is spent once the control has done it.** That is right for a gear that
opens a drawer and wrong for a control whose tooltip *becomes* the answer:
`CopyButton` swaps its content from Copy to Copied on the same click, so the
bubble was being hidden at the exact moment it had something to say. What a
reader saw was a flash, and the confirmation the component had carefully
written was never on screen long enough to read.

So this is not "keep it open", it is "the hint is not spent": set it where
the words change to describe what just happened, and leave it alone
everywhere else. Escape, blur and pointer-leave still close it, because
those are a reader saying they are done rather than a control saying it
worked.

attributes.name: delay
attributes.description:
How long the pointer must rest before the bubble appears, in milliseconds.

Without one, sweeping across a row of controls flashes a tooltip for each
of them, which is noise rather than help. Focus opens with no delay: a
keyboard reader arriving on a control has already committed to it.

attributes.name: delay-out
attributes.description: How long the bubble stays after the pointer leaves, in milliseconds.

declarations.summary: A short description that appears beside what it describes.

examples.description: A word of explanation on hover and on focus.
A tooltip that describes its target rather than naming it.
A bubble that opens on hover and on focus, and says so both ways.
A bubble clamped to a box of the page's choosing rather than to the window.
A glass bubble, for a page whose surfaces are glass.
The twelve positions a tooltip can take around its anchor.
More than a line, for a tooltip that has something to explain.
The rest before it appears and the grace after, and how far it sits from its trigger.

slots.description: The trigger.
The bubble's content, when `content` is not enough. Anything slotted here replaces the property, which is this slot's fallback.
slots.name: content

cssParts.description: The point, resting against the trigger.
cssParts.name: arrow

cssParts.description: The bubble.
cssParts.name: tooltip

events.description: Fired before it hides, and cancelable.
events.name: helix-before-close

events.description: Fired before the bubble shows, and cancelable.
events.name: helix-before-open

events.description: Says the state moved, carrying `newState` and `oldState`.
events.name: toggle

declarations.description: The styled tier of `BaseTour`. It draws the light and nothing else.
declarations.name: HelixTour

cssProperties.description: The darkness outside the lit box.
cssProperties.name: --tour-scrim-color

cssProperties.description: Corner radius of the lit box.
cssProperties.name: --tour-spotlight-radius

members.name: open
members.description: Whether the tour is running.

members.name: index
members.description:
Which stop the reader is on.

**It announced after it moved for two days, which made refusing it
impossible.** `index` was a plain property the tour wrote to directly:
`move` assigned it and *then* announced, so `preventDefault` on the change
arrived after the move it was refusing. It goes through `requestChange`
now, which announces first and applies only if nobody refused, and refusing
is how a consumer takes the decision. See 294.

The shape is `Carousel`'s, which is the nearest thing in the library: a
`default-index` for markup that only seeds and a held state that is
`undefined` until somebody sets one.

members.name: defaultIndex
members.description: Stop to start on, where nothing declared one.

members.name: indexState
members.description: The stop being shown, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the run, such as "Getting started".

members.name: spotlightPadding
members.description: Space left around the target when it is lit, in pixels.

members.name: backLabel
members.description: Label for the control that goes back, handed to every stop.

members.name: nextLabel

members.name: doneLabel

type.text: { height: number; left: number; top: number; width: number } | undefined

members.name: length
members.description: How many stops there are.

members.name: skip

Announced before it is applied, and cancelable because of it. Both closes

members.name: settle

Written onto the stops, which is the one outward write in this family and
is argued for on the class above. The labels go with it, and only where the
root was given one, so a stop keeps its own default unless somebody has

members.name: light

members.name: tag

members.description:

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug

showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

reason that did not hold for the trail or the avatar group: a tour starts
closed, so there is no server state to get wrong. The server renders a
closed tour, a closed tour shows nothing, and nothing can disagree.

members.name: renderActions
members.description:
Skip, back and next, behind a seam the styled tier can move.

They are slot fallback rather than markup a consumer has to write, so a
tour with nothing slotted still has the three controls a tour needs; and
they are a method as well, so a tier above can render its own three without
reimplementing the panel around them. Both are needed: the slot is for the
consumer and the method is for the tier.

members.name: ask
members.description:
Says what the reader pressed and lets the root decide.

A stop cannot move a tour: it does not know what is after it, and a stop
that reached up to its parent to find out would be a stop that only works
inside one. Composed, so the root hears it through its own slot.

members.name: open
members.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

members.name: defaultOpen
members.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

members.name: openState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

Prefixed, and it has to be. These mixins compose onto one prototype
chain, `Select` takes this one and `MixinControllerValue` together, and
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time fiction: two mixins with a field
called `state` share one property on the instance, and the second one
silently overwrites the first. Measured, as a select whose `value` came
back holding its `open` boolean.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, which is what a native
control does when a script assigns to it, and is the behavior an
imperative `element.open = true` should have whatever mode the element is
in. What the write does *not* do is change which mode that is.

members.name: requestOpen
members.description:
Requests an open-state change, and reports whether it was applied.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-open` or
`helix-before-close` is a refusal and nothing moves. Nobody refusing means the
element opens or closes itself, whether or not a consumer declared
`open`: a declared property is a seed and a correction, and a consumer
who wants the decision for themselves refuses it and assigns their own.
See 294.

members.name: announceToggle
members.description:
Says the state moved, under the platform's own name and in its shape.

**`<details>` fires `toggle` and a popover fires `toggle`, and sixteen
families here fired neither.** Two of them render a real `<dialog>` and
ten show a `popover="manual"` panel, so the browser was already firing
something on an element inside a shadow root, where `toggle` neither
bubbles nor composes and so reaches nobody. The rest, the disclosures,
have no native element to fire anything at all: `AccordionItem` and
`TreeItem` are `aria-expanded` and `hidden` written by hand, which is
`<details>`'s job done manually.

**From here rather than from `PopoverController`, which had it first.**
The controller covers eleven families and the mixin covers sixteen, and
the overlap is ten that would have announced twice. What `toggle` reports
is the *state*, and the state is this mixin's; the controller is a way of
putting a panel on the screen.

**`newState` and `oldState`, because that is the platform's shape**, so a
consumer arriving from `<details>` reads the same two words. Not
cancelable: the before events are the request, and a second cancelable
event for one transition is two answers to one question.

members.name: toggleOpen
members.description: Requests the opposite of the current state.

members.name: value
members.description: Identifies the item to the consumer, carried in `helix-select`.

members.name: href
members.description:
Where this node goes, which makes its row a real link.

Unset by default, and unreflected: a tree of choosable nodes is not a tree
of links, and an empty `href` written onto every row would be a link to the
current page on every item a consumer never asked to be one.

members.name: target
members.description: Where the link opens, for the rare row that leaves the site.

members.name: rel
members.description:
What the link declares about where it goes.

Set by the consumer rather than derived from `target`: `noreferrer` is a
decision about their own analytics and a component should not make it for
them. `noopener` is not needed as a default either, since every browser
this library supports implies it for `target="_blank"` already.

members.name: selected
members.description:
Whether this item is the current one.

Not reflected, for the reason `level` below gives in full: the tree assigns
this after it upgrades, so the attribute would be a change to markup the
consumer rendered and hydration would report it. It reflected, one line
from the paragraph saying why it must not.

The stylesheet reads it from the row inside this shadow root, which is the
answer `level` gives one paragraph down: the indent it drives is written
onto the row rather than onto the host, because the row is not part of the
tree React hydrates. Mirroring to `data-selected` on the host instead was
the same fault with a different name, and React said so.

members.name: level
members.description:
Depth from the root, set by the tree so indentation needs no CSS nesting.

Not reflected. The tree assigns this after it upgrades, so an attribute
here would be a change to markup the consumer rendered and hydration would
report it. The indent it drives is written onto the row instead, inside the
shadow root, which is not part of the tree React hydrates.

members.name: focusable
members.description: Whether this item holds the tree's single tab stop.

members.name: branch
members.description:
Whether anything is slotted into `children`.

Read after first render.

members.name: focusItem
members.description:
Moves focus to this node.

Which element that is moves with `href`: the thing carrying `treeitem` is

row rather than the wrapper around it.

members.name: select
members.description: Selects this node and announces it.

members.name: activate
members.description:
Chooses this node the way a reader does, from a press or from Enter.

pointer and the keyboard take one path to the same end. The tree calls this
rather than `select` for the keyboard, which is what fixes Enter: a nav
tree whose rows are links could be walked with the arrows and not entered,
because choosing announced a value and nothing listened for it.

members.name: follow
members.description:

chevron at the far end most of the row's width are all outside the anchor,
so a reader who pressed the row anywhere but on the text got nothing. The
words are the consumer's own content and this does not rewrite them, so

deliberately: a framework's link component is what carries prefetching and
client-side routing, and a plain `<a href>` rendered in here would be a
full page load on a site that had neither. A synthetic click is what those
components listen for, so both keep working.

consumer's, and it is scoped to this item's own name rather than to the

its children.

members.name: renderRow

members.name: tier
members.description:

members.description:

source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per

members.name: internals
members.description:

attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it

The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:

and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a

transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled

members.name: stopInner
members.description:

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches

specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for

still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where

announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:

so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on

makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles

has to remember to include it.

declarations.summary: One node in a tree.

attributes.name: open
attributes.description:
Whether the element is open.

One property, not two. Reading gives the real state whichever mode the
element is in, so `dialog.open` answers the question anyone asking it
meant. Writing hands ownership to the consumer, which is what the
attribute in `<helix-dialog open>` does as well: from then on the element
announces changes and applies none of them.

It reads as an accessor pair rather than a field because those are two
different questions sharing one name, and the alternative was a second
property answering the first. That worked for a boolean, where `isOpen`
reads well; there is no such word for a value or an active item, so all
four of these mixins now have this shape instead of two shapes.

**Not reflected, and that is required rather than tidy.** Reflection
writes the resolved state back as an attribute, and writing the attribute
is how a consumer says they own it. So an uncontrolled element that
opened itself would put `open` on its own host and, from the next thing
that read it, be indistinguishable from one the consumer controls:
cloned, serialised for hydration, or diffed by a framework, it would come
back holding whatever the last reader did rather than what the author
wrote. `:state(open)` carries the resolved state for stylesheets, which
is what the mirror has always been for.

attributes.name: default-open
attributes.description: Initial open state for uncontrolled use, where nothing declared one.

attributes.name: value
attributes.description: Identifies the item to the consumer, carried in `helix-select`.

attributes.name: href
attributes.description:
Where this node goes, which makes its row a real link.

Unset by default, and unreflected: a tree of choosable nodes is not a tree
of links, and an empty `href` written onto every row would be a link to the
current page on every item a consumer never asked to be one.

attributes.name: target
attributes.description: Where the link opens, for the rare row that leaves the site.

attributes.name: rel
attributes.description:
What the link declares about where it goes.

Set by the consumer rather than derived from `target`: `noreferrer` is a
decision about their own analytics and a component should not make it for
them. `noopener` is not needed as a default either, since every browser
this library supports implies it for `target="_blank"` already.

attributes.name: selected
attributes.description:
Whether this item is the current one.

Not reflected, for the reason `level` below gives in full: the tree assigns
this after it upgrades, so the attribute would be a change to markup the
consumer rendered and hydration would report it. It reflected, one line
from the paragraph saying why it must not.

The stylesheet reads it from the row inside this shadow root, which is the
answer `level` gives one paragraph down: the indent it drives is written
onto the row rather than onto the host, because the row is not part of the
tree React hydrates. Mirroring to `data-selected` on the host instead was
the same fault with a different name, and React said so.

attributes.name: level
attributes.description:
Depth from the root, set by the tree so indentation needs no CSS nesting.

Not reflected. The tree assigns this after it upgrades, so an attribute
here would be a change to markup the consumer rendered and hydration would
report it. The indent it drives is written onto the row instead, inside the
shadow root, which is not part of the tree React hydrates.

declarations.description:
Quiet by default: no rules between rows and no fill except on the selected
item. A navigation tree is read by scanning, and every line of chrome added
to it is one more thing between the reader and the label.

members.name: chevronPlacement
members.description:
Which end of the row the branch chevron sits at.

Styled tier, because it is presentation and nothing else: it moves paint
and leaves the markup, the ARIA and the reading order exactly as they were.
It was written on the base class first, which the tier rule forbids for
precisely this kind of property.

On the tree rather than on the item, because it is a fact about the list. A
navigation puts every chevron on the same side, and a per-item version
would make a ragged tree writable and would have to be repeated on every
row to say one thing.

**Optional, with no default.** A reflected property that defaults to a
value writes that value onto every host: `chevron-placement="start"`
appeared in the server's markup for every tree anybody rendered, which is
the same fault `href` and `target` had on `Button`. The resting arrangement
is the absence of the attribute, and the stylesheet only asks about `end`.

It is worth owning rather than leaving to `::part(toggle)`, which a
consumer could reach for: the naive version is `order` plus an auto margin,
and the row's `end` slot already carries an auto margin of its own, so the
two split the free space and the chevron lands halfway along. Measured at
70px short. That is the kind of thing a component should absorb once.

members.name: loading
members.description:
Whether the rows are still on their way.

Reflected, because a stylesheet needs it: the rows that are already there
are dimmed rather than removed while a new set arrives, and only CSS can
say that without the component knowing what a row looks like.

members.name: loadingText
members.description: What is said while they are on their way.

members.name: emptyText
members.description: What is said where there are none, and none are coming.

members.name: slotCounted
members.description: Whether the rows have been looked at yet.

members.name: slotRows
members.description:
How many there were, the last time anyone looked.

**Not `rows`, and the rename is the whole point of this comment.**
TypeScript's `private` is a compile-time claim and the runtime field is
whatever it is named, so a subclass declaring `@property() rows` for the
data a consumer hands it would share one field with this counter: the
slot count would overwrite the consumer's array on every `updated`, and
`hasRows` would read the array's length as a slot count. Nothing would
throw. `helix-data-table` takes exactly that property, which is what
found this before it happened.

members.name: countRows
members.description:
Counts what a rows slot was given.

Emptiness is a fact about light DOM children and the server has none to
count. `slotchange` never fires there, so `counted` is false exactly when
the answer is unknown, and an unknown answer is not "empty": a list that
shipped "Nothing to show" over markup about to have rows in it is the one
thing an empty state must never do. Listbox's spec caught precisely that.

members.name: renderStatus
members.description:
The status line, or nothing where there is content to show.

Loading wins over empty. A collection that has not answered yet is not
empty, and saying so is the most common version of this fault: the reader
is told there is nothing a moment before there is something.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description:
Initial item for uncontrolled use.

Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-activate` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back. Nobody refusing means the set updates itself,
whether or not a consumer declared `active`, a declared property being a
seed and a correction. See 294.

members.name: announceActivated
members.description:

event class said so deliberately: no native word means "a set chose a
different member", so borrowing `change` would be a lie about what moved.

not follow is that a set should therefore announce nothing.

only wants to know which child is current had one channel and it fires

covered because `helix-select` bubbles up from a child, which fires when an
item is *chosen* and not when `active` is assigned, and `Steps` and

state is on the element by the time a handler reads it. Not cancelable:
the decision was taken by the event before this one, and two refusable
events for one transition are two answers to one question. See #325.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:

its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the tree.

members.name: items
members.description:

an array of every descendant element in the tree, labels and icons and
whatever a consumer slotted into a row included, and threw most of it away;
on a tree of any size that is the array a single arrow press rebuilds.

`helix-tree-item` extends the base, so both names are needed, and the
`instanceof` stays as the type guard because a consumer can write either
tag and neither selector proves what the element is.

members.name: visibleItems
members.description: Items a reader can actually reach: not inside a collapsed branch.

members.name: syncItems
members.description:
Pushes tree-owned state down: which item is selected, which holds the tab
stop, and how deep each one sits.

Depth is computed here rather than by each item counting its own ancestors,
so an item moved in the tree gets the right indent without knowing it moved.

attributes.name: chevron-placement
attributes.description:
Which end of the row the branch chevron sits at.

Styled tier, because it is presentation and nothing else: it moves paint
and leaves the markup, the ARIA and the reading order exactly as they were.
It was written on the base class first, which the tier rule forbids for
precisely this kind of property.

On the tree rather than on the item, because it is a fact about the list. A
navigation puts every chevron on the same side, and a per-item version
would make a ragged tree writable and would have to be repeated on every
row to say one thing.

**Optional, with no default.** A reflected property that defaults to a
value writes that value onto every host: `chevron-placement="start"`
appeared in the server's markup for every tree anybody rendered, which is
the same fault `href` and `target` had on `Button`. The resting arrangement
is the absence of the attribute, and the stylesheet only asks about `end`.

It is worth owning rather than leaving to `::part(toggle)`, which a
consumer could reach for: the naive version is `order` plus an auto margin,
and the row's `end` slot already carries an auto margin of its own, so the
two split the free space and the chevron lands halfway along. Measured at
70px short. That is the kind of thing a component should absorb once.

declarations.description:
The arrow takes the judgment color and the number does not, which is the
opposite of the dashboard convention and is measured rather than preferred:
in light mode the success token is 3.8:1 on the surface, enough for a glyph
and short of what 13px text needs, and there is no darker green in the ramp.
The number therefore keeps the page's own foreground and stays the most
legible thing here, which is right anyway, since the number is what a reader
reads and the judgment is a gloss on it.

**No visual axis applies here, and that is the answer rather than a gap.**
This family carries `@groups charts`, so `check:axes` reports it beside eight
that do declare one. Each of the three was asked and each refuses for a reason
about what this is rather than about the axis. `emphasis` is how much ink a
mark claims, and there is no mark: an arrow glyph and two runs of text, whose
weight is `Text`'s business and whose size is the region's. `material` is what
reads through a surface, and a 13px glyph has nothing behind it. `wash` is a
gradient across an area, and there is no area.

The meaning axis is here and is *derived*, which is the more interesting half:
`direction` and `good` together resolve to success, danger or muted, so a
consumer states the metric's polarity once rather than picking a color. A
declared `tone` would let the color disagree with the arrow, which is the one
thing this component exists to stop.

members.name: direction
members.description:
Which way the measurement moved.

Absent is neutral, so a trend with nothing to report draws a bar rather
than picking a direction. Optional rather than defaulted for the reason
`Stat.direction` is: a reflecting property with a default writes its
attribute onto the host the moment the element upgrades, and the host is
markup the consumer rendered, which React compares against what it rendered
and reports as a hydration mismatch.

members.name: good
members.description:
Which direction is the improvement, for this metric.

Absent states the movement without judging it, which is the honest default:
revenue up is good news and latency up is bad news, and only the consumer
knows which one this is. Set it once per metric and it holds while the
direction changes underneath.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

has to remember to include it.

members.description:
The menu's accessible name, and its trigger's.

"Episodes" suits a series and is wrong for a set of camera angles, and the
component cannot know which one it is in.

members.name: placement
members.description:
Where the menu opens relative to its trigger.

`top-end` because a control bar sits at the foot of the picture, and a menu
opening downward from there opens off the player.

members.name: entries
