members.name: watch
members.description:
Watches the playlist for entries arriving, and re-reads it on every open.

Two signals rather than one, because the two facts change on different
clocks and only one of them is observable.

**Which entries exist** is the playlist's light DOM, and a `MutationObserver`
sees it directly.

**Which entry is current** is `active`, a property with no attribute, so
there is nothing to observe: events travel up from the playlist and this
element is below it, and mirroring `active` to a `data-` name is ruled out
on its own merits, `active` being a payload rather than a boolean fact.
Mirroring it was written and reverted here: it put `data-active` onto every
host, which `tree-root.ssr.spec.ts` caught, and the rule it broke was the
one that stops a copied host coming back frozen.

So it is re-read at the moment it is looked at. `helix-before-open` comes from the
menu in this element's own shadow root, which is the one direction events
do arrive from, and a closed menu showing a stale mark is a thing nobody
can see.

members.name: toggleState

`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on

makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: active
members.description:
Which item is current, by its `value`.

Called `active`, which is what this mixin is named for and what it was
not: it declared `value`, so the one mixin whose whole subject is which
item is active had no such property, and `active` meant something else
entirely elsewhere in the library. It still does, and only there now:
`option.active` is the option the keyboard is on, which is a different
question from which one is chosen.

An accessor pair, the same shape as the other three. Reading gives the
real item; writing hands ownership to the consumer, so `<helix-tabs
active="one">` is a set that stays on that tab and `default-active` is
how markup says where to start.

members.name: defaultActive
members.description:
Initial item for uncontrolled use.

Ignored once `active` is written.

members.name: activeState
members.description:
The state, whoever set it, and `undefined` until somebody has.

One field and not two. Writing always applies, the way a native control
does when a script assigns to it. What the write does not do is change
which mode the element is in.

members.name: requestActive
members.description:
Requests a new current item, and reports whether the request stood.

Announces before it acts, so `preventDefault()` on the `helix-before-activate` is
a refusal and nothing moves. Unlike a native control, nothing has moved
by the time this runs, so refusing is simply not writing: there is
nothing to put back. Nobody refusing means the set updates itself,
whether or not a consumer declared `active`, a declared property being a
seed and a correction. See 294.

members.name: announceActivated
members.description:
Says the current child moved, once it has.

**This was the only one of the four mixins with no notification**, and the
event class said so deliberately: no native word means "a set chose a
different member", so borrowing `change` would be a lie about what moved.
That half still holds, and is why the pair is `helix-activate`. What did
not follow is that a set should therefore announce nothing.

The cost is the one 294 fixed for values and left here. A consumer who
only wants to know which child is current had one channel and it fires
*before* `apply`, so `currentTarget.active` is the previous value inside
the handler and `detail.value` is a proposal another listener may refuse.
Measured across the four families taking this: `Tabs` and `Tree` looked
covered because `helix-select` bubbles up from a child, which fires when an
item is *chosen* and not when `active` is assigned, and `Steps` and
`Video Playlist` announced nothing at all.

**After `apply`, which is the whole reason it is a second event**, so the
state is on the element by the time a handler reads it. Not cancelable:
the decision was taken by the event before this one, and two refusable
events for one transition are two answers to one question. See #325.

members.name: resolveActive
members.description:
Which item is current, given what there is to choose from.

The first enabled one when `value` names nothing, which is a set before
its consumer has chosen and a set whose current item has just been
removed. Disabled items are skipped in the fallback but not in the match:
a consumer who names a disabled item meant it, and quietly moving to
another would be the component overruling them.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name for the list, which usually has no visible heading.

members.name: items
members.description:
The entries, in the order the consumer wrote them.

**Found by tag and filtered on the property, never on `[value]`.** The
prefilter used to be an attribute selector, which is redundant beside the
tag match and is the half that broke: React assigns a matching property
rather than an attribute, so a playlist written in JSX carried no `value`
attribute anywhere and `querySelectorAll('[value]')` returned nothing. Every
entry vanished from the list, the active one included, and the component
threw no error because an empty playlist is a legal playlist.

Reading `one.value` answers the same question and answers it the same way
whether the consumer wrote markup or set a property, which is the only form
that works for both. Found by rendering the React twin of this family's
examples beside the markup ones.

members.name: chased
members.description:
Whether the entry changed because somebody moved through the playlist.

All three ways it moves are the reader going somewhere: pressing an entry,
pressing next or previous, or a clip ending and the next one following it.
Every one of those means play, and the one case that does not is the first
render, where the playlist is simply pointing the player at its opening
entry and nobody has asked for anything yet.

A press is also what makes the play legal. Autoplay is refused when nothing
the reader did asked for it, so starting here works because this is inside
the gesture that chose the entry, and where it is refused anyway the player
shows its start control and waits.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

declarations.description:
The player is the headless tier's. What this adds is the bar: where it sits, when
it is there, and what the two ranges look like, which is the whole reason to
replace a control set that cannot be styled.

**The bar is over the picture, not under it.** A bar in the layout would move
everything below the video by its own height and would leave a strip of page
color under a picture that is meant to be the whole of it. Over it, the
video is the component's size and the controls belong to it.

**It goes when nobody is using it, and comes back for the keyboard.** Hidden
once a playing video has gone `idle-delay` without being touched, shown again
the moment the pointer moves, and shown whenever anything inside it has
focus, which is what keeps it reachable without a pointer. A paused video
keeps its bar, because a reader who stopped it is deciding what to do next.

members.name: poster
members.description: A still shown before it plays, which the platform draws itself.

members.name: label
members.description: Accessible name, since a video is not described by its filename.

members.name: loop
members.description: Whether it starts again at the end.

members.name: defaultMuted
members.description:
Whether it *starts* silent, which is what an autoplaying video must do.

**Renamed from `muted`, because that is what it always was.** The platform
splits these two: the `muted` content attribute reflects to `defaultMuted`,
and the `muted` property is live state a reader's click moves without
touching the attribute. This element declared one property called `muted`,
bound it to the attribute, and tracked the live state privately as
`silent`, so `<helix-video>.muted` answered what the author wrote rather
than whether there was sound. A name matching the platform's while meaning
something else is worse than a name the platform does not have, and
`check:platform-fidelity` could not see it: it compares names.

members.name: playsInline
members.description: Whether it plays where it sits rather than taking over the screen.

members.name: controls
members.description:
Whether the browser draws the controls instead of this element.

A fallback rather than a default. Two bars over one video is worse than
either alone, so this one is not drawn at all when it is set.

members.name: preload
members.description: How much to fetch before anything is asked for.

members.name: autoplay
members.description:
Whether it starts on its own, which a browser only allows while silent.

Forwarded rather than acted on. Whether an unprompted play is permitted is
the browser's policy and not this element's, and `play()` already swallows
the refusal: what follows a refused autoplay is a paused player showing its
start control, which is the correct thing to be looking at.

members.name: crossOrigin
members.description:
How the media is fetched across origins, which decides whether a track can
be read.

members.name: disablePictureInPicture
members.description: Whether the browser may offer picture in picture.

members.name: disableRemotePlayback
members.description: Whether the browser may offer playback on a remote device.

members.name: extraControls
members.description:
Controls beyond the ones every player has, named in the order they appear.

A list rather than a property apiece. A bar is a row with a budget, and a
boolean per feature invites a consumer to switch all of them on: naming
them makes the row a decision, and makes the order theirs. Anything
unrecognised is skipped rather than throwing, since the list is markup and
a typo should cost a control, not a page.

`pip` is offered only where the platform has it, checked rather than
assumed: it is absent on iPhone and behind a flag in Firefox, and a button
that cannot work is worse than one that is not there.

The names are `speed`, `pip`, `remote` and `download`.

**`download` is named and never assumed.** Offering the file is a decision
about the content rather than about the player, and plenty of consumers
decline it deliberately. It is also the one control whose success is not
ours to promise: the attribute is ignored cross-origin, so a file served
from somewhere else opens rather than saves, which is the browser's rule
and not something a player can work around.

members.name: overflowControls
members.description:
Controls that go behind one button instead of onto the bar, named the same
way.

**Named rather than measured, and the reason is that a width cannot answer
this.** A media query asks about the window, and the bar's problem is its
own width: a video in a 320px sidebar on a desktop is cramped and a
full-bleed hero on a phone is not. A container query asks the right
question and still cannot answer it, because how many controls there are is
the consumer's, so the threshold is not a width but a width per control,
which is a guess. And a control that moves between the bar and a hidden
menu as the layout shifts is a control the reader has to find twice.

So the consumer says where the fold is, which they can, having already
named the controls in order. A name in both lists is drawn once, on the
bar: two of the same control is worse than either placement.

members.name: startControl
members.description:
The big mark over the picture before anything has played, or `none`.

**On unless it is turned off, because a stopped video has nothing else.**
Measured on the bar as it was: the play glyph is 16 by 16 in a 24 by 24
target, which is 0.12% of a 528 by 396 picture and 0.33% at 320. What a
reader meets first is a still frame with some chrome along the bottom, and
nothing in it says "press to watch".

`none` is for the cases where that is wrong rather than right: a muted loop
behind a hero, a grid of eight thumbnails, anything where the video is
decoration rather than something to start.

**Only before the first play.** A video paused halfway already has its bar
up, because a paused video never idles, so the small control is visible and
the reader has just used it. Covering the picture they stopped to look at
would be the opposite of helpful.

A value rather than a boolean, so the resting state is the attribute's
absence: a boolean defaulting to on would have to be spelled as its own
negation.

members.name: localFile
members.description:
Whether the file this points at is ours to hand over.

`blob:` and `data:` named rather than compared, because the rule `download`
actually follows is same-origin *or one of those two*: a clip a consumer
generated in the page has no origin to match and is theirs to save by
definition. Comparing origins alone called both foreign, so the one case
where a download certainly works was the one case it was not offered.

members.name: speeds
members.description: The speeds offered, slowest first, as multipliers of normal.

members.name: idleDelay
members.description:
How long the bar waits after the pointer stops before it goes, in ms.

It used to leave the moment the pointer did, which is not how a player
behaves: a reader moving across the picture to reach a control watched it
vanish under them. Zero turns the wait off and the bar goes immediately;
a large number keeps it up for as long as anyone is likely to look.

The wait is only ever about *idling*. A video that is paused keeps its bar
regardless, because a reader who stopped it is deciding what to do next.

members.name: playLabel
members.description: What the play control is called while it would start the video.

members.name: pauseLabel
members.description: And while it would stop it.

members.name: loadingLabel
members.description: What a reader is told while the picture is waiting for more of itself.

members.name: errorLabel
members.description: And what they are told when it will not play at all.

members.name: buffering
members.description:
Whether playback has stopped to wait for data.

**Only ever after somebody asked for playback**, which is what `waiting`
means: the element wanted the next frame and did not have it. Before that,
a video that has loaded nothing is a poster with a play control over it,
which looks deliberate and is. A spinner there would say something is
happening when nothing is, on every video on the page.

The case this covers is the one that looks like a bug: a picture frozen
mid-play, the scrubber stopped, and nothing on screen saying why.

members.name: failed
members.description:
Whether the source failed, which is the other thing a frozen frame can
mean.

members.name: captionIndex
members.description:
Which caption track is showing, or `-1` for none.

`@state`, because it is read off the video rather than declared: a consumer
asking for a language would be naming a track that may not have loaded, and
`default` on the `<track>` is the platform's own way to say it.

members.name: captionCount
members.description:
How many caption tracks there are, which decides which control is drawn.

A count and not a boolean, and that is the whole reason it changed. Tracks
resolve after the element renders, so this is what schedules the update
that draws the control at all; as a boolean it went false to true when the
first one arrived and then never moved again, so a second track landing
left the toggle in place and the language menu was unreachable on exactly
the videos it exists for.

members.name: cue
members.description:
The cue on screen now, as nodes, or nothing between cues.

Nodes rather than a string, because `VTTCue.text` is the cue's *source*:
WebVTT carries markup, and a caption file in the wild is full of it. `<v
Hildy>` names who is speaking, `<b>` and `<i>` and `<u>` mark emphasis, and
`<c.loud>` classes a line. Rendered as text every one of those arrives on
screen as visible angle brackets.

`getCueAsHTML` is the platform parsing its own format, so nothing here has
to know the grammar and no cue text is ever treated as HTML: what comes
back is a fragment the browser built, not a string anybody interpolated.

members.name: idle
members.description: Whether the reader has been still long enough for the bar to go.

members.name: remoteAvailable
members.description: Whether anything on the network offers to play this.

members.name: remoteConnected
members.description: Whether it is playing somewhere else right now.

members.name: remoteWatch
members.description: Cancels the availability watch, since it outlives a single render.

members.name: offers
members.description: Whether this platform can do a named control at all.

members.name: extras
members.description: The extras asked for, in order, and only the ones this platform can do.

members.name: overflow
members.description:
The controls asked for behind the overflow button, in order.

A name in both lists is on the bar and not here. Drawing it twice is worse
than either placement, and the bar is the one a reader can see.

members.name: media
members.description:
The sources and caption tracks to copy into the video, as the consumer
wrote them.

members.name: currentSrc
members.description:
The media's own state, under the platform's own names.

**This element already knew every one of these and kept them private.** It
tracks `currentTime` as `position`, `duration` as `knownDuration`, `volume`
as `loudness`, `paused` as `playing` and `playbackRate` as `rate`, paints
them, and published none of them, so a consumer asking where the video had
reached had nowhere to ask: the `<video>` is inside this shadow root and
`querySelector` does not cross it. 295 is that finding across the library
and this is its clearest case.

**Read from the element, with the mirror as the fallback.** The element is
the truth and the mirror is a render cache that a media event refreshes, so
reading the mirror alone would answer with whatever the last `timeupdate`
said rather than with where the video is now. The fallback is what answers
on the server and before the first render, where there is no element and
the mirror holds what markup asked for.

**Accessors rather than reactive properties**, because none of these is a
setting: they are the media's state, and a `@property` would give each one
an attribute that a consumer could write and the element would then have to
disagree with. Where the platform makes one writable this writes it
through, and where the platform does not neither does this.

members.name: currentTime
members.description:
Where playback has reached, in seconds.

Writing seeks, through the same clamp `seek` uses, because a `currentTime`
past the end is the one write the platform answers with an exception.

members.name: defaultPlaybackRate
members.description: The rate playback returns to, which `defaultPlaybackRate` names natively.

members.name: duration
members.description: How long the media runs, in seconds, and `NaN` until that is known.

members.name: ended
members.description: Whether playback has run off the end.

members.name: paused
members.description: Whether playback is stopped, which is the resting state and not an error.

members.name: playbackRate
members.description: How fast it plays, where 1 is the recorded speed.

members.name: preservesPitch
members.description: Whether pitch is held steady when the rate changes.

members.name: seeking
members.description: Whether it is currently moving to a new position.

members.name: videoHeight
members.description: The media's own height in pixels, and zero until the metadata has loaded.

members.name: videoWidth
members.description: The media's own width in pixels, and zero until the metadata has loaded.

members.name: muted
members.description:
Whether there is sound, now, which a reader's click moves.

The live half of the pair above. Writing mutes or unmutes the media itself
rather than the attribute, which is what the platform does and what the
mute control here has always done directly.

members.name: volume
members.description: How loud it plays, 0 to 1.

members.name: play
members.description:
Starts playing, where the platform allows it.

The rejection is swallowed on purpose: a browser refuses `play()` when
nothing the reader did asked for it, and that is a policy answer rather than
a fault. What follows a refused play is a paused player showing its start
control, which is the correct thing to be looking at.

members.name: pause
members.description: Stops, leaving the frame up.

members.name: toggle
members.description: Toggles playback, which is what every key and the button both come to.

members.name: seek
members.description: Moves to a point in seconds, clamped to what exists.

members.name: takeScrub
members.description:
The scrubber's new position, and the reason these two are named at all.

**The stop is the first line.** `input` is composed by specification, so a
range inside this shadow root sends its own straight past the host to
whoever is listening on it, and this component declares no `input`: a
consumer binding one received the scrubber's and the volume rail's under a
name Video never promised, carrying a seconds count or a level between zero
and one rather than anything about the element.

Found by sweeping every family that renders a native control, which is what
308 said and not what it was read as: the first two passes both took "form
control" as the population and a media component with two rails in its
chrome is neither a form control nor exempt from the mechanism. See 308.

members.name: takeVolume
members.description: The volume rail's new level, stopped for the reason `takeScrub` carries.

members.name: handleMedia
members.description:
Rebuilds the copies from whatever the consumer has slotted.

The attribute list is explicit rather than a blind copy of every attribute:
these are two elements with a known and small surface, and copying anything
a consumer happened to put on one would carry their framework's own markers
into a shadow root that has no use for them.

members.name: handleWaiting
members.description:
Relayed, because none of these cross a shadow boundary on their own.

The video is inside this element's shadow root, so a consumer listening on
the element they wrote hears nothing at all without this. Input relays
`change` for the same reason.

members.name: claimSession
members.description:
Takes the page's media session, and tells the platform what is playing.

On play rather than on render, which is the ownership rule: a page with two
players gives the session to whichever one the reader started, so a
headset's buttons land on what they are listening to rather than on
whichever came first in the markup.

The handlers are what make a headset's play, pause and skip work at all.
Without them a platform falls back to guessing which element was meant,
which is right often enough to hide the fault and wrong exactly when there
are two.

members.name: handleCue
members.description:
Draws the active cue ourselves, so it can be put where we want it.

The browser renders cues inside the video's own box and there is no
standard way to inset that box: a caption lands under the control bar and
stays there. `::cue` styles the text and not the region, and the property
that moves the region is a `-webkit-` internal that two of the three
engines do not have.

So the track is set to `hidden` rather than `showing`, which is the mode
that keeps the cues coming without drawing them, and what it reports is
rendered into a part of our own. That also makes captions styleable, which
`::cue` only half allows.

members.name: skipBy
members.description:
Moves by a fixed length, clamped by `seek`.

Separate from the arrow keys, which move by 5 and by 10 with Shift. Those
are a scrub; this is the gesture for "I missed that", and a reader who
presses it twice expects twenty seconds rather than an accelerating jump.

members.name: captionTracks
members.description:
The tracks a reader could choose between, in the order they were written.

Filtered by kind, because `textTracks` also carries `chapters`, `metadata`
and `descriptions`, and a menu offering "Chapters" as a subtitle language
would be offering something that draws no words. Read off the video rather
than off the slot: a `<track>` added later is in one and not the other, and
the video is the one that has resolved them.

members.name: showCaption
members.description:
Shows one track and disables every other, or shows none at `-1`.

Every other, rather than only the one that was on. Two tracks in `hidden`
both fire `cuechange`, so the rendered cue becomes whichever fired last and
a reader who switched language gets the two interleaved. Measured as two
subtitles alternating line by line.

`hidden`, never `showing`. Hidden is the mode where a track still fires
`cuechange` and still fills `activeCues`, and the browser draws nothing,
which is exactly what is wanted when something else is doing the drawing.

members.name: toggleCaptions
members.description: Turns captions on or off, which is what the button means with one track.

members.name: skip
members.description:
Says the reader asked for another item, and does nothing else.

There is nothing else it could do. A `<video>` plays one resource, so what
comes before or after it is a fact this element does not hold: a playlist
has it, or the consumer does. Announcing is the whole of the contribution,
and the event bubbles so a wrapper hears it.

The same call answers the button, the row in the overflow menu, and the
skip keys on a headset, which is why the media session's handlers point
here rather than at anything of their own.

members.name: cycleSpeed
members.description: Steps through the speeds offered, which is what one button can do.

members.name: watchRemote
members.description:
Starts watching for something to play this on, and stops on the way out.

The Remote Playback API is the standard one, and it is what Safari
implements for AirPlay and Chrome for Cast: one call covers both, where the
older `webkitShowPlaybackTargetPicker` covers only the first. Firefox has
neither, and `remote` simply being absent is what turns the control off
there.

`watchAvailability` returns an id that has to be canceled, or the callback
outlives the element that owns it.

members.name: promptRemote
members.description: Opens the platform's own device picker. It has no list of its own.

members.name: toggleFullscreen
members.description:
Into fullscreen and back, and quiet about being refused.

`requestFullscreen` rejects rather than returning false, and the two
refusals a consumer will actually meet are a Permissions Policy that does
not grant `fullscreen` to the frame the player is in, and a call without
user activation. Both are `TypeError: Permissions check failed`, which is
the same message for two different causes.

It was `void`ed, so a refusal became an unhandled rejection: the button did
nothing and said nothing, and the console entry it left named neither the
element nor the reason. Caught here, the state stays honest because
`aria-pressed` follows `fullscreenchange` rather than this call, so a
refused request leaves a button that correctly reports "not fullscreen".

members.name: stir
members.description:
Restarts the wait, on anything that counts as the reader being here.

Pointer movement and focus both count, and both have to: a reader using the
keyboard never moves a pointer, and a bar that only answered the mouse
would leave them nothing to look at.

members.name: handleKeydown
members.description:
The keys every player uses, bound to this element rather than the document.

A video is not a command palette: its keys belong to it while a reader is
on it, and a page with two videos on it would otherwise have both answering
the same press.

Nothing is taken while focus is in a range. The scrubber and the volume are
real inputs and the arrows are already theirs, so intercepting would mean
seeking twice for one press.

members.name: cued
members.description: The track currently being listened to, so the next one can take it off.

members.name: renderExtra
members.description:
One named control, as a button on the bar.

A method rather than four branches inlined, because the same four names are
asked for twice now, once for the bar and once for the menu behind it, and
two lists that have to stay in step is how a control ends up offered in one
place and not the other.

members.name: renderCaptions
members.description:
A toggle for one track, a menu for several, and nothing for none.

No menu at one, because a menu of a single language plus "Off" is a
two-state control wearing a popover, and the button already says which
state it is in through `aria-pressed`. The moment there are two the button
cannot say which one is on, so it stops being a button.

The label comes off the track: `label` where the markup gave one, and
`srclang` where it did not, because a `<track>` with neither is a track
nobody can choose between and that is the markup's fault to fix, not this
component's to paper over with "Track 2".

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.

attributes.name: separation
attributes.description: Whether the bar floats on the picture or sits on its own ground.

attributes.name: src
attributes.description: Where the video is, for the common case of one file.

attributes.name: poster
attributes.description: A still shown before it plays, which the platform draws itself.

attributes.name: label
attributes.description: Accessible name, since a video is not described by its filename.

attributes.name: loop
attributes.description: Whether it starts again at the end.

attributes.name: muted
attributes.description:
Whether it *starts* silent, which is what an autoplaying video must do.

**Renamed from `muted`, because that is what it always was.** The platform
splits these two: the `muted` content attribute reflects to `defaultMuted`,
and the `muted` property is live state a reader's click moves without
touching the attribute. This element declared one property called `muted`,
bound it to the attribute, and tracked the live state privately as
`silent`, so `<helix-video>.muted` answered what the author wrote rather
than whether there was sound. A name matching the platform's while meaning
something else is worse than a name the platform does not have, and
`check:platform-fidelity` could not see it: it compares names.

attributes.name: playsinline
attributes.description: Whether it plays where it sits rather than taking over the screen.

attributes.name: controls
attributes.description:
Whether the browser draws the controls instead of this element.

A fallback rather than a default. Two bars over one video is worse than
either alone, so this one is not drawn at all when it is set.

attributes.name: preload
attributes.description: How much to fetch before anything is asked for.

attributes.name: autoplay
attributes.description:
Whether it starts on its own, which a browser only allows while silent.

Forwarded rather than acted on. Whether an unprompted play is permitted is
the browser's policy and not this element's, and `play()` already swallows
the refusal: what follows a refused autoplay is a paused player showing its
start control, which is the correct thing to be looking at.

attributes.name: crossorigin
attributes.description:
How the media is fetched across origins, which decides whether a track can
be read.

attributes.name: disablepictureinpicture
attributes.description: Whether the browser may offer picture in picture.

attributes.name: disableremoteplayback
attributes.description: Whether the browser may offer playback on a remote device.

attributes.name: extra-controls
attributes.description:
Controls beyond the ones every player has, named in the order they appear.

A list rather than a property apiece. A bar is a row with a budget, and a
boolean per feature invites a consumer to switch all of them on: naming
them makes the row a decision, and makes the order theirs. Anything
unrecognised is skipped rather than throwing, since the list is markup and
a typo should cost a control, not a page.

`pip` is offered only where the platform has it, checked rather than
assumed: it is absent on iPhone and behind a flag in Firefox, and a button
that cannot work is worse than one that is not there.

The names are `speed`, `pip`, `remote` and `download`.

**`download` is named and never assumed.** Offering the file is a decision
about the content rather than about the player, and plenty of consumers
decline it deliberately. It is also the one control whose success is not
ours to promise: the attribute is ignored cross-origin, so a file served
from somewhere else opens rather than saves, which is the browser's rule
and not something a player can work around.

attributes.name: overflow-controls
attributes.description:
Controls that go behind one button instead of onto the bar, named the same
way.

**Named rather than measured, and the reason is that a width cannot answer
this.** A media query asks about the window, and the bar's problem is its
own width: a video in a 320px sidebar on a desktop is cramped and a
full-bleed hero on a phone is not. A container query asks the right
question and still cannot answer it, because how many controls there are is
the consumer's, so the threshold is not a width but a width per control,
which is a guess. And a control that moves between the bar and a hidden
menu as the layout shifts is a control the reader has to find twice.

So the consumer says where the fold is, which they can, having already
named the controls in order. A name in both lists is drawn once, on the
bar: two of the same control is worse than either placement.

attributes.name: start-control
attributes.description:
The big mark over the picture before anything has played, or `none`.

**On unless it is turned off, because a stopped video has nothing else.**
Measured on the bar as it was: the play glyph is 16 by 16 in a 24 by 24
target, which is 0.12% of a 528 by 396 picture and 0.33% at 320. What a
reader meets first is a still frame with some chrome along the bottom, and
nothing in it says "press to watch".

`none` is for the cases where that is wrong rather than right: a muted loop
behind a hero, a grid of eight thumbnails, anything where the video is
decoration rather than something to start.

**Only before the first play.** A video paused halfway already has its bar
up, because a paused video never idles, so the small control is visible and
the reader has just used it. Covering the picture they stopped to look at
would be the opposite of helpful.

A value rather than a boolean, so the resting state is the attribute's
absence: a boolean defaulting to on would have to be spelled as its own
negation.

attributes.name: speeds
attributes.description: The speeds offered, slowest first, as multipliers of normal.

attributes.name: idle-delay
attributes.description:
How long the bar waits after the pointer stops before it goes, in ms.

It used to leave the moment the pointer did, which is not how a player
behaves: a reader moving across the picture to reach a control watched it
vanish under them. Zero turns the wait off and the bar goes immediately;
a large number keeps it up for as long as anyone is likely to look.

The wait is only ever about *idling*. A video that is paused keeps its bar
regardless, because a reader who stopped it is deciding what to do next.

attributes.name: play-label

are the consumer's markup in the light DOM, so they are styled by the
consumer's stylesheet the way any other content is, and this must not reach
into them: a rule here for a row would be a design system styling markup it
did not write.

members.name: place
members.description:
Puts the windowed rows into the light DOM, and takes the rest out.

Cleared and re-cloned rather than reconciled, which is the simple thing and
is measured rather than assumed to be enough: a window is twenty-odd rows
and cloning that many is well under a frame. A reconciler here would be
carrying keys and identity for a set nothing selects into, and is the kind
of optimisation to add against a measurement rather than ahead of one.

members.name: tier
members.description:
The prefix this tier registers its elements under.

**A component that renders another renders its own tier's version of it**,
so `helix-headless-pagination-size` composes `helix-headless-select` and
`helix-pagination-size` composes `helix-select`. One template says
`${this.tag('select')}` and each tier answers with its own name.

It was the public tag in both tiers, on the argument that each imports its
own element under that name. That works and costs three things: the name
means two different things depending on what a consumer imported, the
headless tier composes an element it does not ship, and the composition
cannot be tested there at all, because there is no `helix-select` on that
tier to test it against. Thirty-nine specs had to be moved back to
`helix/styled` for exactly that reason.

**A prefix rather than an override per composition**, which was the first
plan and does not compile. An override re-renders the fragment from the
subclass, and the fragment reads members the base keeps private:
`PaginationSize` alone would have had to widen `options`, `current` and
`handleChange` to `protected` so a subclass could say the same thing again.
Sixteen families of that is a lot of encapsulation spent on saying one
word differently.

members.name: tag
members.description:
One composed tag, as a static value a template can interpolate.

`unsafeStatic` is safe by construction: the name is a literal in our own
source and the prefix is one of two strings this class defines. Called per
render and not cached, which costs nothing, because `static-html` keys its
template cache on the joined string rather than on the object.

members.name: internals
members.description:
The element's semantics, set without touching the DOM.

`ElementInternals` sets the implicit role, which an author's own `role`
attribute still overrides, and it writes no attribute. Setting `role` on the
host directly would: that is an attribute the element gives itself after it
upgrades, which a React consumer's server markup never had, and hydration
reports it as a mismatch.

Available during server rendering. Lit's shim implements `attachInternals`,
so nothing here needs a guard.

members.name: toggleState
members.description:
Records a boolean fact about this element as a custom state.

**The host belongs to whoever rendered it, and a component's own
bookkeeping may not be kept there.** An attribute written on the first
update is markup a consumer's server never sent, so a React consumer
hydrates a DOM that has gained attributes since and reports a mismatch it
will not patch up. A custom state is not in the DOM at all: it carries the
fact to a stylesheet through `:state()` and leaves the markup alone, so the
server's output and the client's agree by construction.

`SETTLED` carries the long version of that argument and was the first to
move. `checked`, `open`, `invalid` and `has-label` followed it on 27 Aug
2026, after the same fault was reported once more from the landing page's
showcase: a `default-checked` switch, a `default-checked` checkbox and a
`default-open` accordion item, each writing its own resolved state onto
itself before React reached the node.

**The deferral that had been holding it is not a fix and could not be.**
The site imports the definitions from an effect so the upgrades fall the
other side of hydration, which works only while hydration is one pass:
anything that splits it, a streamed segment or a suspended boundary, puts
an upgrade back inside the window. Timing cannot be the guarantee when the
fact is kept somewhere React reconciles.

Feature-tested rather than assumed, the way `hostAria` tests element
references. An engine without `CustomStateSet` records nothing and keeps
whatever the resting rule draws, which is the safe direction to fail, and
Lit's server shim is one of them: a custom state is a fact about a running
element, and a server has nothing to say about it.

members.name: whenSettled
members.description:
Resolves a frame after the first update, when transitions are switched on.

**Named `whenSettled` because `settled` was taken four times over.** Image
and Splitter each have a private `settle`, and both color controls carry a
`settled` of their own, all of them older than this and none of them about
transitions. A base class takes the name every subclass then cannot use, so
it takes the one nobody wanted.

**The state it reports cannot be watched, which is why this exists.** A
`MutationObserver` could see `[data-settled]` arrive and there is no
equivalent for `ElementInternals.states`: a custom state is deliberately not
in the DOM, which is the whole reason it replaced the attribute. Anything
that used to wait on the attribute waits on this instead, and gets a better
signal for it, an awaited promise being what the callers wanted rather than
a mutation they had to interpret.

Separate from `updateComplete`, which resolves in the microtask checkpoint
the suppression is still active in. That is the distinction `readyToMove`
in `@fusion.dev/helix-testing` was written around and the reason two checkbox specs
were misread as a token fault for days.

It never resolves where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires, which is a
server, a hidden tab, and happy-dom. Callers that must not hang race it
against a timeout; `readyToMove` does exactly that.

members.name: resolveSettled
members.description: Resolves `whenSettled`, once, from the frame that records the state.

members.name: stopInner
members.description:
Stops an inner control's own announcement at this element's boundary.

**A composed control is one control to a consumer, and the natives had no
equivalent of the stop the prefixed events already get.** `<helix-select>`
renders a `<helix-listbox>`, and both announce: the listbox dispatches
`input` and `change` from its own host, `input` is composed by
specification, and a consumer listening on the select therefore heard one
choice twice. Measured before this existed, on the styled tier, one choice
on the inner listbox: select `input` twice and `change` three times,
combobox, date input, time input and color input twice each. `Command` was
the only one that was right, because it happened to reach for
`stopImmediatePropagation` for a different reason.

Bound on the child in the parent's template, so it runs while the event is
still at the child and before it can cross. The guard is for the case where
a component binds this on itself: an element must never stop its own
announcement, which is the one it exists to make.

This is the same job the `helix-before-*` handlers do with their own
`stopPropagation`, and it is separate rather than folded into them because
a consumer may legitimately refuse a request without the notification ever
happening: the two travel at different times and one can be absent.

members.name: relayNativeEvent
members.description:
Re-emits a native event from the host, under its own name.

A native event fired by an inner `<input>` or `<textarea>` is not composed,
so it stops at the shadow boundary and a consumer listening on
`<helix-input>` hears nothing. Re-dispatching it from the host is what
makes the component behave like the control it wraps.

The relayed event keeps the native name deliberately. `change` is `change`,
which is what a consumer already knows to listen for, and it is what
reaches React: its synthetic system claims `onChange` and wires it to that
name, so a prefixed one would never arrive.

`composed` is not forced. It defaults to the original event's own value, so
a relayed `change` stops at the next shadow boundary exactly as a native
one would. Pass it explicitly only where escaping is the intent, and say so
where you do.

members.name: finalizeStyles
members.description:
Prepends the shadow-root reset to every subclass's styles, so no component
has to remember to include it.
